ch9.name: Bernard Pivot Questionnaire
ch9.description: Interview your character using the ten questions from this questionnaire inspired by Marcel Proust

attributes.name: What is your least favorite word?
If you were reincarnated as some other plant or animal, what would it be?
What sound or noise do you hate?
Who would you like to see on a new banknote?
What sound or noise do you love?
What is your favorite curse word?
What profession other than your own would you not like to attempt?
If Heaven exists, what would you like to hear God say when you arrive at the Pearly Gates?

ch10.name: Big 5 Personality Traits
ch10.description: Identify how your character expresses these five major personality traits

attributes.name: Openness
attributes.description: The degree to which they are creative, curious, and eager to learn or experience life (e.g. high or low)

attributes.name: Conscientiousness
attributes.description: The degree to which they are thoughtful, organized, detail-oriented, or goal-directed (e.g. high or low)

attributes.name: Extraversion
attributes.description: The degree to which they are talkative, assertive, expressive, or thrive in social situations (e.g. high or low)

attributes.name: Agreeableness
attributes.description: The degree to which they are trustworthy, kind, altruistic, helpful, or empathetic (e.g. high or low)

attributes.name: Neuroticism
attributes.description: The degree to which they are sad, moody, anxious, irritable, or emotionally unstable (e.g. high or low)

ch11.name: Character Arc
ch11.description: Use this framework to evaluate how your character changes throughout the narrative

attributes.name: First Impression
attributes.description: What is the character they like as the story begins? How do they typically think, behave, and interact with the world?

attributes.name: Goal
attributes.description: What is the character's goal? What do they want to win, gain, obtain, or achieve?

attributes.name: Flaw
attributes.description: What undesirable qualities or weaknesses are holding the character back from achieving their goal?

attributes.name: Aha! Moment
attributes.description: When does the character recognize their flaw and how it negatively affects them? What is that moment like?

attributes.name: Action
attributes.description: How does the character react to their Aha! Moment? What actions do they take to avoid their flaw or transform it into a strength?

attributes.name: Transformation
attributes.description: What is the character like at the end of the story? How do they change after recognizing their flaw and taking action?

ch12.name: Clifton Strengths Profile
ch12.description: Identify how your character expresses these four personality domains to accomplish their goals

attributes.name: Executing
attributes.description: Which themes represent how they work to achieve their goals? (e.g. Achiever, Discipline, Focus)

attributes.name: Influencing
attributes.description: Which themes represent how they communicate and persuade others to achieve their goals? (e.g. Command, Maximizer, Woo)

attributes.name: Relationship Building
attributes.description: Which themes represent how they build relationships and contribute to a team culture? (e.g. Empathy, Includer, Positivity)

attributes.name: Strategic Thinking
attributes.description: Which themes represent how they think, make decisions, and empower those around them? (e.g. Futuristic, Input, Learner)

attributes.name: Interpretation
attributes.description: What does the character's overall strengths profile indicate about who they are and how they think and behave?

ch4.name: Cognitive Distortions
ch4.description: Ways that our mind sees things that aren't

ch21.name: Online Dating Profile
ch21.description: Interview your character using these profile prompts from real online dating sites

attributes.name: Headline
attributes.description: A short tagline that would intrigue a potential partner to learn more about you

attributes.name: About Me
attributes.description: A few paragraphs introducing yourself in a way that would make potential partners interested in communicating with you

attributes.name: Seeking
attributes.description: What type of partner are you seeking? What age range, gender, and other personal details are important to you?

attributes.name: Age
attributes.description: What age are you?

attributes.name: Sexual Preference
attributes.description: What is your sexual preference? (e.g. heterosexual, homosexual, bisexual)

attributes.name: Gender
attributes.description: What is your gender? (e.g. male, female, nonbinary, transgender)

attributes.name: Pronouns
attributes.description: What pronouns do you use? (e.g. he/him, she/her, they/them)

attributes.name: Location
attributes.description: Where do you currently live?

attributes.name: Relationship Status
attributes.description: What is your current relationship status? (e.g. single, divorced, in an open relationship)

attributes.name: Height
attributes.description: How tall are you?

attributes.name: Body Type / Weight
attributes.description: What is your body type or weight?

attributes.name: Languages
attributes.description: What languages do you speak?

attributes.name: Education
attributes.description: What level of education do you have? Where did you go to school?

attributes.name: Religion / Spirituality
attributes.description: What is your religious or spiritual background?

attributes.name: Ethnicity
attributes.description: What is your ethnic background?

attributes.name: Smoking / Drinking / Drugs
attributes.description: Do you smoke, drink, or use drugs? If so, what type and how often?

attributes.name: Kids
attributes.description: Do you have kids? If not, would you like to start a family?

attributes.name: Pets
attributes.description: Do you have any pets? If so, what type and how many?

attributes.name: Diet
attributes.description: Do you keep a particular diet or have any dietary restrictions?

attributes.name: Zodiac Sign
attributes.description: What is your astrological sign?

attributes.name: Where were you born?
attributes.description: What is your country or city of birth?

attributes.name: What's the first thing people notice about you?
What are you doing with your life? Do you have a job?
What’s the most important thing you’re looking for in a partner?
What are your short-term goals for yourself this year?
What’s one long-term goal you have for the next five years?
What personal qualities make you especially good at your job?
What have you worked hardest to achieve in your life?
What are you most passionate about?
What are you really good at?
What do you spend a lot of time thinking about?
What aspects of yourself are you most proud of?
What are the three things for which you are most thankful?
What are five things you could never do without?
What activities or moments make you happy to be alive?
How do you typically spend your leisure time?
What do you do on a typical Friday night?
How would you describe your ideal weekend?
What do you wish you did more often?
What are your most and least favorite books, movies, shows, music, and food?
What was the last live event you went to? How did you enjoy it?
What’s your favorite thing to cook?
How would you describe your relationship with your family?
What are your favorite things to do with your friends?
What characteristics do your friends have in common?
What are four words your friends would use to describe you?
What people or life experiences have shaped you the most? How?
How have you been feeling about life lately?
How do you feel about your physical appearance?
What's the most private thing you're willing to admit?

ch16.name: DISC Personality Profile
ch16.description: Identify how your character expresses the four personality profiles of this framework

attributes.name: DISC Style
attributes.description: There are four main DISC personality styles: D = Dominance; I = Influence; S = Steadiness; and C = Conscientiousness

attributes.name: Traits
attributes.description: What are their primary traits?

attributes.name: Goals
attributes.description: What are their primary goals?

attributes.name: Fears
attributes.description: What are their primary fears?

attributes.name: Influences Others with...
attributes.description: What traits do they use to influence others?

attributes.name: Overuses
attributes.description: What traits do they overuse to their detriment?

attributes.name: In Conflict
attributes.description: How do they respond when experiencing a conflict?

attributes.name: Could Improve Effectiveness by...
attributes.description: What could they do to become a better version of themselves?

attributes.name: Leadership Qualities
attributes.description: How do they demonstrate their leadership?

ch13.name: D&D Character Sheet
ch13.description: Develop your character based on the Dungeons & Dragons tabletop role-playing game

attributes.name: Class & Level
attributes.description: The character's calling and way of being (e.g. Cleric or Fighter), alongside their experience level (e.g. Level 1)

attributes.name: Background
attributes.description: A representation of how the character lived before the adventure began (e.g. Noble, Sage, Urchin)

attributes.name: Race
attributes.description: The character's species, which influences their appearance and traits (e.g. Human, Dwarf, Elf)

attributes.name: Alignment
attributes.description: A representation of the character's ethical and moral values (e.g. lawful good, neutral, chaotic evil)

attributes.name: Experience Points
attributes.description: A numerical indicator of the character's experience as an adventurer, which increases by completing challenges

attributes.name: Strength
attributes.description: On a scale of 1-30, a score representing skill in physical combat, carrying objects, and breaking physical barriers

attributes.name: Dexterity
attributes.description: On a scale of 1-30, a score representing skill in dodging attacks, avoiding traps, and hiding from enemies

attributes.name: Constitution
attributes.description: On a scale of 1-30, a score representing health, endurance, and general survival ability

attributes.name: Intelligence
attributes.description: On a scale of 1-30, a score representing knowledge, cleverness, and logical reasoning skills

attributes.name: Wisdom
attributes.description: On a scale of 1-30, a score representing awareness, intuition, and ability to spot hidden traps and foes

attributes.name: Charisma
attributes.description: On a scale of 1-30, a score representing skill in social situations, likability, and general persuasiveness

attributes.name: Inspiration
attributes.description: A reward for behaving heroically or true to character or in a noteworthy manner that grants a one-time advantage

attributes.name: Proficiency Bonus
attributes.description: A number used to modify the effectiveness of certain dice rolls, checks, and saves

attributes.name: Saving Throws
attributes.description: A score representing the character's ability to resist or prevent a threat

attributes.name: Skills
attributes.description: The ability score of each character skill (e.g. acrobatics, arcana, medicine, religion, survival)

attributes.name: Passive Insight
attributes.description: A score representing the character's ability to passively discern the motivations and deceptions of others

attributes.name: Passive Perception
attributes.description: A score representing the character's ability to passively scan the environment for hidden objects, threats, and other details

attributes.name: Tool Proficiencies & Custom Skills
attributes.description: Tools the character is adept at using and the ability scores associated with their custom skills

attributes.name: Other Proficiencies & Languages
attributes.description: Weapons and armor the character is adept at using, as well as languages they speak

attributes.name: Armor Class
attributes.description: A score representing how difficult the character is to successfully attack

attributes.name: Initiative
attributes.description: A score representing the character's reaction time, which is equal to their Dexterity modifier

attributes.name: Speed
attributes.description: A score representing the character's raw speed, which is influenced by their Race

attributes.name: Hit Point Maximum
attributes.description: A score representing the character's greatest possible health

attributes.name: Current Hit Points
attributes.description: A score representing the character's current health

attributes.name: Temporary Hit Points
attributes.description: A score representing the character's current temporary health bonus, if any

attributes.name: Total (Hit Dice)
attributes.description: A term representing the number of hit dice the character has available to roll (based on Level)

attributes.name: Hit Dice
attributes.description: A term representing the dice the character rolls to determine their hit points (based on Class)

attributes.name: Death Saves
attributes.description: The location where you track how many successes and failures the character has on death saving throws

attributes.name: Attacks & Spellcasting
attributes.description: A list of the character's favorite melee and ranged weapons (or spells) and describe their attacks

attributes.name: Equipment
attributes.description: The character's inventory of gems, jewelry, magic items, and other loot acquired during the adventure

attributes.name: Currency
attributes.description: The character's copper (cp), silver (sp), electrum (ep), gold (gp), platinum (pp) and other forms of money

attributes.name: Total Weight
attributes.description: The amount of weight the character is currently carrying

attributes.name: Carrying Capacity
attributes.description: The amount of weight the character can carry (equal to the Strength score multiplied by 15)

attributes.name: Personality Traits
attributes.description: Two personality traits that identify the character (choose from the Player's Handbook or create your own)

attributes.name: Ideals
attributes.description: At least 1 ideal, or fundamental belief, that drives the character (choose from the Player's Handbook or create your own)

attributes.name: Bonds
attributes.description: One bond that ties the character's background to the adventure and drives their behavior (e.g. family, traditions, heirlooms)

attributes.name: Flaws
attributes.description: One flaw that could stop the character from achieving their goals (e.g. vices, fears, weaknesses)

attributes.name: Features & Traits
attributes.description: The character's major features (gained via their Class) and traits (gained via their Race)

attributes.name: Age
attributes.description: How old is the character?

attributes.name: Size
attributes.description: What size is the character? (e.g. Tiny, Medium, Huge)

attributes.name: Height
attributes.description: How tall is the character?

attributes.name: Weight
attributes.description: How much does the character weigh?

attributes.name: Eyes
attributes.description: What is the character's eye color?

attributes.name: Skin
attributes.description: What is the character's skin color?

attributes.name: Hair
attributes.description: What is the character's hair color and style?

attributes.name: Character Appearance
attributes.description: Your character's appearance in detail, including images or sources of inspiration

attributes.name: Character Backstory
attributes.description: A summary of the character’s background prior to the adventure (e.g. origin, goals, conflicts, unique qualities)

attributes.name: Allies & Organizations
attributes.description: Friendly non-player characters (NPCs) and factions in which the character is a member (e.g. The Zhentarim)

attributes.name: Additional Features & Traits
attributes.description: The character's minor features (gained via their Class) and traits (gained via their Race)

attributes.name: Treasure
attributes.description: The character's inventory of loot and items of value which cannot be equipped, consumed, or modified (e.g. maps)

attributes.name: Spellcasting Class (Modifier)
attributes.description: The ability the character uses to cast spells, based on their Class (e.g. Charisma, Intelligence, Wisdom)

attributes.name: Spellcasting Ability
attributes.description: The number used to determine the effectiveness of a character's spells

attributes.name: Spell Save DC (Difficulty Class)
attributes.description: The number that targets must roll to resist the full impact of a spell (influenced by the Spellcasting Ability score)

attributes.name: Spell Attack Bonus
attributes.description: The number added to the d20 attack roll to determine if the spell hits the target (influenced by the Spellcasting Ability score)

attributes.name: Cantrips
attributes.description: The lesser spells the character can cast at will, which do not require spell slots (e.g. Mage Hand)

attributes.name: Spells - Level 1
attributes.description: 1st-level spells the character can cast

attributes.name: Spells - Level 2
attributes.description: 2nd-level spells the character can cast

attributes.name: Spells - Level 3
attributes.description: 3rd-level spells the character can cast

attributes.name: Spells - Level 4
attributes.description: 4th-level spells the character can cast

attributes.name: Spells - Level 5
attributes.description: 5th-level spells the character can cast

attributes.name: Spells - Level 6
attributes.description: 6th-level spells the character can cast

attributes.name: Spells - Level 7
attributes.description: 7th-level spells the character can cast

attributes.name: Spells - Level 8
attributes.description: 8th-level spells the character can cast

attributes.name: Spells - Level 9
attributes.description: 9th-level spells the character can cast

ch14.name: D&D Monster Sheet
ch14.description: Develop your monster based on the Dungeons & Dragons tabletop role-playing game

attributes.name: Type
attributes.description: The monster's Type, or species, influences their appearance and traits (e.g. Beast, Dragon, Giant)

attributes.name: Alignment
attributes.description: A representation of the monster's ethical and moral values (e.g. lawful good, neutral, chaotic evil)

attributes.name: Armor Class
attributes.description: A score representing how difficult the monster is to successfully attack

attributes.name: Hit Points
attributes.description: A score representing the's monster's current health

attributes.name: Speed
attributes.description: A score representing the monster's raw speed, which is influenced by their Type

attributes.name: Strength
attributes.description: On a scale of 1-30, a score representing skill in physical combat, carrying objects, and breaking physical barriers

attributes.name: Dexterity
attributes.description: On a scale of 1-30, a score representing skill in dodging attacks, avoiding traps, and hiding from enemies

attributes.name: Constitution
attributes.description: On a scale of 1-30, a score representing health, endurance, and general survival ability

attributes.name: Intelligence
attributes.description: On a scale of 1-30, a score representing knowledge, cleverness, and logical reasoning skills

attributes.name: Wisdom
attributes.description: On a scale of 1-30, a score representing awareness, intuition, and ability to spot hidden traps and foes

attributes.name: Charisma
attributes.description: On a scale of 1-30, a score representing skill in social situations, likability, and general persuasiveness

attributes.name: Saving Throws
attributes.description: A score representing the character's ability to resist or prevent a threat

attributes.name: Skills
attributes.description: The ability score of each character skill (e.g. acrobatics, arcana, medicine, religion, survival)

attributes.name: Damage Vulnerabilities
attributes.description: The damage types that cause double damage (e.g. acid, fire, poison)

attributes.name: Damage Resistances
attributes.description: The damage types that only cause the monster half damage (e.g. bludgeoning, force, lightning)

attributes.name: Damage Immunities
attributes.description: The damage types that cause the monster no damage (e.g. psychic, slashing, thunder)

attributes.name: Condition Immunities
attributes.description: The conditions that cause the monster no adverse effects (e.g. blinded, paralyzed, stunned)

attributes.name: Senses
attributes.description: The monster's Passive Wisdom (Perception) score, and any special senses they have (e.g. Truesight)

attributes.name: Languages
attributes.description: The languages the monster can speak or understand

attributes.name: Challenge
attributes.description: A score representing how difficult the monster is to defeat in combat and the experience points (XP) it awards

attributes.name: Actions
attributes.description: The actions the monster can take in combat

attributes.name: Reactions
attributes.description: The monster's special reactions in combat, if any

attributes.name: Legendary Actions
attributes.description: Special actions the monster can take outside its turn (applies to legendary creatures only)

attributes.name: Size
attributes.description: The monster's Size determines how much space it occupies in combat (e.g. Tiny, Medium, Huge)

attributes.name: Special Traits
attributes.description: Special characteristics and/or abilities that may influence the monster's skill in combat

attributes.name: Equipment
attributes.description: The monster's inventory of gear, gems, jewelry, magic items, and other objects of value (e.g. rope)

attributes.name: Race

attributes.description: The NPC's special reactions in combat, if any

attributes.name: Equipment
attributes.description: The NPC's inventory of gear, gems, jewelry, magic items, and other objects of value (e.g. rope)

attributes.name: Type
attributes.description: Type of personality based on the Enneagram test

ch24.name: Four Temperaments
ch24.description: Identify which classic temperaments best align with your character, using this personality theory developed by Hippocrates in ancient Greece

attributes.name: Sanguine
attributes.description: The degree to which they have an outgoing, cheerful, and optimistic personality. How is this represented?

attributes.name: Choleric
attributes.description: The degree to which they have a results-oriented, independent, decisive personality. How is this represented?

attributes.name: Melancholic
attributes.description: The degree to which they have a loyal, kind, and sensitive personality. How is this represented?

attributes.name: Phlegmatic
attributes.description: The degree to which they have a service-oriented, introverted, and passive/agreeable personality. How is this represented?

ch25.name: Freudian Personality Theory
ch25.description: Identify how your character expresses the three aspects of Sigmund Freud's classic psychoanalytic theory.

attributes.name: Id
attributes.description: The unconscious drivers of basic urges and desires, including sexuality and aggression, the Id seeks pleasure and avoids pain. How is this aspect of the character's psyche represented?

attributes.name: Ego
attributes.description: The practical mediator of personality, the Ego uses reason to negotiate the demands of the Id and Superego and avoid negative societal consequences. How is this aspect of the character's psyche represented?

attributes.name: Superego
attributes.description: The moral conscience of personality, the Superego aims to control the impulses of the Id; it is the internalized voice and values of society (or family) encouraging perfection and punishing failure. How is this aspect of the character's psyche represented?

ch1.name: Goal, Motivation, Conflict
ch1.description: Each character should have one internally and externally

attributes.name: External Goal
attributes.description: Describe the physical outcome the character wants or needs to achieve (e.g. play professional sports)

attributes.name: External Motivation
attributes.description: Describe the outside force driving the character toward their goal (e.g. fame and fortune)

attributes.name: External Conflict
attributes.description: Describe the obstacle preventing the character from achieving their goal (e.g. competition)

attributes.name: Internal Goal
attributes.description: Describe the emotional outcome the character wants or needs to achieve (e.g. finding love)

attributes.name: Internal Motivation
attributes.description: Describe the inner force or emotion that drives the character toward their goal (e.g. loneliness)

attributes.name: Internal Conflict
attributes.description: Describe what stands in the character's way of achieving their inner goal (e.g. fear of failure)

ch17.name: James Lipton Questionnaire
ch17.description: Interview your character using the ten questions from this questionnaire inspired by Marcel Proust

attributes.name: What turns you on creatively, spiritually, or emotionally?
What profession other than your own would you like to attempt?
What sound or noise do you love?
What is your favorite curse word?
What is your least favorite word?
If Heaven exists, what would you like to hear God say when you arrive at the Pearly Gates?
What sound or noise do you hate?
What profession would you not like to do?

ch8.name: Magic Blueprint
ch8.description: Based on the book Magic System Blueprint by C.R. Rowenson

attributes.name: Name
attributes.description: A term or label to reference the magic itself (e.g. Dark or Light Magic)

attributes.name: Type of Magic
attributes.description: Is the magic well understood or mysterious? Are its effects predictable or unpredictable?

attributes.name: Effects and Abilities
attributes.description: Describe the special effects and abilities the magic produces

attributes.name: Limitations and Boundaries
attributes.description: Describe any limitations, costs, consequences, or countermeasures that exist relating to the magic

attributes.name: Source
attributes.description: Describe where the magic comes from, how much is present, and whether it can run out

attributes.name: Transference
attributes.description: The degree to which the magic can be acquired, lost, or transferred to others (e.g. high or low)

attributes.name: Prevalence
attributes.description: The degree to which the magic is widespread and commonplace (e.g. high or low)

attributes.name: Naturalness
attributes.description: The degree to which the magic seems "natural" or "normal" for the setting (e.g. high or low)

attributes.name: Ease of Use
attributes.description: The degree to which the magic can be used safely and effectively (e.g. high or low)

attributes.name: Reliability
attributes.description: The degree to which the magic consistently produces the expected results (e.g. high or low)

attributes.name: Balance
attributes.description: Does the magic create power disparities in the world or between characters?

attributes.name: Perception
attributes.description: How is the magic viewed by others? Is it good or evil? Is it desirable?

attributes.name: Consistency
attributes.description: The degree to which the magic is consistent with the rest of the magic system (e.g. high or low)

ch18.name: Marcel Proust Questionnaire
ch18.description: Interview your character with these famous 35 questions thought to reveal a person's true nature

attributes.name: What is your idea of perfect happiness?
What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?
Which living person do you most admire?
What do you most dislike about your appearance?
How would you like to die?
What is your most marked characteristic?
What do you consider the most overrated virtue?
What or who is the greatest love of your life?
What is your most treasured possession?
Which words or phrases do you most overuse?
Which talent would you most like to have?
What is it that you most dislike?
What is your current state of mind?
What is the trait you most deplore in others?
Where would you most like to live?
If you could change one thing about yourself, what would it be?
What do you most value in your friends?
Which living person do you most despise?
When and where were you happiest?
What is the quality you most like in a man?
What do you regard as the lowest depth of misery?
On what occasion do you lie?
Who are your heroes in real life?
What do you consider your greatest achievement?
If you were to die and come back as a person or a thing, what would it be?
What is the quality you most like in a woman?
Which historical figure do you most identify with?

ch19.name: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
ch19.description: Identify how your character's needs are met using psychologist Abraham Maslow's personality framework

attributes.name: Physiological Needs
attributes.description: Level 1: How are the character's biological needs for survival  being met? (e.g. food, shelter, clothing, sex)

attributes.name: Safety Needs
attributes.description: Level 2: How is the character's need for safety and security being met? (e.g. financially, emotionally, socially)

attributes.name: Love and Belongingness Needs
attributes.description: Level 3: How is the character's need for belonging being met? (e.g. friendship, trust, acceptance, love)

attributes.name: Esteem Needs
attributes.description: Level 4: How is the character's need for self-esteem and respect from others being met? (e.g. status, prestige)

attributes.name: Self-Actualization Needs
attributes.description: Level 5: How is the character's need for self-fulfillment being met? (e.g. achieving their full potential)

ch6.name: Myers-Briggs Type Indicator
ch6.description: Type of personality based on the Myers-Briggs test

ch20.name: Numerology
ch20.description: Identify your character's five core numbers and what they suggest about their personality

attributes.name: Life Path Number
attributes.description: Add up the numbers in their date of birth (e.g. 1/1/2000 = 4) for insights into the path they are on in life

attributes.name: Destiny / Expression Number
attributes.description: Convert their full birth name into numbers using the Pythagorean chart for insights into their goals, abilities, and desires

attributes.name: Personality Number
attributes.description: Convert the consonants in their full birth name into numbers using the Pythagorean chart for insights into how others perceive them

attributes.name: Heart's Desire / Soul Urge Number
attributes.description: Convert the vowels in their full birth name into numbers using the Pythagorean chart for insights into their inner self

attributes.name: Birthday Number
attributes.description: Add up the numbers in their day of birth (e.g. 1/1/2000 = 1) for insight into their unique talents and purpose in life

attributes.name: Interpretation

ch26.name: Five Stages of Grief
ch26.description: Identify how your character experiences grief using this popular model introduced by psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross

attributes.name: Denial
attributes.description: How does your character express denial, the first stage of grief? Denial is a normal initial defense mechanism in the face of overwhelming grief (e.g. avoidance, confusion, numbness, shock).

attributes.name: Anger
attributes.description: How does your character express anger, the second stage of grief? Typically this anger stems from frustration that denial does not stop the grief. This stage may involve questioning who is to blame and why/how it could happen.

attributes.name: Bargaining
attributes.description: How does your character express bargaining, the third stage of grief? This is an attempt to find a compromise to escape the grief (e.g. "If you stop X, I will never do Y again.")

attributes.name: Depression
attributes.description: How does your character express depression, the fourth stage of grief? This stage is characterized often by sadness, overwhelm, silence, isolation, and moving away from loved ones.

attributes.name: Acceptance
attributes.description: How does your character express acceptance, the fifth stage of grief? Once the fog of depression has lifted, a state of calm settles in allowing them to accept their grief, make peace with it, and plan for the future.

ch27.name: Story Genius
ch27.description: Part of the Story Genius method, the Story Genius Character Template helps you identify your character’s misbeliefs and desires, and establish their backstory before you even start writing your first draft.

attributes.name: What is Your Character Like Before the Story Starts?
attributes.description: Who is this person on the inside? What do they believe? What do they want? What are they in life before the story starts?

attributes.name: What does your character already want?
attributes.description: Write a short paragraph about what your character enters the novel wanting. Be as specific as possible even if the character doesn’t think they have a chance of getting it, still list it.

attributes.name: Why does your character want it?
attributes.description: Why does your character want it (desire), and what will it mean for your character to get it? What does she think it will say about her?

attributes.name: What Is Your Character's Misbelief?
attributes.description: What is the misbelief your character has that is preventing them from getting what they want? What’s the fear fueling this misbelief? Given the misbelief, what is the very worst thing that could happen according to your character?

attributes.name: Where did that misbelief come from?
attributes.description: Write a paragraph or two about the moment your character’s misbelief took root. This is a defining moment that will constantly be at war with the character’s desire or what they want in the book.

attributes.name: How is their misbelief holding them back from getting their desire?
attributes.description: Determine how their misbelief is holding them back from getting their desire. Be specific.

ch23.name: Syd Field Character Qualities
ch23.description: Identify these four qualities acclaimed screenwriter Syd Field believes all great characters must have

attributes.name: Dramatic Need
attributes.description: What drives the character? What do they want to win, gain, obtain, or achieve?

attributes.name: Strong Point of View
attributes.description: What is the character's unique point of view? What do they believe that could generate conflict?

attributes.name: Attitude
attributes.description: What are the character's mannerisms, behaviors, and feelings? How do these reveal their attitude?

attributes.name: Change
attributes.description: How does the character change? Is their need, point of view, or attitude transformed by the story's end?

pl3.name: 12 Step Mystery Formula
pl3.description: An outline formula for writing a traditional mystery

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:

This is the opening scene of the mystery where you disclose an extraordinary crime. This section hooks the reader's attention and includes an unusual victim and/or perpetrator; the victim must be well developed, with enough details to ensure the reader cares about the solution of the crime. The Sleuth should also be introduced, with unique character traits that set them apart.
Open with a vivid, dramatic event that transports the reader to the time and place of the crime.
Offer clues that hint at both the physical and psychological aspects of the crime, which will carry the Sleuth to the end of Act 1.
Offer some clues that will point the Sleuth in the right direction, some distracting red-herring clues, and other elements that are not yet obvious as clues.

Introduce the Sleuth with enough information to make them unique and allow the reader to understand their world (e.g. small-town detective, FBI agent, coroner, or journalist), but do not reveal too much of their character, as this will unfold throughout the story.
Ideas to Consider:
Open the story with the Sleuth in a dire situation to allow the reader to see how the Sleuth works under pressure, with details unfolding gradually throughout the mystery.
Identify something unique about the crime which can act as a metaphor and/or be used again at the conclusion to create unity (e.g. the killer's signature, an object, a person, or setting).
Use a prologue to describe the crime in detail or have the information revealed by characters.
Note:
As this is a mystery template and the events of later chapters depend on occurrences in early chapters, it is strongly suggested to review the entire template before beginning your story.

This template's subplot has three distinct chapters which must be kept in mind throughout the entire novel. As you write each chapter, consider how the events impact the Sleuth and continue to push them towards personal transformation by the conclusion.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Disclose the Mystery should take approximately the first 10% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
End of Act 1:

Introduce a subplot, which will carry a theme while the main plot progresses the story. The subplot should represent a universal theme easily identified by the reader; the resolution of the subplot will demonstrate the transformation of the Sleuth, with either a personal or professional climax. Subplots allow the manipulation of the novel's pace by switching back and forth between main and subplots.
The subplot can originate either in a crisis in the Sleuth’s private life or a dilemma the Sleuth needs to face to resolve a matter of character, such as addiction, courage, or honesty.
Consider using this as an opportunity to introduce a love interest or a confrontation of the Sleuth's personal demons.
The subplot climax may occur before or in conjunction with the climax of the main plot.
In the chapters that follow, intermingle the impact of the main plot on the subplot and vice versa – do not lose sight of one over the other in future chapters.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
This section of the subplot should take the story to the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Middle of Act 1:

The Sleuth starts working toward solving the mystery. While considering suspects who appear to have the motive, means, and opportunity to commit the crime, however, the Sleuth encounters a twist about midway through this section that shows the crime is more complex than initially thought.
Introduce suspects who appear to have the motive, means, and opportunity to commit the crime.
Have the Sleuth question the most likely suspects, one of whom will end up being the perpetrator.
Create a twist that is attention-grabbing and makes it clear to the reader the investigation will not be straightforward.
Build suspense and tension by offering hints that allow the reader to see possibilities yet unknown to the Sleuth.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Set the Sleuth on the Path should be from approximately the 10% - 20% mark of the story.

cards.title: Set the Sleuth on the Path

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

During Act 2, the investigation is directed toward a conclusion that proves to be erroneous. In this section, further information about the suspects are revealed, but the investigation runs into obstacles. The stakes are raised, and it becomes clear that there will be terrible consequences if the mystery is not soon solved.
Use interrogations and new clues to offer more information about the suspects.
Have one or more suspects disappear or flee.
Develop a sense of urgency.
Consider how this section develops the subplot.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up the second 25% of the story.
Facts About Suspects should be from approximately the 25% - 35% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Middle of Act 2:
Use this section to introduce other characters, spread suspicion, and introduce new information which will point toward the solution. The relevance of the new information may not be apparent.
Place suspicion on other characters, new and old.
Gather new information and/or physical evidence to subtly point toward the solution (e.g. with interrogations or physical investigations).
Consider how this section develops the subplot.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up the second 25% of the story.
Broaden the Investigation should be from approximately the 35% - 45% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
End of Act 2:

Further develop the subplot by revealing more of the Sleuth's background. Make the Sleuth's personal stake in the outcome clear, and use this as an opportunity to further increase the tension and sense of urgency.
Identify what drives the Sleuth (e.g. Is there something missing from their life, or is there something from their past haunting them?)
Demonstrate what is personally at stake for the Sleuth (e.g. Is there a threat to their life or safety? Do they risk having disturbing personal matters revealed?)
Make the personal stakes hit on an emotional level.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up the second 25% of the story.
Sleuth's Background should be from approximately the 45% - 50% mark of the story.
-- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Beginning of Act 3:

The Midpoint of the story, Act 3 represents a pivotal point, which takes the story in a new direction as an unexpected occurrence makes it clear the Sleuth was on the wrong path. This section introduces new information and details which bring forth hidden motives and secrets.
Begin to clarify the importance of earlier clues by further developing and exposing the meanings behind matters hinted at  in Act 1.
Reveal hidden motives that increase the tension and add a twist to the story (e.g. secret relationships or kinships, hidden business agreements, romantic involvements, or past scores to be settled).
Consider how this section develops the subplot.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the third 25% of the story.
Reveal Hidden Motives should be from approximately the 50% - 60% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Middle of Act 3:

The reader (and other characters) are able to review what is known and consider the possibilities of the case, as the Sleuth reveals the results of their investigation. The crime appears to be impossible to solve, and the Sleuth has been stymied at every approach, largely being led in the wrong direction by misinterpreting clues or faulty conclusions. The Sleuth must use logic to find a new perspective to understand the uncertainties. The reader begins to doubt the Sleuth's ability to solve the mystery.
Logically and clearly lay out the evidence as it is currently understood.
Make it clear that the evidence does not add up and that a new approach must be taken.
What clues has the Sleuth misinterpreted?
What were the Sleuth's faulty conclusions?
Raise the stakes as all appears lost.
Consider how this section develops the subplot.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the third 25% of the story.
Reveal the Results should be from approximately the 60% -70% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
End of Act 3:

In this section, the Sleuth reviews the case in an attempt to find where they went wrong. In reviewing the crime's chain of events, the Sleuth identifies a seemingly inconsequential piece of evidence from Act 1, which has been overlooked until information revealed in Act 3 shows it to be crucial. This new understanding makes the Sleuth (and keen reader) aware of the error ahead of the other characters.
Give an overview of the case and chain of events. What was the critical piece of evidence overlooked in Act 1?
Why was the crucial evidence overlooked, and what new information offered in Act 3 illuminated its importance?
Allow the keen reader to piece together the error ahead of the other characters – this increases reader buy-in and connection to the story.
Consider how this section develops the subplot.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the third 25% of the story.
Review the Case should be from approximately the 70% - 80% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Beginning of Act 4:

Build toward the solution of the investigation. The Sleuth, and perhaps keen reader, weigh the evidence and come to a conclusion yet to be shared with the other characters. They must use their knowledge to find proof of concept.
Have the Sleuth consider the information gleaned from interrogations and conversations with other characters, as well as the evidence, to come to a plausible conclusion.
The Sleuth must use what knowledge they have to seek further evidence and proof to support their conclusion.
Consider how this section develops the subplot.
Breakdown:
Act 4 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Weigh the Evidence should be from approximately the 80% - 85% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Middle of Act 4:

In this section, the subplot is resolved. The Sleuth has been tested through the case and their private ordeal, leading to a personal transformation and preparing them for the final actions leading to the mystery's solution.
Resolve the subplot completely if it's a stand-alone story or leave some threads unresolved if part of a greater series.
Show the Sleuth being tested and overcoming an obstacle that prepares them for the conclusion of the case.
Breakdown:
Act 4 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Subplot Resolution should be from approximately the 85% - 90% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
End of Act 4:

A dramatic confrontation between the Sleuth and perpetrator brings us to the ultimate Climax, with the Sleuth prevailing. The clues are revealed, the deductive process has been shared, and the case is solved; the greater the odds and the more impossible the solution seemed, the greater the payoff and reward will be for readers. A pleasant ending for all involved, save the perpetrator.
Increase the tension right up to the Climax. Is there a chase scene? Does the perpetrator fight back once they realize they are caught?
Reveal the clues and deductive reasoning to portray a clear picture of the whole case.
Demonstrate that the case has been solved and justice has been served.
Ideas to Consider:
Reuse the unique object, item, or killer's signature from Chapter 1 to complete the circle back to the beginning of the case and create a tidy resolution.
If part of a series, add a hook or a teaser for the next book.
Breakdown:
Act 4 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Climax should be approximately the final 10% of the story.

The deepest level of intimate closeness that can be reached is when two people touch genitals to genitals. However, note that there are many ways to touch genitals without intercourse, which starts a whole other level of intimacy.
With permission from the lips (mouth), the mind (head), and the soul (heart), it paves the route to touch another person's intimate areas.

Laying your lips against the chest or breast of someone is a way to get close to their heart. It could be seen as more than just a physical gesture, but an intimate connection to the core of their feelings.

As soon as consent is given for a kiss or to hold someone's head, things can quickly escalate. Putting a hand on someone else's body is arriving at "second base." Note that it has taken nine steps to get this far on these levels of intimacy. We are getting closer and closer to the full extent of physical intimacy.

When we feel threatened or vulnerable, we protect our face. Allowing someone else to touch our face with their hands is a sign of a trusting relationship and closeness. For instance; You gently run your fingers through their locks. They tenderly cup your face in their hands. You softly brush the side of their face.

The first kiss of physically bonding is an extension of the emotional bond the lovers have taken time to establish. Notice focus their attention back on the face before proceeding lower; because consent and respect are essential in any relationship. This is why it's important to fall in love with somebody based on who they are, not just their body or physicality. But really it's because consent is sexy.

The lovers put their arms around each other’s waist. This move is beyond possession. It's now about connection. The intensity between them has grown stronger as they close in on the final act of intimate passion.

One partner wraps their arm around the other's shoulders. Think of when a guy yawns and stretches, putting his arm around his date in the movie theater - this is an affirmation of ownership. It serves to announce the status of the relationship.

The practice of joining hands together between two people falling in love is a lost art in reality. When it's on the page, it speaks volumes without the need for words. In romance, when lovers first touch palms, authors often describe electric sensations that can be felt between them, intensifying their bond even more when they finally clasp hands.

When the two lovers engage in dialogue, this initiates the emotional connection between them as they become more familiar with one another. This could be verbal, written or even telepathic in a paranormal romance setting.
Interest can be expressed in the first glance when two potential lovers' eyes meet. That single look can express a connection without any words being exchanged

The moment two people meet, they become aware of one another's presence. They check out the other person's physical characteristics to see if they fit their sexual preference; gender, height, color of hair, eyes, skin because some may like pale complexions, sun-kissed tans or a deep brown hue.

pl31.name: 24 Chapter Novel Outline
pl31.description: Based on the book The Plot Dot by Derek Murphy

children.text: Ordinary World Notes:
The First Act sets up the Protagonist in their ordinary, mundane environment.

In the first few chapters, introduce their friends and family members, their home, school or workplace. But you need to show what’s missing. You don’t want to start with a perfect, happy character who has everything (unless you’re going to take it all away, which is fine).

You need to give them space to grow. Maybe they have unresolved emotional issues. They’re probably shy, awkward, clumsy or embarrassed, or unpopular. Maybe they hate their job or just got dumped. You need to show what they want, their secret desires. What are they working towards? They probably have daydreams about things they don’t think will ever happen.
How is their environment a reflection of their inner flaw?
What is their favorite object?
Where are the sources of conflict?
Rebirth Notes:
The Protagonist returns, changed. They’ve won – though if this is a series, it’s probably temporary (this Antagonist was defeated, but they or someone new will return).

The Protagonist once again faces challenges or bullies from the beginning of the story, but they may seem trivial now. The Protagonist is no longer lacking; they’ve grown in confidence, have a group of new friends, and a new hope for the future.
The Antagonist has been defeated, but the Protagonist is forever changed.
What have they lost?
What have they gained?
What object(s) symbolize those things?

cards.title: B Story: Internal - Rebirth (Return to Ordinary World)

children.text: First Plot Point Notes:

Things have been getting weirder and/or more intriguing for several chapters. Your Protagonist tries to ignore the problems, but they keep interfering with their normal agenda. They get roped in, and something happens that forces them into the action. Everything changes, and there’s no going back to the Ordinary World.

They might have met a teacher, or seen something that changes their perspective: a revelation of supernatural abilities; a murder or death; an accident or robbery or attack or disaster. Something pretty big that shatters what they thought they understood of the world and makes them feel vulnerable and exposed. This will be one of the major scenes in your book, so make it unforgettable.
This is your Protagonist stepping off the cliff or going into the rabbit hole. It may not be a physical change of location.
What object symbolizes this transition?
How does the environment reflect the inner change?
What flash of color conveys the mood?
Act One has ended and is about 25% of your book—by now, all the major characters should have already been introduced, or at least hinted at.

This is a section break: something big changes, so be aware that this is a big turning point of your story. Take a breath. Figure out how it impacts your Protagonist. Then continue writing the next chapter.

cards.title: B Story: Internal – First Plot Point

children.text: Inciting Incident Notes:
In most books, the inciting incident should happen in the first few chapters. Start your book as near to the inciting incident as you can. But don’t think of it as just one scene or chapter.

It’s an intrusion on the Ordinary World. Something big changes. Maybe a stranger moves to town, or a family member dies, or there’s an earthquake. It might be an invitation or a friend inviting your Protagonist to a party. It can’t be a huge crisis, but it will be annoying and noticeable, or exciting — it’s the beginning of your plot.

The “Call to Adventure” is usually followed by denial or refusal. The Protagonist doesn’t trust it or doesn’t want to make a decision. They’ll ignore it and continue focusing on their previous goals. They just want things to go back to normal.
What object symbolizes the event and deepens character?
How does the setting reflect the mood of the conflict?
What’s remarkable and novel about the character and their setting?

This is a section break: something big changes, so be aware that this is a big turning point of your story. Take a breath. Figure out how it impacts your Protagonist. Then continue writing the next chapter.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3:
Optional: Hints of future challenges or antagonist lives.

This chapter may be used to fill in any remaining plot holes (perhaps by having the Protagonist in the hospital and visited by someone who fills in any information they may have missed). While optional, this chapter can be very powerful and can be a coming full circle or represent the rebirth of the Protagonist, as they have shifted from ambition to service. They always wanted their own thing, tried to get what they wanted, but ultimately sacrificed it to save others and defeat the Antagonist. This represents a very big shift and may even deserve an acknowledgement ceremony or public recognition of their service. This is also a great place to offer hints at future challenges if part of a series.
Show how the Protagonist is recovering and dealing with the emotional fallout of their journey.
Reaffirm the completion of the character arc for the Protagonist.
Show how the Protagonist now functions in the changed Ordinary World.
Wrap up any loose ends.
Acknowledge the Protagonist with a ceremony, being called up on stage, or other public celebration.
Hint at future problems or that all may not be well.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Optional: Rebirth occurs around the 99 to 100% mark.
End of Act 3:
Temporary victory. Innocents saved. How far they’ve come.

The Protagonist has won the battle, and it is now time for a joyful celebration or bittersweet reflection. If part of a series, they may not have defeated the Antagonist; they may have just driven them off or been in a battle with a powerful but lesser henchman. In a standalone book, they may have a symbolic object they have held from the beginning, which they now discard because it is no longer needed. Either way, they foiled the Antagonist's plans and are a changed person. There may be a deliberate letting go scene or perhaps an acknowledgement ceremony as they return to the now changed Ordinary World.
Decide the wrap-up of the battle – will there be a joyful celebration or bittersweet reflection?
Show how the Protagonist has changed and close all loose ends in their storylines, perhaps with a "letting go" scene.
Conclude the storylines and character arcs of the other Main Characters and Allies.
Tie up any loose ends (unless moving on to the optional next chapter).
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Bittersweet Return occurs around the 96 to 100% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Late in Act 3:
Secret weapon or ability, deep resolve, new understanding, unlikely ally. Remove glass shard. Sacrifice.

Here is where the Antagonist believes they have won. However, the Protagonist now has a new understanding of themselves and the unhealed wound that was holding them back, and they decide to let it go or move past it. Their want versus need comes to a head here: they realize they may never achieve their want, but they are going to sacrifice it and fight anyway. The Protagonist has a secret weapon, one unexpected thing that was overlooked for the duration of the story, that will get them out of trouble and bring them victory.
Demonstrate the Protagonist's new understanding and willingness to leave their wants behind to attain victory.
Allow the Antagonist time to continue gloating until the Protagonist pulls forth the secret item, ability, or hidden Ally to get them out of trouble.
Have the Protagonist take the final steps in their character arc as they finally transform into their new self.
Create the payoff for readers by presenting a satisfying ultimate victory over the Antagonist – all the struggles have led to this moment.
Do not be afraid to sacrifice more Allies and characters in this scene, perhaps even the Protagonist.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Unexpected Victory occurs around the 92% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Mid Act 3:
Triumph of Villain. All hope is lost. Confront fatal flaw.

This is the "All is Lost" moment for the Protagonist and the reader. The Protagonist thinks they understand their Fatal Flaw but really do not. They go into the battle confident, which leads to their undoing. The Protagonist may be at the mercy of the Antagonist, may be suffering through the Antagonist's gloating speech where plot holes are filled in and plans are laid bare, because it doesn't matter since they are about to be killed. This is a great place to wrap up some loose ends. It's where the Protagonist comes to a full understanding of their flaw and lets go of whatever was holding them back; it may even be the Antagonist who points the flaw out. The Protagonist has no hope of winning until they are able to face it.
Display the Protagonist's confidence as they enter the battle and then showcase how their fatal flaw defeats them.
Consider using this as a humiliation scene where the Protagonist is at the mercy of the Antagonist (e.g. tied up, at gunpoint, or other dire circumstance).
Show the Protagonist react to their defeat, including the mental trauma of being caught, losing Allies, and being shown their true flaws by the Antagonist.
Bring the Protagonist to their lowest point – show how they have lost all they wanted and dreamed of, and make the reader believe there is no way forward.
Show the Protagonist finally realizing their flaw and understanding what needs to be done to overcome it.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Ultimate Defeat occurs around the 88% mark.
Final Battle Notes:

The Final Battle scene often includes a “Protagonist at the mercy of the Antagonist” scene, where the Protagonist is caught, so the Antagonist can gloat (or this can come earlier, just before the Second Plot Point). All is lost, the Protagonist is captured, the Antagonist gloats, then the Protagonist perseveres… usually simply by not giving up. In a sudden twist, the Protagonist reaches into themselves and finds the motivation and tenacity to persevere, unlocking access to their secret weapon and defeating the Antagonist.

Often the Final Battle scene also includes a “death of the Protagonist” scene, where the Protagonist, or an Ally/Romantic Interest, sacrifices themselves and appears to die… but then is brought back to life in joy and celebration. (Or if you want to keep it dark, just have them die, so the victory will be bittersweet). This doesn’t have to be a literal “battle.” It’s just the last, final straw, the most dramatic part of your story. It’s what forces the Protagonist to make a realization, change or grow – and it’s the place where they have a victory.

This is a section break: something big changes, so be aware that this is a big turning point of your story. Take a breath. Figure out how it impacts your Protagonist. Then continue writing the next chapter.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Mid Act 3:
Deliberate choice to continue, even if slim chance of success.

While the Fatal Flaw realized in Chapter 20 may not be fully healed, it has at least been addressed, and the Protagonist now has the courage to Seize the Sword and make a deliberate choice to continue,  no matter how slim the odds of success. This is a good opportunity to reveal a piece of critical information that has been hidden to this point to give them an extra boost. As the Protagonist gears up for the Final Battle, they may need to complete tasks, like getting a special weapon or gathering troops or forces. Now it's time to confront the Antagonist.
What object or information does the Protagonist receive?
Bring the reader along for the decision to move forward despite slim chances.
Showcase the Protagonist and Allies gearing up for the final battle. What do they need to prepare? What do they need to attain? What is their plan?
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Seizing the Sword occurs around the 84% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Early in Act 3:
Encouragement from an Ally. Vulnerable share, inclusion. What’s at stake; choice.

The Protagonist no longer believes in themselves and needs someone else to pull them out of their depressive cycle. This often comes in the form of a pep talk, encouragement from an Ally, or a vulnerable share; for example, this could be a revelation about the Protagonist, their past or true identity, or their fatal flaw – a blind spot the Protagonist has that explains why things have been going wrong and people keep getting hurt around them. Typically the fatal flaw is not brought fully to light, but this is a good point to have the Protagonist attempt to face it. Having this pep talk rebuilds their confidence, reaffirms what is at stake, and presents the choice of how to move forward.
Who offers the words of encouragement to the Protagonist? Why do their words matter and have an impact?
What information is shared, and how does it confront the Protagonist's fatal flaw or lack?
What steps can the Protagonist take to face their flaw?
How can this new information inspire them and give them courage to fight back?
Reaffirm what is at stake and why the reader should care if the problem is resolved.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Pep Talk occurs around the 80% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 3:
Lead loses confidence; the forces are too great. What they want is unattainable.

Having lost the battle, the Protagonist loses their confidence and essentially gives up as they face the Dark Night of the Soul. They underestimated the Antagonist, their plan didn't work, and they lost their one shot at getting it right. They feel powerless as whatever hope they had is gone, leading them to self-doubt and feeling like a failure. Adding to their problems, they may also feel guilt and responsibility for the outcome.
What is the fallout from their failure?
How did they underestimate the Antagonist?
Display the Protagonist's mental state – are they angry, depressed, forlorn, or wracked with guilt?
Further increase the stakes and create the impression that victory is impossible.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Giving Up occurs around the 76% mark.
Second Plot Point Notes:
The plan failed.
The secret weapon backfired. The worst has happened. The Antagonist has won.

Alternatively, the Second Pinch Point can be elevated conflict, followed by the Protagonist's reaction – leading to a total, devastating loss. Usually, this process happens over several chapters. But at the Second Plot Point, everything the Protagonist feared could happen has happened. They are destroyed. They cannot win. They give up. There’s no hope.

They lose the battle, with serious consequences. Usually, the failure is due to the Protagonist's character flaw or a lack of knowledge. This marks a period of depression, prompting a change in mindset; the Protagonist has to give up what they want. They realize the thing they’ve been holding on to (often it’s just wanting to get back to the Ordinary World, back to normal) is completely gone. There is no chance for victory. The only way forward is through.

They are forced to go in a new direction. This is tied to the Protagonist's flaw/lack of knowledge. When they figure out what they’ve been holding onto, what’s been holding them back or limiting them, and when they’re prepared to sacrifice what they want for the greater good, they finally become the Hero they need to be to defeat the Villain.

The Protagonist knew this was coming and felt somewhat prepared, but they were wrong. Make this scene heart-wrenching by taking something permanent from them or one of their Allies (destroyed house, lost limb, a death, etc).
What object focuses the scene?
What object does your Protagonist cling to afterwards, as a reminder?

This is a section break: something big changes, so be aware that this is a big turning point of your story. Take a breath. Figure out how it impacts your Protagonist. Then continue writing the next chapter.

cards.title: B Story - Internal: Second Plot Point

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2B:
The Antagonist’s full plan/true identity is revealed. Stakes are raised. Guilt and anger.

The Protagonist learns new information in the new predicament they are facing, such as the true identity of the Antagonist or their full plan. The Protagonist may experience guilt and anger – anger at themselves for failing and/or anger at the Antagonist for outsmarting them or getting away. They may also feel personally responsible for letting everyone down. The stakes are raised as the worst has happened.
Who is the Antagonist, and what is their full plan?
What new information do the Protagonist and Allies learn? How did they learn it?
How does this information inform future plans and decisions?
What is the emotional state of the Protagonist, and how does this impact their wants and/or needs?
Use this chapter to build tension, raise the stakes, and plant seeds of doubt.
Breakdown:
Act 2B makes up 25% of the story from 50% - 75%.
Socking Revelation occurs around the 72% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Late in Act 2B:
The plan goes horribly wrong, faulty information or assumption. Consequences.

The Protagonist's plans go horribly wrong, and they fail at their mission. Being in direct contact with the Antagonist's forces means their identity is revealed, and real consequences may arise, such as the death of an Ally, permanent disfigurement, or the loss of an important object. The plan may fail for a variety of reasons. In the end, they have failed, they are in real danger, and their plan has been shattered, leaving them at square one.
Deepen the problems for the Protagonist and their Allies.
Do not be afraid to be aggressive in this scene – kill off characters, injure characters (including the Protagonist), or remove a key to their success.
Shake the Allies and the reader in the face of this failure.
Raise the stakes by having identities revealed, plans shattered, and the group at a loss for what to do next.
Breakdown:
Act 2B makes up 25% of the story from 50% - 75%.
Surprise Failure occurs around the 68% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Mid Act 2B:
They execute the plan and come in direct conflict with the Antagonist’s forces.

While the First Battle may have been a bit of an accident involving low-level henchmen, in which the Antagonist didn't know who the Protagonist was, the enemy forces no longer underestimates them and their Allies. The Second Battle will bring the Protagonist and Allies in direct contact with higher-level forces of the Antagonist – forces with more agency. This could be an infiltration scene, for example, in which the Protagonist tries to sneak into the Antagonist's lair or perhaps tries to steal something the Antagonist wants or needs.
How are the Protagonist and their Allies putting their plan into action?
What is the goal they are trying to achieve? (e.g. stealing an artifact or trying to evaluate the Antagonist's defenses.)
What level of forces do they meet? (e.g. is the team ambushed, do they stumble into a surprise attack, etc.)
Use this scene to increase tension and leave the Protagonist in a dire situation.
Breakdown:
Act 2B makes up 25% of the story from 50% - 75%.
Direct Conflict occurs around the 64% mark.

cards.title: A Story: External - Second Battle / Second Pinch Point

children.text: Second Battle Notes:

The Second Battle which is about to unfold in the next chapter may not be against the Antagonist; it could just be forces that represent the Antagonist’s interests. The battle could be a real battle or a conflict that is the result of the Protagonist taking action, such as setting a trap for the Antagonist that doesn't work.

The Protagonist is determined to see this Battle through and feels responsible for the outcome, although the chances of success are slim. This confrontation makes the Protagonist realize they’ve underestimated the Antagonist’s power.
The Antagonist defeats the Protagonist’s forces or foreshadows what’s at stake in the next major encounter.
What object symbolizes the danger and conflict?
Where’s the flash of color?
What is remarkable about the setting?

This is a section break: something big changes, so be aware that this is a big turning point of your story. Take a breath. Figure out how it impacts your Protagonist. Then continue writing the next chapter.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Mid Act 2B:
Trusted with an important task.

Once they have mapped out their strategy, the Protagonist will be given a crucial role. This is their chance to prove themselves and be tested in the real world as the other characters are beginning to trust the Protagonist. To really develop emotional angst and conflict, the Protagonist must be responsible for what happens.
Show how the team is beginning to trust the Protagonist more.
What is the crucial role the Protagonist takes on? Why were they given that task?
Decide if the Protagonist will take on personal responsibility or stay arm's length from the conflict.
Breakdown:
Act 2B makes up 25% of the story from 50% - 75%.
Crucial Role occurs around the 60% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Early in Act 2B:
Plan of action to thwart the Antagonist’s forces or overcome the main problem.

The Protagonist is all in, so they formulate a plan of attack. They are going to work around the problem presented in Chapter 11 and take action against the Antagonist. Perhaps they have to stop the Antagonist from doing something, maybe they don't quite understand the Antagonist's plans, or perhaps they don't truly know their identity.
Create a planning session where the Protagonist works with their Allies to use their information to form a plan.
What are the Antagonist's plans? What needs to be done to stop them?
Will the Protagonist and Allies face off against the Antagonist's forces, or will they try to solve a central problem?
Consider pre-planning for future chapters, keeping the Antagonist one step ahead for the time being. How will the Antagonist stop the Protagonist from foiling their plans?
Breakdown:
Act 2B makes up 25% of the story from 50% - 75%.
Plan of Attack occurs around the 56% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2B:
Self-realization or a discovery. Victim to Warrior.

This is where the Protagonist goes from Victim to Warrior, from reluctant to deliberate. Up to this point in the story, the Protagonist has been passive and reactive. Now armed with new information, backstory, and the actual risks, they make a conscious decision to move forward. This is also a good point for a big revelation or surprise twist; the Protagonist may discover the extent of the conspiracy against them, making them second guess if they want to continue or if they are the right person for the task. It may be a reevaluation of themselves, leading them to confront their weaknesses and define themselves and the person they want to be. Ultimately, they decide to move forward.
What is it that makes the Protagonist decide to continue on in the face of all they have learned?
Consider creating a plot twist or revelation that causes the Protagonist to second guess their decision.
Show the Protagonist displaying true self-reflection, recognizing weaknesses, and deciding who they want to be, but remember they are not yet ready or willing to confront their fatal flaw.
Breakdown:
Act 2B makes up 25% of the story from 50% - 75%.
Mirror Stage occurs around the 52% mark.
Midpoint Notes:

After the First Battle/First Pinch Point (see Chapter 9), the Protagonist faces new challenges, but remains in a defensive role. They might make some plans, but mostly are waiting for something to happen and reacting to events or circumstances beyond their control. If they try to solve an issue, they are thwarted or make things worse. They might accidentally hurt someone, or their friends and family begin to fear and distrust them (because they have secrets now). They question their identity and worldview, which leads to a personality crisis, which leads to a shift in perspective.

About halfway through the novel marks the point where the Protagonist decides to be proactive. They decide to stop being a victim and vow to do whatever it takes to win. They’ll probably form a new goal, and even if they aren’t sure how to achieve it, they’ll feel a deep conviction toward it. This might be based on rage or anger towards the Antagonist, a newfound perspective, or increased self-confidence.

This could even literally be the Protagonist looking at themselves in a mirror, wondering who they’ve become. So far, they’ve been refusing their quest. But now, with new determination, they decide to fight back.
What object symbolizes that shift?
Where’s the flash of color?
What’s remarkable about the setting?

This is a section break: something big changes, so be aware that this is a big turning point of your story. Take a breath. Figure out how it impacts your Protagonist. Then continue writing the next chapter.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2A:
New information, vulnerable share. In or out?

The Protagonist learns critical new information that changes their whole worldview. Now they know the full extent of the Antagonist's forces, the backstory of the problem, and what they are up against. They may also have a new perspective on the Allies, realizing they were not as good as originally thought, or perhaps they realize the Antagonist has a sympathetic point of view. With this new and complete information, the Protagonist must consciously decide whether or not they are "in" for the rest of the journey. If they are, they will be committed to going forward with their eyes open.
What is the new information, and how does it change the Protagonist's worldview?
What is the Antagonist's perspective? What are their reasons for doing what they are doing?
How has the Protagonist's perspective changed in regards to the Allies and Antagonist?
Create a difficult and intriguing choice on whether or not to move forward – use this as an opportunity to further hook the reader.
Breakdown:
Act 2A makes up 25% of the story from 25% - 50%.
Truth & Ultimatum occurs around the 48% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Late in Act 2A:
Surprise problem or situation. Demanding answers.

The Protagonist feels down and overwhelmed once more as they realize how much they don't know. This has been revealed by the challenges in the previous chapter, and the Protagonist realizes they have been left in the dark; their Allies knew the danger and true level of threat but did not tell the Protagonist. The Protagonist, feeling left out, misunderstood, or like they don't belong, confronts the Allies and demands answers. They may be brushed off initially and told they are not ready or need to further develop their powers, but they will insist.
Demonstrate how the Protagonist reacts to the discovery they have been left in the dark.
How do the Allies react to being confronted?
Create a tense scene that balances the Protagonist's shaken confidence in the Allies and themselves, with a newfound strength to defend themselves and stand up for what they deserve.
Breakdown:
Act 2A makes up 25% of the story from 25% - 50%.
Problems Revealed occurs around the 44% mark.

cards.title: A Story: External – First Battle / First Pinch Point

children.text: First Battle Notes:

After the First Plot Point (see Chapter 6), there are several chapters where the Protagonist is learning about the New World. There needs to be conflict and tension, which builds up to the First Pinch Point.

This doesn’t have to be a literal battle, but it is the first major interaction with the Antagonist or the forces of evil. The Antagonist might not be visible yet, but they should be the one wielding the strings. The Antagonist is after something, and that something is tied to the Protagonist. Maybe the Antagonist wants something the Protagonist has, or needs them to do something, or has a score to settle. The Protagonist probably still has no idea what’s happening, but they find themselves at the center of a conflict. They may not win, but they do survive. Now the stakes are clear.

You should make the stakes as dire as possible. Ask yourself, what’s the worst thing that could happen? Then ask, how can I make it even worse for my Protagonist? The stakes should always seem like life and death to the Protagonist… they represent a complete change, the “death” of the former self. If your Protagonist doesn’t have their self-identity shaken to its roots, you need to make this scene bigger.
What can you add to make the setting reflect the mood?
What can you add to make it epic?
What can you add to deepen character?
What’s remarkable about the setting?

This is a section break: something big changes, so be aware that this is a big turning point of your story. Take a breath. Figure out how it impacts your Protagonist. Then continue writing the next chapter.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Mid Act 2A:
Stakes are raised, antagonists revealed.

In the previous chapter, the Protagonist reached a status quo and feels a bit more confident. But now the forces of evil make themselves known and a new threat is realized. The Protagonist comes to truly understand what they have become involved in and its real dangers for the first time. This could be a face-to-face battle or a remote attack on a larger scale, but it creates a clearer picture of the Antagonist and their ultimate goal. The Protagonist is humbled by the event.
Show the Protagonist and their Allies having small successes as they work towards their goal.
Detail how the Antagonist forces are working toward the same goal, building tension.
Create a point of conflict where the two forces meet, perhaps in surprise.
Demonstrate the Protagonist's new understanding of the Antagonist and hint at the Antagonist's ultimate goal.
