Portray how the Protagonist is humbled by the attack and their realization of what is actually happening.
Breakdown:
Act 2A makes up 25% of the story from 25% - 50%.
Forces of Evil occurs around the 40% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Mid Act 2A:
Small victory as lead proves capable. Fun and games. Begrudging acceptance.

Even though the Protagonist may not have complete control over their abilities, they experience a small victory that proves to Allies and Enemies that they are not incapable or hopeless, and gain some begrudging respect. They prove that they do belong and are beginning to build confidence in themselves.
What is the small victory the Protagonist achieves?
How do their Allies react to it?
How does the Protagonist's self-confidence grow? What does it look like?
Breakdown:
Act 2A makes up 25% of the story from 25% - 50%.
Earning Respect occurs around the 36% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Early in Act 2A:
Struggle to belong. Frustration and doubt. Trials and challenges. The promise of the premise.

This is where the most interesting and exciting things the New World has to offer are presented. As the Protagonist explores the New World, they meet new characters and learn how to navigate it. It is often not all fun and games, as it may also present their main conflict with the Love Interest. There is often also some form of training and/or learning required to harness their powers or use the new information they have gained. As a result, the Protagonist may experience a lot of frustration and self-doubt and like they are not good enough to succeed.
What new abilities does the Protagonist have?
What do they need to do to grow or control those abilities?
Clearly demonstrate how the Protagonist feels and doubts themselves, allowing the reader to sympathize and connect with the struggles and feelings of not belonging.
Showcase what the world has to offer through the Protagonists' actions and training – use this as an opportunity to wow readers.
Breakdown:
Act 2A makes up 25% of the story from 25% - 50%.
Games & Trials occurs around the 32% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2A
Explore new world; meet characters, find their place and role. Introduce all main characters.

The Protagonist has passed the Point of No Return and is now in the New World. This can be a magical world or simply an unfamiliar locale or situation. Moving forward, the Protagonist's daily life will be different. There will be new surroundings and circumstances they must adapt to, proving themselves in their new role. By the end of this plot point, most (if not all) the main characters should be introduced, and the Antagonist should at least be hinted at. The enemies in this section do not need to be the Antagonist or their minions; they could be new team members or Allies who feel threatened by the Protagonist's presence. This is also a good time to introduce new Mentors or a Love Interest who may act as a guide.
What is the Protagonist's new role? How are they uncomfortable and fumbling in finding their way?
Who are the other characters in the story? Are they Allies, Enemies, Mentors, or something else?
Does the Protagonist face hazing or bullying? Do their new Allies meet them with fear and skepticism, or do they take the Protagonist under their wing and support them?
Introduce the Antagonist and set expectations for what is to come.
Who is the guide for the Protagonist to assist in traversing the New World?
Breakdown:
Act 2A makes up 25% of the story from 25% - 50%.
Enemies & Allies occurs around the 28% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1:
Trying to fix ordinary world problems while resisting the lure of the supernatural world.

The Protagonist is still trying to fix issues in the Ordinary World and resist the pull of the Call to Adventure, but now something happens to pull the rug out from under them and send them tumbling into the Point of No Return. They are torn out of their comfort zone and forced into action. This could be a theft, a kidnapping, killing of a pet, loss of financial security, and they must take the mission, or they could be placed in a life or death predicament. Whatever it is, they become personally motivated and have to get involved, even though they still do not want to.
Create a big event that the Protagonist cannot ignore, and make it personal.
Be sure to use this scene to hook the reader – they have to care about the outcome to continue reading.
Make sure the stakes and tensions are high.
Remember, the Protagonist is not bold at this point – this is still against their will and they feel out of sorts.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Pull Out Rug occurs around the 24% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Late Act 1:
The new interrupts the old and causes conflict. Reveals dissatisfaction with ordinary.

The Protagonist refuses to deal with or accept the reality of the Call to Adventure. Intrigue, tension, and mystery – perhaps supernatural events as well – are building, but the Protagonist is trying to put their head in the sand. They do not want to face the new challenge or the New World; they want things to return to how they were. Regret and doubt build as the Protagonist resists the Call to Adventure.
Continue to build events the Protagonist cannot ignore – how do the events conflict with the Ordinary World?
Show what makes the Protagonist unable to continue in the Ordinary World.
What is the Protagonist's emotional response to the new developing reality?
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Head in Sand occurs around the 20% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Mid Act 1:
Something extraordinarily different happens they can’t ignore. Major setback.

The Call to Adventure can be an invitation, a mission, or an event. Whatever form it takes, it cannot be ignored and sets the Protagonist on the path to the New World. This event must be something major that cannot be dismissed and cannot be resolved on its own. The door to the Protagonist's old problems is closed, and they have no choice but to focus on the new issues arising.
What is the Call to Adventure? For example, it could be the arrival of a mysterious stranger with paranormal abilities, a natural disaster, a kidnapping, etc.
How does the Call prevent the Protagonist from focusing on their previous goals?
With the character and their flaws in mind, how does the Protagonist react to the Call? How do they begin to push back against it?
What is the Protagonist's emotional state in light of the Call? Are they mad or perhaps depressed over having their original plans foiled?
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Call to Adventure occurs around the 16% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Mid Act 1:
Trying to regain control of the Ordinary World, but setbacks mount.

Things are really starting to fall apart. Whatever it is the Protagonist wants, they're not having success; while trying to regain control, their problems are worsening. The Protagonist is given a peek into a different world and begins to feel a pull toward something else, and they start to second guess their choices. This development may make them critical of the Ordinary World and their relationships within it. However, they cannot yet be fully honest with themselves and want to maintain control and stay in the Ordinary World.
Consider the Protagonist's flaw and create new events to distract them from their original goal.
How do these events offer a glimpse of the New World and what is to come?
How does the Protagonist's perspective of the Ordinary World change?
What does the Protagonist do to try to maintain control?
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Grasping at Straws occurs around the 12% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Early in Act 1:
Something unique or strange happens, but they dismiss it.

Something peculiar happens – something that's unusual for the Protagonist in the Ordinary World. It doesn't fit in the Protagonist's main worldview, so they'll probably dismiss it or ignore it. Readers might be clued in, but the Protagonist is too distracted or busy thinking about other things (such as trying to fulfill a want or deal with a problem) to really recognize the full consequences of what this peculiar event means.
Create an event that foreshadows future problems.
Decide upon and portray the distraction(s) for the Protagonist that keeps them from realizing the actual ramifications of the event.
To help build tension, consider allowing the reader to fully understand the implications of the peculiar event while the Protagonist remains oblivious.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Something Peculiar occurs around the 8% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:
Ordinary World, Empathy, Conflict. Flaw and Lack. Want, Problem, Need.

The first chapter introduces the Ordinary World. On this particular day the Protagonist wants something but immediately runs into a problem or a conflict which stops or prevents them from getting it. This allows readers to connect with the Protagonist and shows they are missing something they need to achieve their goal, though they may not be fully aware what that something is.
Introduce readers to the Protagonist and their Ordinary World
Establish a three-dimensional character with flaws, desires, problems, and a unique personality.
Show the Protagonist behaving as their normal self in the Ordinary World – demonstrate what they want, a problem they have, and hint at what they will need to achieve it.
What does the Protagonist need but is not self-aware enough to realize?
What is the Protagonist's character flaw? The shard of glass from years before, healed over, no longer recognized, but still causing harm.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Really Bad Day should comprise approximately 4% of the story.

pl28.name: Three Act Structure
pl28.description: The classic story structure for plotting novels and screenplays

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
End of Act 3: Resolution

The Protagonist is successful in their goal and can now return home with their reward – unless they have a few more minor obstacles to overcome before success is complete. This section ties up loose ends, completes the Protagonist's character arc and transformation, and the arcs of any other major characters. As the changed Protagonist revisits their Ordinary World, the tension releases, and the central theme is emphasized one final time.
Has the Protagonist completed their goal, or is there more work to do? If so, what are the final obstacles?
Clearly demonstrate the conclusion of the central conflict or question of the narrative.
Demonstrate how the Protagonist has grown and is now in an opposite state of being from the start of the story.
Wrap up any loose ends and complete the character arcs for the Protagonist and other major characters, resolving any subplots at the same time.
Show the changed Protagonist back in their Ordinary World and what life looks like for them now.
If the story is part of a larger series, leave some room for growth and set the hook for the next story.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Denouement occurs around the 95% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Middle of Act 3: Resolution

Having suffered a significant setback, the Protagonist must use all they have learned and gained from the experience of their Darkest Hour to gather themselves and prepare for the final confrontation. This is the moment of payoff the reader has anticipated from the start of the narrative, so it must be gripping and rewarding. The Protagonist emerges changed but victorious, and the Antagonist is vanquished, killed, or driven off to return another day. Generally, the central conflict or question has been resolved by the end of this beat.
Demonstrate how the Protagonist has rebuilt themselves from their Darkest Hour and how they have grown to use all they have learned along the way to be victorious.
Consider how the Protagonist will overcome the Antagonist's newly showcased strengths.
Create a compelling and gripping final conflict that offers a strong payoff for the reader.
What is the fate of the Antagonist - are they killed, destroyed, vanquished, or merely driven off?
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Climax occurs around the 90% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Beginning of Act 3: Resolution

Through trials and obstacles, the Protagonist has finally made their way (with gusto) to confront the Antagonist. However, the Antagonist's true strength has been hidden until now. Caught off guard, the Protagonist fails in the confrontation and faces an All is Lost moment. This is sometimes referred to as the Dark Night of the Soul or The Hero's Darkest Hour. As a result, the Protagonist's chance for success should now seem in doubt both to readers and to the character.
Hint at how the Protagonist and (especially the) Antagonist have grown and become more powerful.
Create a surprising show of strength for the Antagonist and connect it to the Protagonist's inner conflict or flawed thinking.
Have the Antagonist's victory be not just physically, but mentally destructive for the Protagonist as well.
Structure this section in such a way that there appears no hope of victory.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Pre-Climax occurs around the 80% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
End of Act 2: Confrontation

The Protagonist has been thrown off balance and is now unsure of how they will reach their goal. The Midpoint punctured their belief that they were getting close, and now they must formulate a new plan of attack. After reflection – and possibly a kick in the side by a Mentor or Ally – they become proactive rather than reactive, restore or even raise their confidence, and strike off to face the Antagonist and defeat them once and for all.
Give the Protagonist time to consider the story's conflict and how they will move forward.

Consider having the Protagonist and Allies achieve a series of successes, even if they are small, to build their confidence, equip them with the proper toolkit, outlook, or information, and prepare them for the final confrontation.
Consider how the Protagonist reacts to these events and the impact on their overall character arc.
Don't forget to develop the character arcs of the other main characters – and Antagonist(s).
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Plot Point 2 occurs around the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Middle of Act 2: Confrontation

The Midpoint of the story re-establishes the Protagonist's main goal and the central question of the story. While the Protagonist feels as though they are closer to their goal, this is the point where success is threatened, and the stakes for failure are raised. This beat changes the Protagonist's perspective moving forward, reinforcing their need or want to continue their journey despite the challenges they must face.

Consider having the Protagonist reach their goal only to have success stripped away (e.g. they reach the address where the kidnapper is holding the hostages only to find they have left or were never there).
Raise the stakes in a way that changes the Protagonist's perspective (e.g. they visit an informant to find them murdered and the critical information missing).
Restate and remind the reader of the central question or problem of the story.

Remember, while this section creates a setback for the Protagonist, it does not completely destroy their faith in themselves and their abilities (that comes later), but rather refocuses them on their overall goal and re-establishes and raises the stakes.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Midpoint occurs around the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Beginning of Act 2: Confrontation

The Protagonist has entered into the New World and now faces challenges and roadblocks. New characters and enemies are introduced as the Protagonist successfully navigates (or fails to navigate) the challenges before them, leading toward a final confrontation with the primary Antagonist. With each challenge, the Protagonist grows, learns, and perhaps recoils as they undergo character transformation. Make sure this character change is not a straight path; the Protagonist learns and grows, slides back to old ways, and perseveres again.
Introduce difficult challenges and enemies to show how dangerous the New World is.

Remember the Protagonist is not yet fully comfortable with any new abilities or knowledge they have gained, or the role set before them, and they will not always be successful when they face challenges.
Introduce Allies and friends who can help the Protagonist move toward their goal – and test them severely. Which Allies will survive this section?
During each challenge and with each obstacle the Protagonist faces, keep in mind how the events propel the Protagonist and main characters forward or backward in their character arcs.
If there is a subplot, each conflict builds it, while the subplot supports the overall narrative.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Rising Action occurs around the 30% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
End of Act 1: The Setup

Plot Point 1 presents the moment or event that influences the Protagonist to take up the call to action and "cross the threshold" into the story – this could be a symbolic threshold or a physical one like going through a door and leaving home. By the end of Act I, the Protagonist leaves their Ordinary World to enter into the special New World.
Ask yourself if a Mentor gives the Protagonist the tools, training, or motivation needed to accept the challenge before them.
Create a gripping event that pulls the Protagonist into the story (e.g. they visit their Mentor only to find them murdered and the villains escaping).
Re-establish the central theme or question of the story.
Have the Protagonist take up the challenge – willingly or begrudgingly – and break into the special New World.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Plot Point 1 occurs around the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Middle of Act 1: The Setup

The Inciting Incident is the event that drives the character out of their comfort zone and into the story. The Protagonist may initially be unwilling to take up the call to adventure presented by the Inciting Incident, but they ultimately have no choice. This event disrupts their life in such a way that it cannot be overcome on its own and requires direct intervention, leading them into the main storyline and setting up their external goal. The Inciting Incident must be intriguing to hook the reader and keep them interested in the story's resolution.
Introduce a dramatic event that disrupts the Protagonist's life/world (e.g. a natural disaster, a developing romance, an assault on their town, a kidnapping/murder, being sent on a quest).
Clearly present how this event impacts the Protagonist and why they must step into action and solve the problem (e.g. their child is kidnapped and they have a very particular set of skills).
Consider how this event collides with the Protagonist's flawed thinking or inner conflict.
Remember, the event must be compelling to hook the reader into the story.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Inciting Incident occurs around the 15% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Beginning of Act 1: The Setup

The Exposition sets the scene of the story. It introduces the Protagonist in their Ordinary World, gives an example of their everyday life, offers a sense of what is important to them, and hints at something in their world that challenges or displeases them. It should also offer the reader a glimpse at the Protagonist's internal conflict, setting it up to collide with their external goals later in the story. The Protagonist is in a different state of being here than they will be at the end.
Introduce the Protagonist and what their life is like in their Ordinary World.
Develop a three-dimensional character with flaws, desires, problems, and a unique personality.
Present the Protagonist's flawed thinking or internal conflict (this may be connected to something about the Ordinary World that upsets them).
Set the scene and atmosphere in an interesting way – the reader must care about what is happening!
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Exposition should take approximately 10% of the story.

pl1.name: Seven Point Plot Structure
pl1.description: A plot structure popularized by Dan Wells

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:

The Hook is the opening scene and your opportunity to engage the reader and draw them into your story. It is the beginning of the Protagonist's character arc and must show them in an opposite state from where they are at the end of the story.
Establish the setting, introduce the Protagonist, and showcase what their life is like under normal circumstances.
Develop a three-dimensional Protagonist with flaws, desires, problems, and a unique personality.
The Protagonist is in the opposite state from the ending of the story (i.e. fearful vs brave, brash vs respectful, uncertain vs confident.)
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Hook should take approximately 12% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1:

The inciting incident and point of no return. In this section, the status quo is shaken up by something drastic, which forces the Protagonist out of their comfortable life and into the adventure. The world has changed in such a way the Protagonist is compelled to willingly - or reluctantly - take up the challenge.
The status quo is shaken up (e.g. a loss, an attack or natural disaster, a threat to their way of life, or acquisition of new knowledge.)

The Protagonist may initially refuse to engage, but Plot Turn 1 cannot be corrected by itself. The Protagonist is forced into action, past the point of no return, and must start the movement towards the eventual climax and resolution.
Ensure the Protagonist's reactions are in line with their character development.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Plot Turn 1 should take your story to the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

The Protagonist sets off on an adventure, leaving the comfort of their ordinary world behind, but they are not yet comfortable in their new role. While trying to adapt, the Protagonist is put under pressure and must face challenges and an obstacle, such as the Antagonist or other villains. The process of dealing with the obstacle solidifies the Protagonist's dedication to the quest and stopping the Antagonist. This Pinch Point continues to push the Protagonist forward, leading to the resolution and their transformation.
Show the Protagonist being uncomfortable in their new role, and how that leads to missteps and difficulty in facing their challenges, while creating tension and personal growth.
Introduce obstacles such as an Antagonist and other enemies.
Show the Protagonist either overcome the obstacle(s) or simply survive with lessons learned.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The Protagonist's reaction to previous events lasts from around the 25% to 37% mark.
Pinch Point 1 occurs around the 40% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

A major event occurs, which changes the Protagonist and their perspective for the remainder of the story. The event must be dramatic enough to drive the Protagonist to switch from reaction to action and reinforce their need to stop the Antagonist. The tension and intensity begin to ramp up.
Introduce a major dramatic event (e.g. an attack, new knowledge, a change of direction, or a realization of the true stakes.)
Show how the event alters the Protagonist's perception moving forward (e.g. learning the Antagonist plans to poison a water supply, threatening the Protagonist's loved ones.)
Raise the stakes, forcing the Protagonist to decide they must stop the Antagonist.
The dramatic event should capture the reader's attention and carry them to the climax.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The Midpoint occurs around the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2:

The Protagonist faces another major obstacle, bigger than the first, and everything seems to fall apart; it appears as though the Protagonist will be defeated and lose everything. They either find the confidence to move on and face the Antagonist or need allies to support them. At the end of this section, the Protagonist gains a new perspective which emboldens them to defeat the Antagonist.
Show the Protagonist moving forward with confidence and speed from the Midpoint, only to have it fall apart in the face of this obstacle.
Allies may become trapped, mentors may be killed, powers may fail, a critical item is lost or broken, or the Antagonist reveals themselves to be more powerful than anticipated.
The Protagonist fights and struggles but ultimately suffers a major defeat.
Decide if the Protagonist finds their own strength to continue or needs to revisit a Mentor or allies.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Pinch Point 2 occurs around the 60% - 65% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 3:

The second Plot Turn leads to the climax and must offer readers high stakes and high rewards for a satisfying payoff. Everything ties together, and the Protagonist receives or realizes they have all they need to defeat the Antagonist and emerge victorious. The Protagonist and Antagonist meet face to face for the final - dramatic - confrontation. The entire story has been leading to this point. It is important to have the Protagonist in a position of strength, now confident in their abilities.
Determine what is the new piece of information or ability granted to the Protagonist that helps rebuild their confidence (i.e. discovering the new potential of an idea or object they have.)
Show the Protagonist newly emboldened for the event/battle before them and make clear why they have regained their confidence and how they can use what they have learned to succeed.
Lead the Protagonist to the final confrontation with the Antagonist, and make it explosive or dramatic, bringing the story to its climax.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Plot Turn 2 occurs around the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3:

The Antagonist is defeated (or not) after the final confrontation. This concludes the character arc of the Protagonist; they have been transformed by what they have learned and experienced. If the book is a part of a series, leave some storylines unfinished and leave room for further growth for the Protagonist.
Show the Protagonist transformed and in an opposite state from the opening scene.
Show the Protagonist's return to a sense of normal (or as close to normal as the story allows).
Consider showing the Protagonist's return to the normal world and how they are received and celebrated.
If Part of a Series:

Consider having the Antagonist not be defeated, just driven off to rebuild... OR the sense of normalcy be off-balance (i.e. the first challenge has been defeated, but it leads to potentially greater danger).
If the Antagonist has been defeated, begin to set the hook for the new Antagonist.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The climax occurs around the 85% - 90% mark
The Resolution occurs around the 98% mark.

pl2.name: Eight Sequences Method
pl2.description: An outline formula for a feature script

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:

The opening section of a film introduces the Protagonist and show them living and interacting in their Ordinary World; typically there is something about the Ordinary World that displeases the Protagonist. This section is the hook that draws in the audience and allows them to connect to the Protagonist and the story, and it often ends with an Inciting Incident that drives the Protagonist into the story.
Begin this sequence by introducing the Protagonist, other characters, and their Ordinary World.
Show how they interact with their normal world and possibly include something which displeases them about it.

Develop a three-dimensional Protagonist with desires, problems, flaws, and a unique personality – developmentally, they will be in an opposite position from what they transform into by the end of the narrative.
End this sequence with the Inciting Incident – this will be a significant event that cannot be resolved on its own.
Consider having the Inciting Incident occur in the first few minutes of the film for a bit of twist.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Status Quo brings the story to about the 12% mark.
The Inciting Incident occurs around the 12% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1:

Sequence 2 introduces the Central Conflict and the incident which compels the Protagonist to take up the challenge. When first presented with the call to action, the Protagonist may attempt to solve the Central Conflict on their own (with dire consequences), or outright refuse the call until mounting pressure forces the decision. The Lock In is the moment of no return. The Protagonist's actions show they have accepted the challenge and make it impossible for them to walk away as they take their first steps into the adventure.
Show the Protagonist struggling whether to resolve the Predicament or not (they always do, though the level of coercing required can differ).
Consider having the Protagonist attempt to resolve the Predicament but fail, creating an even worse situation.
What is the Protagonist's moment of Lock In, or point of no return, in your story? For example, it can be embarking on a voyage, chasing down the villain, or tackling the first challenge.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Predicament occurs around the 17% mark.
The Lock-in occurs around the 20% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

The Protagonist's first steps into their New World are met with a series of challenges that test them while raising the stakes and tension. The Protagonist struggles in the face of their First Obstacle, but having crossed the point of no return, they cannot turn back and ultimately suffer a defeat.
Show the Protagonist entering the new world and quickly being tested – introduce enemies and challenges to showcase the new world's dangers.
Let the Protagonist falter and fail to succeed in facing their First Obstacle.
Introduce Allies to support the Protagonist during this section as the stakes rise, but remember that loyalties waver, and not all true motivations of the Allies may be apparent.
Use any remaining exposition to raise the stakes for the central conflict and subplots, showing that there is more to lose.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The First Obstacle occurs around the 25% mark.
Raising the Stakes occurs around the 40% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

The Protagonist's defeat from the First Obstacle leads to a greater obstacle that adds to the rising action and leads to the First Culmination. The Protagonist may continue to try to solve the Central Conflict and restore the Ordinary World. This Sequence ends with the Protagonist obtaining a major revelation, knowledge, or item which alters their perspective as the story comes to its midpoint/crisis. The Midpoint mirrors the resolution. If, in the end, the Protagonist is defeated, this section should end in a defeat or low point; if they succeed at the end, the Sequence should end with a small victory.
This section is the Protagonist's first major encounter with the Central Conflict or Predicament from the beginning.
The method used by the Protagonist to survive the First Obstacle fails them in the face of this greater Obstacle.

The Protagonist attempts to solve the Central Conflict and learns valuable information or gains an object which changes their perspective – they go from passive to active, with a renewed sense of vigor.

This is a moment of crisis for the Protagonist – they may suffer a significant loss, even though victorious, or they may suffer a defeat from which they must be resurrected, either figuratively or literally.
Consider the loss of an Ally or Mentor or essential item, raising the stakes, and increasing the tension.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The First Culmination occurs around the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

Avoid a second act sag by building a strong subplot to continue the rising action. Use this Sequence to explore conflicts in the subplot and perhaps introduce new characters; often the troubles keep piling up for the Protagonist to increase tension and help set up the next Sequence. This is also a good point to increase the stakes to maintain the audience's interest.
Show events continuing to worsen for the Protagonist after facing the Central Conflict for the first time and suffering a crisis.
Use this section to continue to strip the Protagonist (e.g. perhaps they lose their love interest or the support of an essential Ally).
Let the deepening tension of the subplot contribute to the Protagonist's transformation and lead to further clarity and strength that aids in the final confrontation.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The Subplot & Rising Action occurs around the 60% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2:

Return to the Main Plot with force. This Sequence contains the largest Obstacle, the final option, and the lowest point for the Protagonist. The stakes, tension, and drama are at their highest as the Protagonist is put through the absolute worst circumstances; despite all the efforts of the Protagonist, victory seems completely out of reach. The tension set up in this section will carry the story to its conclusion.

Raise the tension and stakes so that the Protagonist's objective seems beyond reach (e.g. the Villain has returned with the full force of their armies, they are close to completing their nefarious plan, or perhaps they obtained an object which gives them incredible strength).
Show how the full complement of the Protagonist's toolkit and abilities seems to fall short in the face of the increased threat, as all hope appears lost.
The audience should doubt that ultimate victory can be achieved.

Since most midpoints and endings are paralleled, the plot point at the end of Act 2 is usually at a polar opposite of those points; if our hero wins at the midpoint and at the end of the film, they are usually at their lowest point here.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The Main Culmination occurs around the 70% mark.

cards.title: Main Culmination / End of Act II

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 3:

This sequence contains fast-paced action with short rapid scenes and minimal set-ups, as the solutions to the Central Conflict found at the end of the last Sequence falter. The stakes are raised as the Protagonist faces a new Twist that sends them and the story in a new direction. The Twist comes at the end of this Sequence and presents a new goal for the Protagonist, with the audience being quickly brought up-to-speed, with minimal exposition.

The Protagonist has faced their lowest moment in Act 2 and is determined to defeat the Villain, but they are pursued by danger and face several small obstacles on their way to the final confrontation.
Show that the Villain is at their strongest, as is the Protagonist, who is ready to use all they have learned and experienced to get themselves to and past the final conflict.

Introduce a Twist at this point in the story which adds to the tension or shifts the Protagonist's goal – they may realize the goal they have achieved is not what makes them happy or ends in success (e.g. they may have foiled the Villain's plan, only to realize it was a small part of a much larger plot with more dire consequences).
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
New Tension occurs around the 75% mark.
The Twist occurs around the 85% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3:

The Resolution comes as the Protagonist faces the final battle, and the stakes are crystal clear. If they lose, the world faces disaster; if they win, they can return to the Ordinary World transformed and ready to be celebrated. The Resolution must tie up all loose ends, conclude the character arcs for all main characters, and set the hook for the next story in the series (if there is one). The Resolution also mirrors the Midpoint: a previous small victory ends in a great victory, and a previous small defeat ends in devastation.
Dramatize the final battle and demonstrate how the Protagonist has used all they have learned throughout the journey to be successful.
Vanquish the Villain or have the Protagonist succeed in their ultimate quest.
Wrap the character arc of the Protagonist and major characters – be sure to demonstrate how they have transformed from the beginning.
Show how the Protagonist and their Ordinary World has been altered by their success (or failure).
Remember to mirror the tone of the Midpoint.
If part of a greater series, be sure to leave room for further character development of the Protagonist and set the hooks for the next installment.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Resolution occurs around the 90% mark.

pl5.name: Seven Romantic Comedy Beats
pl5.description: An outline formula for romantic comedy based on ideas by Billy Mernit

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3:

Both the Protagonist and Love Interest are forced to decide if they will stick to their external goals and succumb to their false beliefs... or work through their inner conflicts and sacrifice for love. By section's end, they work to fix their internal and external conflicts, leading to a reconciliation that reaffirms the primal importance of the relationship. The central question of will they end up together is answered, usually with a happy ending that implies marriage or a serious commitment, often at the cost of some personal sacrifice to the Protagonist. Hence the term Joyful Defeat. Both must admit defeat and embrace change to save the relationship.

What brought the Protagonist and Love Interest back from the brink? Perhaps they realized it was a misunderstanding, there was an ex manipulating the situation, or they came to realize the relationship was more important than any external goal.
One or both of the characters apologize to each other, and they make amends – be sure to keep this scene in line with their characters and arcs.
Resolve the internal and external conflicts while showing how the Protagonist and Love Interest have transformed so that the relationship may work.
Give the reader and the characters a moment of happily ever after.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Joyful Defeat occurs around the 88% mark.
Resolution occurs around the 98% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 3:

This section introduces the "all is lost" moment where everything seems to fall apart. The consequences of the swivel decision yield disaster as private motivations are revealed, seeming betrayals are uncovered, and either the relationship and/or the Protagonist’s goal is seemingly lost forever. This is when previous false beliefs and doubts come back to the surface, and the relationship falls apart, leading to a breakup and doubt as to whether they will ever be able to find their way back to each other.

What event or betrayal triggers the Protagonist's fears about their relationship, forcing them back into their false beliefs and doubts? For example, this could be the return of an ex, the resurfacing of a previous belief of the Love Interest, or an unexpected opportunity to achieve their external goal.
Consider deepening the tension by having more than the relationship end (e.g. the Protagonist may also lose friends, the support of family, or even their job as they cope with this new stress).

Offer the reader an opportunity to see how the characters have returned to their old lives in an unsatisfactory way, so that everything is as it was, but a little darker and with less enjoyment. Did they make a mistake?
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Dark Moment/Crisis occurs around the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2:

The Protagonist and Love Interest have grown closer and may have shared an intimate moment. The stakes reach their highest point as the romantic relationship’s importance jeopardizes the Protagonist’s chance to succeed at their stated goal—or vice versa—and their goal shifts. This is the "Finally" moment for readers, where they get to see the relationship begin to take a physical step forward.
How have the Protagonist and Love Interest deepened their relationship? This can be a physical connection, a verbal discussion, or an acceptance that this is love.
How does the deepening relationship conflict with the external goals of the characters?
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Swivel: Second Turning Point occurs around the 60-62% mark, three-quarters of the way through Act 2.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

The Protagonist and Love Interest are still committed to their goals, but their growing emotions for each other begin to create conflict. A situation irrevocably binds the Protagonist with the Love Interest, often while tweaking sexual tensions. This situation alters the perspective of the Protagonist and has further implications for the outcome of the relationship. The Protagonist begins to consider a relationship but realizes that it cannot work because of their external goals or false beliefs.

What event glues the Protagonist and Love Interest together? This could be an illness, friends seeing each other in a new way, or an act of selflessness, seemingly contrary to the Love Interest's personality.
Depict the Protagonist's consideration of the relationship and "what if" moment. How and why do they cling to their external goals and/or false beliefs?
Give the readers a 'this could actually work, but no' moment to increase the tension and stakes.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Midpoint/Raising the Stakes occurs around the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

A new development raises the stakes and clearly defines the Protagonist’s external goal. This works best when it sets the Protagonist and Love Interest at cross-purposes and/or their internal needs at odds with their external goal. One or both characters begin to see each other in a different light, raising the romantic tension. More sparks are beginning to fly, but in a state of denial, and conflict is on the horizon.

Consider how the characters' internal needs and external goals conflict with each other (e.g. the Protagonist owns a struggling café, and the Love Interest is opening a fancy new café down the street).
Remember: Internal needs could include love, patience, humility, or courage, while external goals could include a job promotion, saving their bookstore, taking a trip, moving to a new city, etc.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Turning Point occurs around the 25% mark as we begin Act 2.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1:

The Catalyst (or Inciting Incident) brings the Protagonist and the Love Interest together and into conflict. The Meet is brought about by a creative but credible event, often amusing, which sets the tone for the action to come. There may be an instant attraction, with an obstacle, or more often, an instant dislike due to misunderstandings, social miscues, or a clash of personalities. Sparks may fly, but the Protagonist is not ready for the relationship.
Decide upon the Catalyst / Inciting Incident, which sets the tone for future interactions / conflict.
Make the Inciting Incident intriguing and amusing, as the reader must connect to the scene and care about the outcome for the Protagonist and Love Interest.
What is the root of the conflict? Does one have a significant other? Are they brash and overbearing?
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Meet/Inciting Incident should take the story to the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:

This is the opening scene or sequence identifying the Protagonist's internal and/or external conflict. It introduces the reader to the current status quo of the Protagonist with something "wrong" implied as the reader views their ordinary world. The Protagonist and their Love Interest have goals and desires, which will come into conflict.
Introduce the reader to how the Protagonist functions in their ordinary life.
Include something about their life that displeases the Protagonist or appears wrong to the reader.
Identify the Protagonist's conflicts and goals as you develop a three-dimensional character.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Setup/Hook should take approximately 12-13% of the story, or the midway point of Act 1

pl4.name: Action Adventure Plot
pl4.description: An outline formula for writing an action and adventure story

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:

The beginning of the novel allows the reader to learn about the Hero's ordinary world and how they interact within it. For example, they may be looking for adventure, avoiding adventure, content with their life, unhappy, retired, or dreading their next mission. This section sets the hook and connects the reader to the Hero for the remainder of the story/series.
Identify what about the Hero's ordinary world that makes them happy or displeased.
Decide if the Hero is comfortable or uncomfortable with their current circumstance.
Identify what makes the Hero want to stay put or set off on a new adventure.
Emphasize why they are set in their decision and make them sympathetic to the reader.
Create a three-dimensional Hero with hopes, flaws, problems, and a unique personality.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Hero's Circumstance should comprise approximately 8-10% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1:

This section triggers the rest of the story. While living their ordinary life, the Hero encounters a problem or is given a mission. The triggering event includes a multitude of options: the Hero may inadvertently stumble into the Villain's scheme; there may be an assault on the Hero's city; their mode of transport may be hijacked, attacked, or otherwise disrupted; or perhaps damaging information about them is released. This event must be such that it will not resolve independently, and the Hero is left no choice but to take on the mission.
Identify a dramatic triggering event for the Hero.
Consider introducing other characters – is there an ally, mentor, or love interest? Are they in danger? Or have they switched allegiances and are responsible for the disrupting triggering event?

Make the triggering event enticing and ensure the Hero reacts to it according to their current circumstance and character (e.g. a happily retired Hero may be disgruntled and push back at the idea of another mission).
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Receives a mission occurs at approximately the 8-12% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1:

The Hero has answered the call to action and begins toward the goal. New Allies are introduced or already strategically placed, while other Allies may be recruited as the plot progresses. The Hero and Allies begin to form a plan of action and prepare for the journey ahead.
Identify how the Hero will gather Allies.
Increase the stakes and consider adding a small twist here (e.g. perhaps the Hero loses the support of an Ally OR an important new Ally is recruited).
Have the Hero devise and begin to implement a dangerous or risky plan – and if Allies are already strategically placed or to be recruited, decide how/where that fits into the story.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Begins Toward Goal occurs around the 12-15% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1:

Having devised a risky plan, the Hero sets off to an interesting or exotic location, crossing the story's first threshold and beginning the mission in earnest. The Hero must locate an important object, person, location, or information; in their search, they may attempt to infiltrate the Villain's organization. The tension and danger increase in this section as the Hero seeks to meet with allies - who may turn their back - and others to gain resources needed for the mission.
Consider the mission and what items or resources the Hero needs to be successful. For example, do they need to locate a specific person, object, the Villain's headquarters, or piece of information?

Decide how the Hero will attain their needed information and equipment (e.g. infiltrating the Villain's organization, meeting with an informant or previous ally, or locating an object which gives them information, such as a diary).
Consider adding a twist to aid or hinder the Hero (e.g. a missing ally/informant, loss of an ally's support, or gaining the support of an important ally)
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Travels to Exotic Location occurs around the 20% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1:

While gathering information and putting the plan into action, the Hero encounters another obstacle in the form of the Damsel and a relationship forms. Depending on the nature of the relationship, it may help or hinder the Hero along their journey. The Damsel may appear in distress, or as an ally or adversary, though the true nature of the Damsel may change or take time to unfold.
Decide if the Damsel should appear in distress – and if it is actual distress or a ploy.
Consider what form the relationship will take (e.g. romantic, friendship, adversarial, a combination of all, or a relationship of deceit).
Decide who makes the advances and if they succeed or fail, keeping in line with the Hero's character.
You can add depth to the plot by having both make advances, with each adding more detail to the story.
A romantic relationship may lead to a form of consummation – consider having this interrupted or postponed, increasing tension in the romantic subplot.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Encounter the Damsel brings the story to approximately the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

The tension continues to rise as the Hero encounters the Villain's Henchman and is faced with an obstacle. This section is a turning point in the story and serves to alert the Villain to the Hero. Allies or adversaries may switch sides, the Hero may end up on the wrong side of the law, or the authorities may be corrupt. The obstacle threatens the mission, but once overcome, it provides vital information. This new information may interrupt the Hero's mission, turn it into a larger mission, provide deeper insight into the Villain's capabilities, or place the Hero on the run.
Consider using this section to place the Hero in serious danger or raise the stakes.
Have the Hero make a narrow escape when it seems there is no way out (e.g. with the aid of Allies, the Damsel, or a Mentor).
Ensure the newly gained information from overcoming the obstacle is enticing and vital to the plot.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Encounters Henchman occurs around the 30% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Early in Act 2:

Increase the tension and the stakes with an extended chase scene. Having obtained vital knowledge and slipping their dire situation, the Hero is now pursued by evil forces. The Chase generally involves the Hero, Allies, Damsel, and several enemies. This scene provides an opportunity to further showcase the Hero's abilities and hook the reader with stunning physical feats, fantastic vehicles, daring maneuvers, etc.

The chase scene must be extraordinary and intense – allow your imagination to run wild as motorcycles are jumped into helicopters, cars are driven through shopping malls, and pedestrians are jumping every which way to safety.
Aim to amaze the reader's mind and increase their heart rate – the more dramatic and fast-paced the scene, the more the reader will be drawn in.
Have each side appear as though they may succeed.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The Chase occurs around the 40% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Early in Act 2:

A Major Complication arises to cast doubt on the Hero's chances of success. The Hero makes a significant error or suffers an unexpected setback, demonstrating that they may not be ready or capable of completing the mission. The Hero begins to doubt themselves and considers abandoning the mission, bringing them to their lowest point thus far. This scene serves as another turning point for the overall plot, with many options to consider.

The Major Complication must be shattering for the Hero – perhaps they lose an ally, mentor, or love interest to betrayal or death, or they realize they have been chasing a decoy Villain, or the Villain gains a powerful ally.

The Complication does not need to come from an external source – the Hero may make an error in judgement by trusting a traitorous ally, fall in love with the Villain, or may be tricked/required to work with the Villain.

The tide must turn in favor of the Villain, though it may also be by chance (e.g. a natural disaster derails the Hero's plan, a previous enemy returns for revenge, or the Hero losses an item of vital importance).
Consider having the Villain force the Hero into an impossible decision, like sacrificing a few innocent lives to prevent a much larger loss of life.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The Major Complication arises around the 45% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

Having suffered a defeat during the Major Complication, the Hero receives assistance and inspiration that emboldens them to return to the fight. The assistance may come in the form of a pep-talk by a Mentor or Love Interest, the return of an Ally, completing a dangerous task, or realizing the importance of a previously undervalued item, piece of knowledge, or clue. This significant event re-ignites the Hero's fire and will to fight as they regain their self-confidence.

Consider the Hero's character and the type of Assistance that would best re-invigorate their passion after a serious defeat – do they need to prove their self-worth to themselves, do they need encouragement from a Mentor, or perhaps a loved one is thrust into danger?
Does the emotion of the loss drive the Hero to do something atypical, like blackmail, coerce, or threaten a key person to obtain what they need?
Rebuild the Hero and have them ready to fight by the end of this section.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Assistance occurs around the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

Newly inspired, the Hero travels to and infiltrates the Villain's secured Fortress, usually in a remote and difficult to access location. The Hero uses their renewed confidence and knowledge to battle their way past security, henchmen, and impressive guard animals. They are determined to defeat the Villain. As a twist, the Villain may infiltrate the Hero's base, leading to a confrontation where the Hero is in a defensive, rather than an offensive position.

Don't be afraid to go over the top – the Fortress must be challenging to access and is generally awe-inspiring (e.g. a black marble castle on a mountaintop, carved into the side of an active volcano, a rig in the middle of the ocean, or an abandoned temple in the jungle).
Give the Villain a crack security team and intimidating guard animals (e.g. tiger, pack of dogs, sharks, hyenas, or perhaps a moat full of alligators).
If the Villain infiltrates the Hero's base of operations, consider the Hero's defenses – have they already been hinted at, or do they need to be introduced?
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Infiltrate the Fortress occurs around the 55% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Late in Act 2:

Perhaps overconfident or simply overwhelmed by the odds, the Hero finds themselves captured by the Villain. The Hero is in a dire situation as the Villain begins to torture the Hero and possibly attempts to kill someone close to the Hero, like a Love Interest, Ally, or Mentor. The tension and stakes are high as the Hero's success and future are cast into doubt.
Decide under what circumstances the Hero is captured – were they overwhelmed by enemy forces, cornered by an attack animal, or overly confident, causing an error in judgement?
Consider having your Hero intentionally be captured as part of their plan, only to have the stakes rise and the Hero lose control of the situation.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Captured occurs around the 60% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Late in Act 2:

Through guile, planning, or luck, the Hero manages to escape the Villain's grasp and rescue their Allies, Mentor, Damsel, or Love Interest; if the Hero cannot free themselves, they may be rescued by them. Either way, the Hero escapes the clutches of certain doom.
Considering the Hero's character and how they are being held/tortured, decide how the Hero will escape their predicament.
Decide who needs rescuing and by whom, accounting for what will not only fit into the ongoing narrative but what will be satisfying for the reader.

Consider ramping up the tension and the stakes by having the Hero fail at rescuing one of their group (e.g. perhaps they save the Damsel but enter the room just in time to see the Mentor die), and then tie this emotional response into the rest of the narrative.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The Narrow Escape occurs around the 70% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2:

Now free (and angry), the Hero seeks out and obtains the item, person, or information they were seeking. Once the item is obtained, the Hero proceeds to wreak havoc in the Villain's lair; if what they seek is not found or is not on-site, they still wreak havoc in the Villain's lair. If the Villain has infiltrated the Hero's lair, they obtain the object or item they seek and wreak havoc in the Hero's lair.
Showcase the Hero/Villain seeking the needed item, knowledge, or person – whether it is obtained or not, unleash the havoc.
Have fun with this scene and use it as a bit of a pressure release for the narrative.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Attain the Goal occurs around the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 3:
The Hero's escape is not yet complete as they confront or are confronted by the loyal henchman of the Villain. An exciting battle occurs with the Hero ultimately defeating the henchman.

Consider the narrative to this point in the story and decide what outcome to the battle fits best and will be most enticing for the reader (e.g. the Hero captures the henchman, kills the henchman, or the henchman narrowly escapes).
After the quick pressure release in the previous section, the tension and stakes begin to rise again.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Battle the Henchman occurs around the 80% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 3:

The Hero faces off with the Villain in a fantastic battle. The Villain may attempt an escape, be captured or killed. Alternatively, the Hero's attempt to defeat the Villain may go terribly wrong, resulting in a severe injury or even their death; in this instance, the Villain may escape, be rescued, or captured/killed by the Hero's Allies, Mentor, Damsel, or Love Interest.
Showcase an exciting battle between the Hero and Villain.
No matter the outcome, make sure the Hero (or Allies) lays waste to the Villain's fortress.
Include massive explosions and destruction – have fun with it!
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Battle the Villain occurs around the 85% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 3:

The Hero has battled the Villain and destroyed their fortress, but the story is not yet over. The Plot Twist must capture the reader's attention and let them know that the mission is not yet complete, as it presents one final obstacle to be overcome.
Introduce a plot twist in this section that is in line with the narrative of the Villain escaping, being captured, or killed.

There are many ways to add a Plot Twist but keep in mind, there is more work to be done: if the Villain escaped, they must be tracked down; if the Villain is captured, they may escape or be rescued by henchmen; and if the Villain is killed, their nefarious plans must still be stopped.

Raise the stakes and capture the reader's attention – consider having the Hero be tempted by an opportunity which would make it impossible to foil the Villain, or have the henchman attempt to bribe or coerce the Hero, or have a trusted Ally turn and begin working with the Villain.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Plot Twist occurs around the 88-92% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 3:

The final obstacle presented by the last Plot Twist is overcome, and the Hero moves on to the Resolution, the climax of the story. Not all Resolutions occur as planned: the Hero may foil the Villain's evil schemes; they may fail in their attempt to thwart the schemes; or they may negotiate an agreement with the Villain. No matter how the Resolution occurs, the initial threat/problem is over by the end of this section.
Ensure the reader is given a satisfactory solution in line with the Hero's development and the overall narrative of the story.
Detail how the Hero brings about the Resolution and give them - and the reader - a moment to pause and reflect over all they have experienced and learned.
Consider the state of the Hero at the end of this section – are they victorious, defeated, injured, killed, or ready for the next adventure?
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Resolution comes at the 93-97% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3

The mission is concluded, and the Hero may now return to their ordinary world. The Hero has grown and transformed over the course of the adventure, and their character arc ends here, though not always with a happy ending. The story is wrapped by showcasing how the newly transformed Hero fits into the ordinary world once more and may be celebrated by those at home.
Consider the consequences of the resolution – the Hero may deepen their relationship with a Love Interest, enjoy a larger group of Allies, or simply enjoy the rewards of a mission well done.

Not all stories end on a purely happy note, so consider having the Hero recovering from injuries, struggling with the results of their failure, or losing their Love Interest through a breakup or tragedy.
If the Hero caused international incidents, broke laws, or angered authorities, consider if they need to atone in some way.
If this story is part of a series, be sure to leave room for further character development and set a hook for the next installment.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Conclusion occurs around the 98% mark.

pl39.name: Bromancing the Beat
pl39.description: Much like romance, bromance is the basis for stories from buddy cops to partner comedies. This template follows romancing the beat, but more geared toward same gender companion stories.

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Set Up

Hook the reader's attention and draw them into the story by introducing the first Hero/Heroine while showing them in their everyday life. Offer a glimpse of their life and the internal struggle that is holding them back from love.
Introduce H1 in a way that makes that character compelling (e.g. desires, flaws, success, a unique personality).
Show your character’s slice of life but throw a hitch in it.
Give or introduce your character’s external goal – for example, a promotion, vacation, or to attain an object.
Introduce or hint at what your character needs – for example, courage, patience, or the ability to work as a team.
Breakdown:
Phase 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Introduce H1 should be about the first 4-5% of the story.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)
Roger Murtaugh is turning 50, and just wants to quietly work his case for the police department alone. He doesn't want a partner again, ever.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 2: We Gotta Make This Work
This is the false high. It appears as though the Protagonists have a solution or at least the start of one. But that hope is dashed
Show the Protagonists getting along and accomplishing a goal
Showcase H1 and H2 displaying at least one skill they will need to make the resolution possible but only hint at how valuable it might be.
Give the reader the impression that all will end well with the Protagonists together, and the main story problem solved.
Breakdown:
Phase 2 makes up 25% of the story from 25% - 50%.
Turning Point occurs around the 50% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)

Riggs and Murtaugh go to the firing range and discuss a potential suspect. But when they arrive at her home, it explodes. They get a description for another suspect though, the one they think blew up the house.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Go Get the Bad Guys

Everything seems to be headed in the right direction until the protagonists learn something or an event happens that derails the current path of the investigation but also reveals a new clue or new information.
Take away some of the confidence the two have felt in the solution to the problem (e.g. a suspect dies, trust is betrayed, or new information reveals errors in their thinking).
Raise the stakes and threaten the relationship between H1 and H2 due to new conflict and tension.
Breakdown:
Phase 3 makes up 25% of the story from 50% - 75%.
New Information occurs around the 55% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)
Muirtaugh confronts Michael Hunsacker while Riggs waits outside. Hunsacker is killed, and now the bad guys know who Riggs is. His life is now threatened.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Go Get the Bad Guys
The relationship of the partners is threatened, usually by external events that trigger the internal fears of both H1 and H2. The peace of the previous beat is now disrupted.
Show the threat to the growing relationship and partnership.
Allow the threat to trigger fear and threaten the desires of H1 and H2.
Raise the stakes for the partnership forcing them to either trust each other and work together or split up to find solutions on their own.
Breakdown:
Phase 3 makes up 25% of the story from 50% - 75%.
Danger Zone occurs around the 60% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)
Riggs is nearly killed and Roger's family is in danger. In fact, his daughter has been kidnapped, raising the stakes, and the pair must now find and rescue her.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Go Get the Bad Guys
Trust Me is where H2 actually says to H1, "You have to trust me" or "You have to do things my way this time." H1 is left with no choice and must follow their partner's lead.
What is the event that forces H1 to trust and rely on H2?
Show H1 move from distrust to trust of H2, but not always without questions. Show the fear of both protagonists and clearly outline the stakes if they fail.
Breakdown:
Phase 3 makes up 25% of the story from 50% - 75%.
Trust Me occurs around the 65-70% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)
Riggs tells Murtaugh he has to trust him. Murtaugh asks if he is as good as he says he is, and Riggs reassures him. They embark on a brave plan to save Murtaugh's daughter.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Go Get the Bad Guys

The worst-case scenario. The fears and false beliefs of H1 seem to have come true, and the partner's carefully laid plans fail. They are not back where they started in this scenario - the situation is now much worse.
H1's worst fears actually come true, and they find themselves in the worst possible position
Failure means the bad guys get away with the evil they are doing, and the good guys suffer as a result
In the Failure beat, H2 says, "I should have known things would never turn out well for me. What was I thinking trying to help/save/work with H1?" Both protagonists now feel ultimate despair.
Breakdown:
Phase 3 makes up 25% of the story from 50% - 75%.
Failure occurs around the 70-75% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)
The plan fails and Riggs and Murtaugh are captured. His daughter also fails to escape. Both men are tortured, and neither will give up any information.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Go Get the Bad Guys
The darkest moment. H1 and H2 have failed. They no longer believe they can rely on each other, and the bad guys appear to have achieved victory.
Always tie the black moment to the internal conflicts of the protagonists and the external events that have led to this moment.
Show how the old way of doing things did not work, and how H1 and H2 now have no hope.

The larger the event, the further the protagonists are separated (whether that is physical or emotional distance), the greater the stakes for both them and the reader. Make this moment completely devoid of hope and as dark as possible.
Breakdown:
Phase 3 makes up 25% of the story from 50% - 75%.
The Dark Night occurs around the 75% mark.
Example:
Riggs is tortured. He tells the men he knows nothing, and they promise to kill him at that point. He appears to be on the verge of death.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Finish Them

The Dark Night is the worst moment for H1. They are under threat of death or something even worse, and there seems to be no hope for escape. The bad guys have not only won but appear to be able to crush H1 entirely.
Show the protagonist at the lowest possible point so that what appeared to be the worst thing ever is now even worse.
Hint that there may be some hope, but show that it is unlikely or will be really difficult to make this happen.
Breakdown:
Phase 4 makes up the final 25% of the story.
What Have I Done? occurs around the 80% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)
Murtaugh is tortured and resists until his daughter is brought in and threatened. He seems on the verge of breaking.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Finish Them

The glimmer of hope from the last beat has now become a flame. One or both of our protagonists have escaped and the bad guys are now on the run. There is finally hope and victory seems to be possible, even if it is not yet likely.
What is the triggering event that allows our protagonists to escape or rise up from defeat?
Decide which challenges or sacrifices must be made to achieve the victory the protagonists so desperately want.
Build tension as the heroes now pursue the bad guys, and raise the stakes for both.
Breakdown:
Phase 4 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Send them Running occurs around the 85% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)
Riggs escapes, rescues Roger and his daughter, and the three of them run toward freedom, taking out bad guys along the way.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Finish Them

It’s life or death now. The Protagonist must be willing to put it all on the line now or risk losing the one thing they need to survie this ordeal with the least amount of damage possible. The Life-or-Death Moment, the great sacrifice, is here, but will it be enough?
Create a Life-or-death scenario that nearly solves the problem
Don't let them off the hook too easily - the life-or-death scenario only solves part of the problem. There is usually at least one more problem standing in the way.
Portray the celebration of victory, but throw a hitch in it. Something else is wrong.
Breakdown:
Phase 4 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Life or Death occurs around the 90% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)

Riggs goes after Mr. Joshua who escapes by stealing a car. Murtaugh goes after and kills General McAllister. As they celebrate, Murtaugh realizes that Mr. Joshua knows where he lives and will go after his family.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Finish Them
In the last beat, a false victory occurred, but show the reader that things are not quite over. You’ve put them through the wringer, but there is one more challenge they must solve together.
Close the character arcs of the two Protagonists and show how they have changed and now trust each other
Resolve the internal and external conflicts.
Show the Protagonists now are and how that enables the resolution of the final problem.
Ensure you are fulfilling reader expectations – the harder the challenges and difficulties before, the greater the final victory must be.
Breakdown:
Phase 4 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Final Solution occurs around the 95% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)

Riggs and Murtaugh head to Murtaugh's home to catch the final bad guy (Mr. Joshua). They capture him and Riggs subdues him on Roger's lawn. Mr. Joshua makes one last escape attempt, and Murtaugh and Riggs shoot him at the same time.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Set Up

Continue to hook the reader's attention and draw them into the story by introducing the second Hero/Heroine while showing them in their everyday life. Offer a glimpse of their life and the internal struggle that is holding them back from achieving what they want, including fulfilling their need for friendship.
Introduce H2 in a way that makes that character compelling (e.g. desires, flaws, success, a unique personality).
Show your character’s slice of life but throw a hitch in it.
Give or introduce your character’s external goal – for example, a promotion, vacation, or to attain an object.
Introduce or hint at what your character needs – for example, courage, patience, or healing and closure.
Breakdown:
Phase 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Introduce H2 occurs around the 5-8% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)

Martin Riggs has lost his wife in an auto accident. He's suicidal and depressed, but the only thing that keeps him going is the job - his work with the police department. No one wants to be his partner because they either thing he is a psycho or is faking it.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Finish Them

It’s up to you, a master at your craft, to manage a scene with little conflict that is still intriguing. This is the return to the ordinary world; each Protagonist has changed and fits in their world a little differently and with a new perspective.
Show how each Protagonist fits back in the ordinary world and how they have transformed.
Have a moment of celebration – the Protagonists have been through a lot, so let them unwind a party a bit.
How do those around them react to their new partnership and cooperation and their new selves?
If part of a series, consider planting a hook or foreshadowing a future difficulty.
Breakdown:
Phase 4 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Epilogue occurs around the 98-100% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)
Riggs shares Christmas dinner with Murtaugh's family at their damaged but soon-to-be restored home. We see the two of them have formed a new bond and a new partnership.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Set Up

The two Protagonists meet for the first time on the page, brought together by external forces, chance, or a life event. There is usually an instant dislike with one or both of the Heroes feeling a reservation about their new partner, but some respect can also show through.
Decide the Inciting Incident that leads to the Meet Cute.
Make it memorable—this is the story they will share with their grandchildren one day.
Hint at how well the Protagonists might work together, but hint at the fact that the timing or some other factor is off.
Show the immediate development of conflict between the Protagonists.
Breakdown:
Phase 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Meet Cute occurs around the 10-12% mark.
Example:
Roger Murtaugh sees a man with a gun in police headquarters. He runs to subdue the suspect, who throws him to the ground with a judo move and then is introduced as his new partner, Martin Riggs.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Set Up

This is the argument H1 voices against cooperation with H2. This sets up the relationship arc for the reader - the two clearly must work together to achieve a common goal, but the character basically says, (usually out loud but could be through internal dialogue) the reason this will not work, not now, not ever, but especially not with H2.
What is the reason H1 thinks that a partnership or cooperation will never work?
Depict the argument H1 has either vocally or internally, and make it compelling.
Breakdown:
Phase 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
I Don't Think So occurs around the 18-20% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)

Neither Roger Murtaugh nor Martin Riggs wants to work together, but the department has compelled them to do so, so they are stuck. Murtaugh thinks Riggs is crazy, and Riggs thinks Murtaugh is an old man.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Set Up
This beat is the plot thrust that brings the story into the second act.

An event or situation forces the two Protagonists together to achieve a goal or solve a problem; this event not only raises the stakes but also clearly defines each Protagonist's goal. While still at odds with each other, they begin to respect and understand each other. The two Protagonists cannot walk away from each other now—not until they see this conundrum through.
Make sure your glue is sticky here – the event that forces them together must be one that cannot be resolved on its own, nor by only one Protagonist; they must be stuck together to succeed.
Consider what event forces them together and what actions or choices create mutual respect, even if it is reluctant.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Stuck Together occurs around the 20% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)

Riggs and Murtaugh are called out to a jumper situation. Riggs volunteers to talk the man down, but instead handcuffs himself to the suicidal man, and they jump together into the fire department's airbag. Riggs is hailed a hero, but Murtaugh is not so sure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 2: We Gotta Make This Work

We see that H1 is sticking to their old ways and is not yet ready to accept the way that H2 does things, especially after either a stunt they pulled or something they said. They do not want this partner or any partner for that reason.
Restate the argument against the need for a partner at all.
