Establish how the external goals of H1 conflict with their internal needs.
Breakdown:
Phase 2 makes up 25% of the story from 25% - 50%.
Absolutely No Way occurs around the 25% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)

Murtaugh discovers that Riggs truly is suicidal and a little bit crazy. Riggs states that the job is the only reason he does not take his own life. Murtaugh learns more from the police psychologist and decides he really needs to watch his back around Riggs.
Phase 2: We Gotta Make This Work

H1's false beliefs and arguments begin to be challenged as H2 becomes a vital part of their success. They need this new partner whether they like it or not, and despite their issues, they also have some good qualities.
Begin attacking your character’s false belief about what he or she stated in either No Way Beat 1 or No Way Beat 2.
Include little moments between the two Protagonists that show the false beliefs being challenged and H1's changing respect and admiration for H2.
Breakdown:
Phase 2 makes up 25% of the story from 25% - 50%.
Maybe You're Not So Bad occurs around the 30% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)
Riggs and Murtaugh share laughs as they head to the home of a suspect in Beverly Hills. Riggs offers to buy Murtaugh a birthday present.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 2: We Gotta Make This Work
The protagonists are starting to work together as a team. In fact, things are pretty good. H2 does something that really makes H1 think about their reluctance when it comes to accepting H2
What external and internal actions force H1 to reconsider their first impression of H2?
Show examples of how the false beliefs discussed earlier are either unfounded or irrelevant considering the situation they find themselves in.
Breakdown:
Phase 2 makes up 25% of the story from 25% - 50%
In Fact, You're Pretty Good occurs around the 40% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)
Riggs and Murtaugh head to a suspect's home in Beverly Hills. Murtaugh subdues the suspect, but the suspect attempts to kill him. Riggs saves his life, and Murtaugh expresses his thanks begrudgingly.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 2: We Gotta Make This Work

The Protagonists begin to question their first opinions of each other and their previous No Way arguments. Each Protagonist is still working toward their own goals, but working together is helping them in this process. H1 and H2 begin to see a path forward toward a solution to their current problem.
What actions or events cause them to begin questioning their opinions of each other and their previous No Way statements?
Grant a glimpse at the opposition between the Protagonist's inner and outer conflict.
Depict the two Protagonists relationship improving as they move forward.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
We Can Solve This Together occurs around the 45% mark.
Example: (Lethal Weapon)
Murtaugh takes Riggs home to meet his family. The two discuss the case and share some beers. The partnership seems to be working out for the better.

pl38.name: Character in a Situation Short Story
pl38.description: The classic Seven Point plot structure, adapted for short stories

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:
This section introduces the reader to a character and their everyday life–and hints at something that will disrupt that normalcy.
This is the hook and the moment the reader becomes invested in the character and the storyline.
Introduce a character with flaws, desires, problems, and a unique personality.
Hint at some issue or problem in their world that makes them unhappy or impacts them in some way.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the short story.
Introducing the character should take approximately 10-15% of the story, 500-750 words in a 5,000-word story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle to the end of Act 1:
Describe the situation the character finds themselves in, and why it is disrupting their life or ordinary world.
Introduce the situation and how it impacts the character. This must be an issue that cannot be resolved on its own.
Show the character's discomfort with their new situation and how it guides their actions.
Ensure that the situation is interesting and continues to hook the reader into the story.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
A situation happens from the 15-25% mark in the story, from 750-1,250 words in a 5,000-word story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:
The Situation creates a problem for the character that they must solve. This sends their life in a new direction.
Introduce the problem in detail and show how it arises out of the situation.
Show the depth of the problem, and how it impacts both the character and their situation.
Illustrate why the hero must solve the problem themselves, and that it will not resolve itself and cannot be solved by others.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25%-75%.
With a Problem happens around the 25-35% mark of the story from 1,250-1,750 in a 5,000-word story.
-- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:
In this section of the story, the hero will try to solve their problem in a variety of ways, seeking to correct their situation and return to the ordinary world.
Show the hero trying a number of approaches and tactics to try to solve their problem.
Reveal any allies who try to help them and any adversaries who try to stop them from solving the problem.
Keep in mind the length of the story to determine how many attempts the character makes.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Who Tries Repeatedly to Solve the Problem occurs around the 35-50% mark in the story, from 3,750-2,500 words in a 5,000-word short story.

cards.title: Who Tries Repeatedly to Solve the Problem

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2:
Show the character failing. Each time they fail, show the problem becoming worse than it was before.
Show each time the character tries and fails, and increase the tension and the stakes along the way.
Reveal the darkest moment, when it feels like the problem is at its worst, leaving the reader wondering how or if it can be resolved.
Highlight the emotional, mental, and/or physical impact the problem has on the character and just how bad their situation has become.
Hint that the character may have discovered a solution to the problem. This may come from themselves or with the help of an ally or mentor.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The Ordeal occurs around the 50-75% mark, or 2,500-3,750 words in a 5,000-word story.

cards.title: But Fails, Making the Problem Worse
The Final Attempt to Solve the Problem

children.text: -- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 3:
Using what they have learned along the way, the character makes one last attempt to solve the problem, which can either succeed or fail.
Dramatize the consequences the character faces whether they solve the problem or not.
Reconfirm what is at stake for the character and their situation, and increase the tension right before the climax.
Show the outcome of the character's final attempt, either good or bad, and how that has impacted their situation.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Final Attempt to Solve the Problem occurs around the 75-95% mark, from 3,750-4,750 words in a 5,000-word story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3:

Show the character's return to their situation in the ordinary world. Demonstrate whether the situation is changed and made better as a result of their actions, made worse, or if the situation remains unchanged. However, be sure to show the resolution of the problem, whether or not the character was successful.
Redefine the situation and show how things are different or have stayed the same.
Show the resolution of the problem or the failure of the character and how the problem persists.
Define how the character has or has not grown, and how that has changed their feelings about their situation and the problem.
Wrap up the story in a way that is satisfying to the reader.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Result of the Final Attempt occurs around the 95% mark, or 4,750 words in a 5,000-word story.

cards.title: The Result of the Final Attempt

pl19.name: Children's Book Plot
pl19.description: An outline formula for writing books for children

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3:
Using all they have learned, the Protagonist works to find another solution, which is finally successful. The story's Resolution must be driven by the Protagonist, not an adult.
Let the Protagonist come to the solution on their own – for example, in a moment of reflection, with the help of friends, or by an idea triggered by an object or something else in the vicinity.
Use all they have learned to solve the problem.
Show the Protagonist enjoying the fruits of their labors and how they have changed.
Wrap up storylines and character arcs now that the problem has been solved.
Example:

As the girls get to the bottom of the stairs in the basement, they hear Amala's dog barking and growling at something. They run into the playroom and find the dog in its bed playing with Amala's boots! Apparently it had taken the boots from the top of the stairs. Amala runs over and hugs the dog as Carolina saves the boots. They then run upstairs and go outside to play, while Amala promises herself and Carolina that she'll keep her boots in her closet from now on.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Resolution occurs around the 90% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 3:
The Climax and the darkest moment for the Protagonist, which sets up the Resolution. Being a children's book, the darkest moment is relative.
Create a relatable and age-appropriate darkest moment for the Protagonist.
How has the Protagonist lost hope? What is their false belief?
Bring the Protagonist to, or just past, the point of giving up.
Example:

Amala wants to cry. With the sun now shining brightly outside, Amala apologizes to Carolina for not being able to find her boots. She is resigned to being punished for losing the boots, as the friends give up hope on playing in the puddles outside. They begin to walk back to Amala's bedroom and stop partway, deciding to go downstairs to play in the basement instead.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Climax occurs around the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2:

The third attempt at the solution is unsuccessful as well. The Protagonist was certain that their third attempt would work, and is deeply disappointed when they have to head back to the drawing board, as a solution seems out of reach.
Identify a "foolproof" solution to the problem and have it fail as well.
Show the Protagonist running out of ideas and losing faith.
Don't forget the problems, solutions, and reactions must be relatable and within the range of a child.
Example:

As they clean the room again, Carolina suggests that Amala stop and close her eyes, think about when she last had them, and then mentally retrace her steps. It's a technique Carolina's father taught her, and it works for her almost every time. Amala does that and remembers she saw her boots the previous day by the backdoor, close to the basement steps. The girls run to the backdoor to get the boots and once more see that they are not there.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Solution 3 occurs around the 55% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:
With each attempted solution, the stakes continue to rise. But keep in mind that this is a book for children – the stakes generally will not include the fate of the world.
Make the stakes relatable and age-appropriate (e.g. not finishing the homework assignment, not finding a lost toy, or still not being able to reach the cookie jar).
Consider what the Protagonist has learned from Solution 1 and create another attempt that builds on it and teaches a new lesson, without being too obvious or preachy.
Male this solution a bit more complicated while ultimately making the situation worse.
How is the Protagonist reacting to each attempt and failure?
Example:

Remembering that Amala's mom and dad get upset when she leaves her stuff lying around, she thinks maybe her mom put her boots in her bedroom closet. They return to Amala's room, open the closet, and find it is a mess. The girls pull everything out of the closet, but the boots are not there – and time is slipping by as they have to put everything back.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Solution 2 occurs around the 40% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

Whether on their own or with the help of friends, the Protagonist considers the problem facing them and thinks of a possible solution. Unfortunately, this first solution does not work. In children's books, the Rule of Three applies: the Protagonist should attempt and fail three times before succeeding in finding a solution.
Think about the problem from a child's point of view and how they would approach a solution.
Don't be afraid of silly solutions – remember that children do not have the same level of understanding, world perspective, or life experience as adults.
The first attempt at a solution can be simple or obvious, leading to increasingly more sophisticated attempts.
Remember that while initial attempts are doomed to fail, they should bring the Protagonist closer to the solution with lessons learned.
Example:

After the initial shock of discovering the boots missing, Amala runs out to the front porch with Carolina to see if she left them there to dry after the last rain. They look around everywhere, but the boots are nowhere to be seen.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Solution 1 occurs around the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1:
After the Protagonist's introduction, introduce the reader to the Central Problem that needs to be solved. There are limited pages in a children's book, so be sure to reveal the problem early.
Make the Central Problem age-appropriate and relatable to the reader (e.g. needing to finish difficult homework, wanting an expensive toy, dealing with a school bully).
Create a Central Problem that can be easily identified by the reader.
Identify what's a stake if the problem isn't solved.
Example:

The rain stops, and the girls run to the front closet to get their boots – only to find Amala's new boots missing! Amala knows she'll be in trouble if her parents discover she's lost the boots, and they only have a short period of time to play before Carolina has to go home.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Problem should take your story from approximately 12% to the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:

The opening of the story hooks the reader and introduces the Protagonist, who is usually a child or an animal. If possible, have the story start in a state of action, grappling with something that will turn into the story's main conflict. Children's books are often short and don't require a significant amount of exposition.
Create a Protagonist who is age appropriate and relatable, with a compelling personality and motivation.
Start the story in the midst of action.
Briefly show the Protagonist in their Ordinary World.
Example:

Amala is playing with an old set of toys in her bedroom with her friend Carolina as it rains outside. They are bored and biding their time until the rain stops so they can go outside and play in the puddles.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Introduction should take approximately 12% of the story.

pl18.name: Cozy Mystery Beat Sheet
pl18.description: A beat sheet for cozy mysteries by Sara Rosett

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2: Reactive
Act 2 is the
reactive

phase. Because cozies are about amateur sleuths, Protagonists usually become gradually more involved in the investigation. They are getting their bearings and figuring out who is a suspect, and discovering clues and motives. During Act 2, the Protagonist is investigating, but they are reacting to events and discoveries instead of being proactive.
The Protagonist may be a reluctant sleuth and have to be convinced to get more involved.
The Protagonist may think of themselves as simply helping out/providing information to the police in the early stages of the investigation.
Why are they only partially invested in the investigation?
How are their actions reactive instead of proactive?
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up approximately 35% of the story from 25% to 60%.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 4: Confrontation

With the murderer revealed, now justice must be done – for example, through the arrest of the murderer or death of the murderer. Readers want to see a functioning, healthy community at the close of the novel. If there are any lingering questions about red herrings, this is where you clear them up.
How will justice be done?
How will equilibrium be restored to the community?
How will the subplots be wrapped?
What glimpse of the Protagonist's new world will be given to the reader?
What new relationships have been created over the course of the story?
What possibilities are in store for the Protagonist now that the murderer has been caught?
If part of a series, this is a good place to give a hint about the next book.
Breakdown:
Act 4 makes up the final 20% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 4: Confrontation
What form does the final confrontation take?
Battle of wits.
Actual physical battle.
How will the Protagonist confront the Antagonist?
Directly?
Forced into it?
Surprised by Antagonist?
What unique skills/tools will the Protagonist use to win the battle?
Have those skills/tools been worked into the story from the beginning?
Breakdown:
Act 4 makes up the final 20% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 4: Confrontation
When the story reaches the final confrontation, the killer is revealed. How will the murder method be shown and answer any questions the readers might have about it? Make sure these things are clear:
Who committed the murder
How the murder was committed
How the Protagonist figured it out (what clues unlocked the mystery)
Explain any red herrings, if needed.
Breakdown:
Act 4 makes up the final 20% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3: Proactive
The turning point of Act 3 is an event that will set the final conflict in motion. Often it is a clue/knowledge/discovery that reveals the identity of the murderer.
What is the turning point?
What does the turning point reveal?
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up approximately 20% of the story from 60% to 80%.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 3: Proactive
As the Protagonist tests theories, some suspects are cleared.
What theories are tested?
Which suspects are cleared?
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up approximately 20% of the story from 60% to 80%.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 3: Proactive
The Protagonist develops a final theory and attempts to identify the murderer, but fails spectacularly.
What is the Protagonist's final theory?
Why does the theory not work?
How does testing the theory lead to the biggest failure, the “all is lost” moment?
What is the Protagonist's reaction to the large failure?
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up approximately 20% of the story from 60% to 80%.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2: Reactive

This is the next big event in the story that turns everything on its head and makes the Protagonist reevaluate everything they have discovered. The turning point of Act 2 is often the death of the primary suspect, which means the Protagonist must reassess everything and form a new theory.
What is the turning point of this act?
Does the primary suspect die?
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up approximately 35% of the story from 25% to 60%.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Late Act 2: Reactive (Continued)
The Protagonist forms a new theory:
What is the Protagonist's new theory?
Does it work?
Why does the theory not work?
Are any suspects cleared?
If the theory fails, what is the Protagonist's reaction?
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up the second 25% of the story from 25% to 50%.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Late Act 2: Reactive
The Protagonist develops a theory and attempts to identify the murderer, but fails. The try/fail cycle repeats as many times as needed for the story.
What is the Protagonist's first theory?
Why does the theory not work?
What is the Protagonist's reaction to the first failure?
Some suspects are cleared as the Protagonist works through the try/fail cycles. Which suspects are cleared in this act?
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up the second 25% of the story from 25% to 50%.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Mid Act 2: Reactive
In Act 2, the Sleuth gets involved in investigating the murder, and that makes the Antagonist (the murderer) nervous. The Antagonist takes action to prevent the Sleuth from discovering the truth.
Possible actions that the Antagonist might take to confuse the Sleuth and manipulate the direction of the investigation:
Plant false clues that implicate other people (often the Protagonist).
Move the body.
Create a scenario that makes it look as if the death occurred at a different time than it actually happened.
Makes an effort to get the case closed (puts pressure on officials).
Frame someone.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up approximately 35% of the story from 25% to 60%.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2: Reactive
During Act 2, the Protagonist is discovering information – clues and red herrings – and developing theories about who the murderer is and how the crime was committed.
What clues does the Protagonist find in this act?
What red herrings does the Protagonist find in this act?
What theory do they develop?
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up approximately 35% of the story from 25% to 60%.

cards.title: Suspect Pool Narrows to Closed Community

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Mid Act 2: Reactive
As your Protagonist investigates, it becomes clear that the suspect pool is limited to a small group of people. But how is the suspect pool narrowed to the closed community? Some possible factors:
The window of time the crime could have been committed.
Access to the murder weapon.
Weather - storm limits travel, and only those in the immediate area could have committed the murder.
Moreover, as the investigation narrows to the closed community that the Protagonist is part of, it impacts the Protagonist's relationships.
Are any family or friends (or both!) suspects?
Is the Protagonist a suspect?
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up the second 35% of the story from 25% to 60%.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1: Ordinary World

A turning point is an event that sends the story in a new direction. Often the turning point of Act I is the discovery of the dead body or the decision to investigate. Once a murder occurs, your protagonist can't go on with their ordinary life.
What is the turning point of this act?
How does the turning point change everything for the protagonist and launch her on a new path?
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Late Act 1: Ordinary World
Do you have a change or disturbance? A change or disturbance shows the reader that something isn't right, and hints at the murder to come. For example:
Someone doesn't show up at work
Someone receives a threatening letter
Someone behaves in an out-of-character manner
Do you need one?
You don't need to have a change or disturbance.

A disturbance signals to the reader that there is something going on in the background. If your murder takes place farther into the first act, a disturbance is a great way to keep readers turning pages until the murder.
If you have one, how does it foreshadow the turning point?
For more information on the disturbance, check out James Scott Bell's book Plot and Structure.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1: Ordinary World

This is where you show the protagonist's ordinary life. It is the "before" view, before everything changes. This section may be a chapter to two or even just a few sentences. You want to give your reader a taste of what the protagonist's normal life is like before murder invades the community and messes everything up.
What is the Protagonist's ordinary world/story setup?
What situation is the story born out of?
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Early Act 1: Ordinary World
What is the setting of the book? How is it cozy?
Tone is important in a cozy, and one way to make sure you hit the right tone is with your setting. Cozy readers want to read about pleasant places, places they'd like to visit:
A small town with close-knit community
A fun beach town
A quaint village
You're not limited to geographical communities. Your setting could be a college campus, a cruise ship, or a workplace like a flower shop or a bakery or a museum.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 4: Confrontation

Act 4 is about the final confrontation between the Protagonist and the Antagonist. This is the lowest point of the novel. What is the worst thing (event/situation) that could happen to the Protagonist with the case?
Perhaps it seems that the murderer will escape justice, either with a physical escape (leaving town) or with a legal loophole that prevents the authorities from arresting or charging the murder.
Perhaps evidence that would prove the murderer's guilt is destroyed.
Perhaps a witness dies.
How could this "worst thing" play into the Protagonist's external and internal goals?
Perhaps the low point helps them reassess their goals/desire, possibly making a shift to a new goal/desires.
Or perhaps the low point lets them see that they are on the right track and makes them more determined than ever to carry on.
Breakdown:
Act 4 makes up the final 20% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 3: Proactive

The stakes rise for the Protagonist and the Antagonist. Often there's been a second murder, and the Protagonist realizes the killer must be caught so that the community can feel safe again. The Antagonist is more determined to make sure they aren't caught. Now, the Protagonist is
Proactive
and fully invested in catching the killer.
What changed so that the Protagonist is now fully invested in catching the killer? Some possibilities:
Protagonist was threatened/nearly killed.
Someone close to the Protagonist was the second victim.
Threat of more violence unless the killer is caught.
Someone close to the Protagonist is arrested for the crimes.
How does the Antagonist up their game in this act? Some possibilities:
Threatens the Protagonist.
Tries to kill the Protagonist.
Tries to get the Protagonist arrested for the crimes.
Plants more false clues.
Pressures to get the investigation closed.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up approximately 20% of the story from 60% to 80%.

cards.title: Reason to Investigate / Death Wasn't Random

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Early Act 2: Reactive
In Act 2, you need to establish two important factors:
Your sleuth's reason for investigating.
The fact that the crime wasn't random.
First, unlike a police detective who is assigned a case and sets off to investigate it, the sleuth needs a
compelling reason to get involved in the search for the killer. Some reasons might be:
They discovered the body and are a suspect.
A friend/family member is a suspect, and the Protagonist wants to help them clear their name
The investigator/investigating agency is incompetent, and the crime will never be solved unless they get involved

Second, cozy mystery readers want a whodunit puzzle they can solve. They don't want the crime to be committed by a random madman. No one likes to think that murder could happen in their community, so the initial reaction to the death may be that it was random violence or an accident. Establishing that the death was murder and that the crime was intentional helps move the story forward.
What is the Protagonist's reason for investigating?
What draws them into the investigation?
How is it established that the crime wasn't random violence or an accident?
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up approximately 35% of the story from 25% to 60%.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1: Ordinary World
What does your protagonist want?
What is her external goal?*
What is your protagonist's internal goal? Does she have one?
What opposes these goals?
Your protagonist's
external goal
may be straightforward or complex. In
Murder on the Orient Express
, Poirot's original goal is simply to get back to England, but once the murder happens, his goal is to solve the case. Your protagonist's goal might be to get a job or to run a marathon.
An
internal goal

is something deeper and often relates to theme. Some internal goals could be to reconnect with an estranged friend/family member or to right a wrong. Seeing that justice is done is a common internal goal for mysteries.

Some mysteries, in particular from the Golden Age (1920s and 1930s), often have a protagonist without an internal goal other than solving the case, so you're not required to have an internal goal that relates to theme.

Once you've figured out your protagonist's goals, you can layer in roadblocks that will oppose and challenge her. The antagonist will create some opposition, but your protagonist may also create roadblocks that prevent her from reaching her goal. For instance, the antagonist may sabotage the protagonist's relationship with a key suspect or witness, which prevents the protagonist from getting information about the case. Or the protagonist may do something that sabotages the relationship and results in the same situation.
*For a deeper dive on goals, check out Debra Dixon's book Goal, Motivation, Conflict.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.

pl21.name: Fichtean Curve
pl21.description: A classic story structure that begins with a series of crises

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Part 1:

The lessons learned and fallout resulting from Crisis 3 may not seem too severe. It may even appear as though things are beginning to look up a little for the Protagonist. However, they quickly slide into Crisis 4, which leads them directly into the story's Climax.
Display how the Rising Action to this point is changing the Protagonist (e.g. perhaps they are not quite as set in their old ways and are willing to tone down their flaws).
Allow this Crisis to offer a glimmer of hope – each Crisis should produce a slight dip in tension to prevent an exhausting rise in tension.
Then, shred the glimmer of hope and drive the Protagonist into Crisis 4 and to the Climax.
Consider any subplot(s).
Example:

While trying to hide from the human, the squirrel sneaks around the house, lost and trying to find its way to safety. The human, meanwhile, is running through the house trying to find the squirrel, getting more and more upset. The squirrel finally makes its way through the house and finds the back door. It only needs to make it across the living room and through the kitchen. It begins to run across the open space of the living room when, too late, it sees a cat in the corner.
Breakdown:
Part 1 makes up approximately the first 65% of the story.
Crisis 4 should occur around approximately the 45% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Part 1:
The fallout from Crisis 2 may not be as severe as the fallout from the first, but things continue to worsen for the Protagonist as they are thrust into another Crisis. Troubles continue to compound.

Continue to make things worse for the Protagonist while raising the stakes and the tension – for example, this could be a difficult state resulting from the fallout of the previous Crisis (e.g. being embarrassed, having to apologize publicly, losing rights or privileges, or other uncomfortable situations).
Include some falling action, lessons learned, character growth, and perhaps include a glimmer of hope.
Keep the subplot(s) in mind and how it continues to interact with the Main Plot and develop the character arc.
Example:

Hearing the commotion, the human runs into the room and grabs the dog to lock it away. The squirrel is given a moment to pause before it tries to head back to the peanuts and the back door. En route, the human comes by and gives chase to the squirrel. Frightened, it runs into another section of the house but away from the danger of the dog.
Breakdown:
Part 1 makes up approximately the first 65% of the story.
Crisis 3 should occur around approximately the 30% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Part 1:
The fallout from Crisis 1 leads directly into Crisis 2. Things continue to worsen for the Protagonist as they move into the story, and the Rising Action continues. Troubles begin to pile up.
Demonstrate how the fallout from the actions in the previous beat impact the Protagonist, including how it affects their character arc.
Show what lesson they learned, if any, and how they try to recover from the previous Crisis.
Continue to include bits of exposition and backstory to fill in the blanks that occurred before Crisis 1.
Remember to consider any subplot(s) and how these scenes further the Protagonist's transformation. How are the Protagonist's reactions connected to their past experiences and inner conflicts?
Example:

Seeing the backdoor left open once again, the squirrel sneaks back into the house, watching for any sign of the human. It runs in with the coast clear, grabs a few peanuts, and brings them back to the nest. It returns for more and pauses to nibble a peanut in the kitchen, where it is suddenly cornered by the family dog. The dog barks furiously and chases the squirrel deeper into the house where it can get safely out of reach.
Breakdown:
Part 1 makes up approximately the first 65% of the story.
Crisis 2 should occur around approximately the 15% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Part 3:

The Falling Action wraps up the remaining storylines, loose ends, and character arcs of all main characters. The fallout from the Climax creates a transformation and change of perspective for the Protagonist, for better or worse. The end of the Falling Action brings about the Resolution, which shows how the Protagonist now interacts in their Ordinary World.
Wrap up any remaining storylines and conflicts.
Demonstrate if / how the Protagonist has transformed and what they have learned.
Show the Protagonist back in their Ordinary World having transformed (or not) and succeeded (or failed) at their task.
Example:

The squirrel plays dead as they are chased into the kitchen. Thinking its prey is dead, the cat drops it and dodges the human. Now, the squirrel makes a break for it and runs out the back door. The human follows after it, grabs a handful of peanuts and throws them on the ground outside. The human calls out, "I don't mind feeding you out here, but stay out of my house. It is too dangerous, and you don't belong there." Then closes the door. The squirrel gathers the nuts and brings them back to its hungry family in the nest.
Breakdown:
Part 3 makes up approximately the final 25% of the story.
Falling Action should occur at approximately the 75% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Part 2:

The Protagonist has made it past the conflicts and complications of the Rising Action, yet now faces a complication that cannot be easily overcome. To succeed, the Protagonist must use what they have learned during the previous crises. If they are able to grow and learn, they will be successful; if they chose to remain mired in their old ways, they will fail or remain stagnant.
Set the Protagonist against a difficult situation that cannot be easily remedied.
Decide if the Protagonist learns from past mistakes or slides back to old ways.
Consider how the Climax will turn the rest of the story and impact the Protagonist's character arc.
Weigh the above points against any existing subplot(s) – this beat of the story has a pivotal impact on the Protagonist's transformations.
Example:

Seeing the cat ready to pounce, the squirrel has to decide whether to keep running, change course, or stop and turn back. The cat pounces and grabs the squirrel by the back of the neck. The human runs into the room and gives chase to the cat before it can harm the squirrel.
Breakdown:
Part 2 makes up approximately 10% of the story from 65% - 75%.
Climax should occur at approximately the 60% - 65% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Part 1:

The story begins in the middle of a Crisis, with several more to come and little to no narrative exposition to start. Typically, Rising Action has three or 4 crises but can contain more if the narrative calls for it. Each Crisis acts as a plot point, working to raise the tension and stakes and offer exposition, backstory, and learning lessons for the Protagonist.
Introduce the Protagonist as they are dealing with a Crisis.
Hint at the Protagonist's internal and external goals and begin setting up their character arcs.
Include context and some backstory.
Any subplot(s) must be interwoven throughout the story, but during the Rising Action, be sure to include the Protagonist's backstory and other elements that impact their character arc.
Example:

A squirrel is inside a kitchen trying to get to a bag of peanuts. A human enters the room, sees the squirrel, and attempts to chase it out of the house, creating tension and drama as the squirrel escapes. The squirrel makes it outside and gets back to its nest and family, but they are still hungry. The squirrel begins working on another plan.
Breakdown:
Part 1 makes up approximately the first 65% of the story.
Crisis 1 should make up approximately the first 15% of the story.

pl26.name: Foolproof Pulp Formula
pl26.description: An outline formula for writing pulp short stories by Nelson Bond

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Fifth 1,000 Words
The fifth section of the story starts with the climax. The entire phase includes the solution, of final explanation, and
denouement

. It begins with violent action, tears along swiftly, leading to a swift, decisive conclusion – and ends happily. In the detective story, here’s where your cop or shamus explains whodunit, why, and how they figured it out. In the western, science, sport or action story, this is where the Hero fights free and, tying up loose ends, explains to their public how they knew just what to do.
Watch your timing here! Pace your final conflict so that the action of it consumes approximately 500 words or more.
Previous action may have been truncated to move the story along – but not this final scene.
Your readers have suffered with the Hero for 4,000 words, so give them a blow-by-blow description of the Last Stand, and let their empathies jump with glee as the Villain flinches, cowers, and dies.
Breakdown:
Fifth 1,000 Words ends on page 21 - 25, the final 20% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Fourth 1,000 Words

Herein, two things happen. The Hero finds, thinks, or fights their way out of the complication. This consumes almost all of the fourth phase. And when we’ve suffered with them, bled them into open country again... up pops the Villain with their deepest, most dastardly plot, unfolded, finally, in all its dire ramifications!
Show the Hero overcoming the complication of the previous section.
At the end of this section, reveal the Villain's most sinister plan yet, which the Hero will need to overcome next.
Breakdown:
Fourth 1,000 Words ends on page 17 - 19, covering from the 60-80% portion of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Third 1,000 Words

In a longer story, this section would be called the midpoint. Here’s where the Hero stubs their toe. Things looked good – now the Villain heaves a monkey wrench into the works! Trouble-with a capital “Boo!” pops up. Technically this is known as a “plot complication,” which is just a literary way of saying it’s a mess. In short, then, this complication is generally something the Hero did not nor could have possibly expected; it may even be a break the Villain did not count on. But it makes a hell of a situation for the Hero.
Genre Examples:
Sports:

The Hero is a flashy player, without whom his team cannot win championship vital to the athletic future of the small college. In phase one, the main problem is set forth. In phase two, the path looks easy – Hero going like house afire. Phase three, complication: vital blocking back breaks leg before the crucial game!
Science Fiction:

The Hero is hastily finishing a spaceship with which to visit Mars; must get special Martian desert weed to stave off dreadful scourge which threatens to destroy Earth. Complication: enemy scientists corner market on beryllium, vitally essential metal for construction of spaceship.
Detective Fiction:

The Detective Hero is hunting Red Jornegan, a gangster, whose fingerprints were found all over a gun that murdered a cop. Tracks Jornegan to hide-out. Complication: Finds Jornegan dead, killer’s gun lying across the room with Jornegan’s fingerprints on it!
Love Story:

The Hero admires a movie idol, wangles an introduction, succeeds in making him very, very interested. The soft odor of orange blossoms in the distance, and then... complication! Learns his contract has a no wedding clause.
Adventure:

The Hero, a Foreign Legion Lieutenant, is besieged by a mob of howling Bedouins. Must carry news of uprising to post. Remembers cache of ammunition in the desert. Finds it. Complication: Bullets are for a different rifle!
Breakdown:
Third 1,000 Words ends on page 13 - 15, from the 40-60% mark in the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Second 1,000 Words

This is the phase wherein the Hero’s star is in the ascendancy. Things move along with the reasonable assurance of eventual success. Looks like the problem wasn’t so terrible after all. With matters moving smoothly, this section may also be used for brief, telling “flashbacks” (if required), and for strengthening characterizations.
When writing scene changes, bridge time by using a quadruple space between paragraphs.
To quicken the pace and avoid boring the reader, don't reference everything that happens in between scenes.
Save words, save time.
Breakdown:
Second 1,000 words ends on page 9 - 10 moving from the 20% mark to the 40% mark in the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
First 1,000 Words
Get going with a bang! Remember, you’re writing a short story, not
Gone With the Wind.
You can’t waste words, nor will the editor permit you to waste their or the readers’ time. Your first thousand words must tell
who
are to be the central characters of this work-of-art,
when
the story takes place,
where
the scene is set,
what
the problem is, and set the question as to how the Hero expects to take care of it.
Start with something happening to somebody, not with mental maunderings.
Grab the Hero by the neck and shove them smack into a mess of trouble.
Then show who started that trouble and why.
Introduce the other persons involved in the problem, make their opening speeches depict their characters.
As you write, keep an eye on your page numbers.
Remember that this phase of the story must be finished by the middle of page 5.
Breakdown:
First 1,000 Words ends on page 5 or 20% of the way through the story.

pl22.name: Freytag's Pyramid
pl22.description: A classic story structure for writing dramatic plays

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3:

The Denouement wraps up all storylines and character arcs, and presents the Ordinary World from a new perspective. This is a short scene to finalize the story's details and show what life is like in the new normal of the Ordinary World.
Wrap up any remaining storylines and character arcs.
Demonstrate the atmosphere and setting of the new Ordinary World.
Offer readers a final event that neatly ties up the story and overall theme.
Example – Hamlet:
Only Horatio remains alive to tell the truth of Hamlet's death. Fortinbras, King of Norway, arrives to find the Danish Royal Family dead and claims the throne of Denmark.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Denouement occurs around the 95% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 3:

The story's Central Conflict is resolved, and the Protagonist has either succeeded and transformed or failed and remained stagnant. In a tragedy, the catastrophe creates suffering for not only the Protagonist but also those close to them. The Resolution continues the story's themes and leaves the reader with something to think about.
Tie up any remaining loose ends from the Climax and Falling Action.
Conclude the character arcs for all remaining Central Characters.
If a comedy, have the Protagonist achieve their goal.
If a tragedy, have the Protagonist fail and possibly suffer, die, or have their internal conflict remain unresolved.
This is the final payoff for the reader – make it dramatic and memorable.
Example – Hamlet:

The play ends in catastrophe, with nearly all the Central Characters dying and Hamlet's internal struggle incomplete. Queen Gertrude is poisoned accidentally. Laertes and Hamlet are both killed by a poison-tipped rapier, and Hamlet finally kills King Claudius as he is dying.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Resolution occurs around the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2:

The Falling Action explores the aftermath of the Climax and contains a series of events that untangle the main conflict and lead to the Resolution. Events continue to trend in a new direction for the Protagonist as loose ends begin to be tied up. Unexpected incidents add suspense to the final outcome, and the story starts winding down to its conclusion.
Introduce further complications that mirror the new normal of the world after the Climax.
How do the Characters respond to the results of the Climax?
Increase tension and stakes as the story rushes towards the Resolution and final suspense.
Continue to make things worse for the Protagonist, but leave room for a bit of hope.
Example – Hamlet:

Hamlet is sent away. Laertes returns from France to avenge his father's death, and Claudius and Laertes conspire to kill Hamlet. Hamlet returns to Elsinore. Ophelia goes mad and dies when she falls from a willow tree into a brook and drowns.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The Falling Action occurs around the 65% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

The crux of the story and the height of suspense and tension. This is the turning point for the story and Protagonist, and it is important to put full effort into writing this scene. In a tragedy, here is where everything turns and begins to fall apart. In a comedy, things have been difficult for the Protagonist, but they start to improve at this point.
The Protagonist is at full capacity and ready to act – consider how their actions at this juncture will transform the story and their character arc.
Address the Central Conflict and demonstrate the fate of the Protagonist.
Turn the tides on the Protagonist: if they have been succeeding, here they fail; if they have been failing, here they succeed.
Example – Hamlet:

The play has successfully proven to Hamlet that the King is guilty of the murder... and Hamlet actually goes mad. Hamlet wants to kill the King but does not want to do so while the King is in confession and praying. Hamlet accidentally kills Polonius when he mistakes him for King Claudius.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The Climax occurs around the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

Major events lead toward the Climax while increasing the tension and stakes. This section explores the story's conflict and complications while offering the reader key pieces of backstory. The Protagonist's motives are revealed as well as their inner conflict and the central theme of the story. The Protagonist sees things go from bad to worse.
Introduce any Central Characters not yet revealed.
Create several points of conflict and complications as things get worse for the Protagonist.
Create each conflict and complication to lead to the Climax and its aftermath.
Example – Hamlet:

Hamlet pretends to be mad but begins to descend into actual madness. Growing suspicious, King Claudius begins spying on Hamlet, sees him as a threat, and decides he should be sent away; time is running out for Hamlet as the stakes rise. Hamlet presents the Mouse Trap play within a play to gauge the reaction of King Claudius and assess his guilt.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The Rising Action occurs around the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1:
The first point of conflict and the moment that propels the Protagonist into the story. This event begins the Central Conflict of the story and must be one that cannot be resolved on its own.
Tie the Inciting Incident to the basic conflict within the story, hinted at in the Exposition.
Create a strong Inciting Incident that ultimately forces the Protagonist's hand toward taking action.
Ensure the Incident and the Protagonist's reaction to it are intriguing enough to keep the reader's attention and hook them deeper into the story.
Example – Hamlet:

Hamlet meets the Ghost and learns that King Hamlet was, in fact, murdered by his brother Claudius, now on the throne and married to Hamlet's mother. The Ghost of Hamlet's father demands Hamlet seek revenge for his murder. Hamlet is unsure whether the Ghost is trustworthy or a Devil trying to trick him.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Inciting Incident occurs around the 15% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:

The Exposition introduces the Protagonist, Central Characters, and the Ordinary World, and hooks readers into the story. There is no true action in this beat as it sets the scene and allows readers to see how things currently stand. In the end, it sets up the Inciting Incident.
Introduce the Central Characters of the story, creating a Protagonist your readers can connect with and care about.
Introduce the basic conflict of the story – the basic conflict is that which makes the Protagonist unhappy in their Ordinary World.
Establish mood and atmosphere.
Lead to the Inciting Incident.
Example – Hamlet:

Opening of play, the introduction of Hamlet and most Central Characters. The King, Hamlet's father, has been killed. Denmark is under attack from the Norwegian Prince Fortinbras, Hamlet's family is in ruins, and his mother has remarried his uncle Claudius, whom Hamlet dislikes. Prince Hamlet is miserable, and the audience learns, possibly suicidal.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Exposition should take approximately 15% of the story.

pl34.name: Haiku
pl34.description: A template for writing traditional Japanese short form poetry in three lines and 17 syllables.

children.text: A traditional form of Japanese poetry that originated in the 17th century, the Haiku is characterized by its strict syllable count of 17 syllables. Divided into three lines of 5-7-5 syllables, it is known for its focus on nature and the changing seasons, and features a "cutting word" (kireji) that separates or contrasts different parts of the poem.

Typically composed of three lines, a Haiku does not rhyme. The first line, containing 5 syllables, sets the scene or introduces the main subject of the poem. The second line, containing 7 syllables, provides additional details or imagery related to the first line. While the third line contains 5 syllables and concludes the poem, often with a twist or a moment of insight.

A Haiku is a short form of poetry and provides economy of language by providing a lot with few words. Striving to use the fewest words possible to convey the most meaning, Haiku poets often rely on imagery and metaphor to create a sense of depth and complexity.
Fill in each part of this template to successfully complete your haiku.
Example:
Blank page under pen,
Words refusing to flow free,
Sudden spark ink flows.

The first line of a Haiku contains 5 syllables. Use this line to set the scene or introduce the main subject of the poem, establish the context, and provide a sense of the overall tone and atmosphere.
Example:
Blank page before me
Write the first line of your haiku below:

The second line of a Haiku contains 7 syllables. Use this line to provide additional details or imagery related to the first line, expand upon the main subject, and provide a more detailed description of the scene or moment being described.
Example:
Words refusing to flow free,
Write the second line of your haiku below:

The third line of a Haiku contains 5 syllables and concludes the poem. Often with a twist or a moment of insight, this line provides a sense of resolution to the poem, while offering a sense of closure. Use this line to convey a deeper meaning or to provide a moment of reflection for the reader.
Example:
Sudden spark ink flows.
Write the third line of your haiku below:
Write your final poem below:
What is the message your haiku is trying to convey? Is it being successful? Why or why not?
Note your thoughts below:

pl36.name: Hero's Journey Short Story
pl36.description: The classic Hero's Journey plot structure, adapted for short stories

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:
Introduce the Hero and their ordinary world. The Hero has a well-defined need or want, but there is something specific preventing them from acquiring it.
Introduce readers to the Hero, their world, and what they need or want.
Establish the character's flaws and strengths and show their unique personality.
Hint at a problem or disruption to their ordinary world that the Hero faces and must solve.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Ordinary World should take approximately 12% of the story, the first 600 words of a 5,000-word story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1:
Something (perhaps something shocking) happens to break the status quo, revealing the obstacles the Hero must face.
Introduce a significant disruption to the Hero's everyday life that only they can solve.
Show the disruption this event causes in the Hero's world and life.
Hook the reader into the story and show the overall conflict quickly. This is where the central question/theme of the story is established.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The inciting incident occurs around the 10-20% mark, between 500-1,000 words in a 5,000-word story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 3:

The one thing that absolutely can't fail for the plan to work does fail. All hope is lost. It appears the Hero will never be able to solve the problem or defeat their enemy. But wait, all hope is not lost. It's an incredible long shot, but there is a potential way the Hero's plan could work.
Allow the Hero to fail and sit in the moment when all is lost before they glimpse the way forward.
Allow the reader and the Hero to believe there is no way to solve the problem.
Re-confirm the danger and urgency of the mission–this is where the stakes and tension are at their highest.
Create an unexpected turn or twist in the story and surprise the reader.
Make clear how these events lead toward the climax and final confrontation.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story
All is Lost occurs around the 75% mark, or around 3,750 words in a 5,000-word short story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 3:

It is essential that the Hero act immediately. It is now much harder for the Hero to succeed than it was at the mid-point, and the stakes are much higher. Something spectacularly improbable yet plausible happens, and the Hero must execute their plan. Here, they will either triumph over whatever was keeping them from attaining their goal or suffer a final defeat.
Dramatize the final battle. Show how the Hero is victorious or defeated using what they have learned along the way.
Show how the final battle changes the Hero and reveals their strengths and weaknesses and how they have changed.
Reveal any sacrifices the Hero will have to make to achieve their goal.
Ready the Hero to return to the ordinary world.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Final Attack occurs around the 80-85% mark, 4,000-4,250 words in a 5,000-word short story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3:

Have the Hero say goodbye to their allies and return to the ordinary world. Show how the ordinary world has been transformed because of their journey and how the Hero has also changed. The Hero can be successful or not, and they may not willingly return to the ordinary world. If not, provide a good motive for them to reluctantly return, such as being chased back or to care for someone they were forced to leave behind.
Show the Hero's return home and reveal how they are different.
Highlight the Hero's growth, the reasons for the journey, and their new hope (if the story ends well for them).
Show how they have achieved their goal or met their needs and how that has changed the world.
Resolve any story threads and wrap up any loose ends.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Wrap Up occurs around the 95% mark, or 4,750-5,000 words in a 5,000-word story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1:

The Hero might vacillate for a short time while they weigh what accepting the call to adventure will mean for them, but ultimately, the Hero accepts the call and enters a new, strange, and intensely unfamiliar situation/world. The Hero may also be willing but face an obstacle that must be overcome to accept the call to adventure.
Have the Hero hesitate or try to refuse the Call.
Raise the stakes so the Hero cannot refuse.
Include the Hero's emotional response–are they feeling guilty, angry, or annoyed?
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Refusal of the Call occurs around the 25% mark, around 1,250 words into a 5,000-word story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

The Hero enters the new world and tries to attain their goal, to meet the need revealed at the beginning of the story. They fail, perhaps spectacularly or humorously. Even though the Hero failed, they succeed in either gaining an ally or learning new information. This is a place to show that your character will not give up no matter what and continues to grow.
Create doubt in the Hero regarding their ability to succeed.
Have the Hero go through at least one try/fail cycle.
Show how the Hero is learning and growing in the face of failures.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story, from 25% - 75%.
Trial and error occurs around the 25-40% mark, from 1,250-2.000 words mark in a 5,000-word short story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:
The Hero tries to defeat the obstacle that is preventing them from getting what they need.

If the Hero succeeds, then there has to be a twist. The person/thing they thought was the Big Bad or the problem they thought they were facing isn't the real issue. Reveal the true Big Bad or problem.
If the Hero fails, raise the stakes. Perhaps they lose an ally, become injured in battle, or lose an important item/artifact. Reveal the weakness that caused the Hero to lose this battle.
Reveal the real need or want of the Hero and show how the current conflict sets those things against each other.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story, from 25% - 75%.
Midpoint/point of no return occurs around the 40-50% mark, around 2,000-2,500 words in a 5,000-word story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

Our Hero has failed. They try to go back to the status quo but realize that's not possible. This is a good time for reflection or perhaps the Hero reaches rock bottom and is energized to fight their way out of it.
Show the Hero facing their most difficult setback so far and reaching the darkest moment of the story, the dark night of the soul.
Dramatize this moment of change and the Hero's shift in perspective due to this setback.
Hint at how the Hero's perception of the future and the rest of the story is altered by this setback and what will enable them to move forward.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story, from 25% - 75%.
Setback occurs around the 50-70% mark, 2,500-3,500 words in a 5,000-word story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2:

The Hero accepts their fate and trains or otherwise works on removing what is keeping them from reaching their goal. Their weakness is usually internal, but they are getting it under control. Make sure the readers know how the Hero plans to defeat what is preventing them from reaching their goal and solving their problem.
Show the Hero accepting their failure and acquiring what they need to move forward – this can be an object, knowledge, new abilities, or reconciliation.
Indicate how this acceptance and acquisition of new knowledge and training will play a key role in the Hero's plan.
Allow a moment for the Hero to celebrate and perhaps reflect back on all they have been through to get to this point.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Acceptance occurs around the 70% mark, around 3,500 words into a 5,000-word short story.

pl40.name: Heroine's Journey
pl40.description: Gail Carriger's Heroine's Journey focuses on the way in which a male or female protagonist uses networking and connection to achieve goals and overcome conflict. For best use of this template, consider Gail Carriger's The Heroine's Journey book as a companion guide for navigating this template.

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
The Beginning of Act 1:

(Special note: The Heroine's journey can be for both male and female leads. For the sake of ease, we will refer to the protagonist as she/her, but keep in mind that biological gender is completely irrelevant when writing a Heroine's Journey. All references to the masculine and the feminine are also not gender specific as masculine and feminine traits are found in both genders.)
This section introduces the heroine and shows us she believes she exists in a perfect world
. The heroine employs feminine coping strategies like the belief that nothing bad will happen to them, they will be protected by a group, and they can fit in and excel in a masculine role or group.
Show the heroine feeling comfortable with societal norms or...
Feeling she will be able to break out of them easily to create her own path or "journey" while maintaining her current sense of identity.
Reveal your heroine's character and what she believes the world to be or what it could be.
Define your heroine's goals (what she wants), and her motives to achieve those goals.
Hint at the conflict that will drive the story.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.

cards.title: The Illusion of the Perfect World/Heroine's Circumstance

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
The Middle of Act 1:

The Heroine's network and familial ties are disrupted by either betrayal, disillusionment, or the realization that the world is not what she assumed it to be. Whatever the cause of the disruption, it sets the Heroine on her journey.
What disrupts your Heroine?
How does this affect her and her current worldview?
Breakdown:
Act 1 takes up 25% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 1 Continued:

The heroine may initially become hopeless in this beat, but a Heroine is all about connection and networking. Rather than go it alone, your Heroine will naturally gravitate toward help and assistance. However, what she will soon discover is her immediate network and seat of power is not the solution. The disruption event forces decisions upon the Heroine that she would otherwise not willingly take upon herself. The choice to leave her familial ties and close network is an
involuntary
choice forced upon her by circumstance and the necessity to solve the problem, save a family member, or pursue a quest for the greater good.
How or who does she turn to for aid, and in what way (can also be metaphorical)?
Give the heroine a solid motive to embark on the journey, however unwillingly, driven by something greater than herself.
Breakdown:
Act 1 takes up the first 25% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
The End of Act 1:

To move forward, the Heroine must not only give up control, but she must re-evaluate and, in some cases, abandon all of the tools, defenses, and “weapons” (coping mechanisms) she used before. In this beat, she descends into the new world, and it's a world that is often driven by patriarchy and masculine ideals. The descent is thrust upon the Heroine involuntarily, and it moves her away from her seat of power into a world of risk and isolation. This can also be seen as a loss of identity.
Show that the Heroine's connections with the "perfect world" have been severed, and reveal her feelings of abandonment.
Show how your Heroine has experienced a loss of identity.
Show your Heroine experiencing a fear of what is new.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up 25% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
The Beginning of Act 2:

The Heroine faces isolation and risk as she begins her newfound journey, but most of this is very reactive. A loss of her world means a loss of control and adjusting to new circumstances while trying to achieve her quest. The same rules no longer apply. Social norms, beliefs, and even cultural ideas and values are challenged. Her original sense of self, whether right or wrong, is also challenged and left for her to reconcile and either come to terms with or evolve and grow from. This is a series of events with repeated progress and retreat (try/fail cycle).
Those around the Heroine do not want to be led by a woman/minority for very long, no matter how hard she tries to fit in.
Show masculine forces who may be jealous of her success working to undermine her efforts.
Show the Heroine floundering in her environment. Reveal how she feels lost, isolated, and without any allies, and as a result, she is unsure of what to do next.
This isolation creates moments of despair, and we see the loss of strength and confidence when her network is taken from her.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 25-50% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 3 Continued:

There is a moment in your Heroine's journey where it seems forces and events will be too much to overcome. The odds are stacked against the Heroine and the family created. In this beat, despite her best efforts, she fails and is forced to accept defeat. While the Heroine has conquered one crisis, she comes to the realization that she cannot maintain the status quo as is. Perhaps things were not actually right or good as they had been before. Perhaps more is required to achieve the ultimate goal.

Have your Heroine realize that she has achieved what she set out to achieve, but this new "accomplishment" is not what she needed nor what she expected. It does not allow her to be true to who she is or assist others as she had thought.
How does this once again isolate her?
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up 50-75% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
The Middle of Act 2:

In this beat, the Heroine shows a desire to return to the world as it was before, but she doesn't see a clear path for doing so. Then she meets someone (who may also be a spirit/goddess/muse within rather than an actual "person") who offers support.
Show your heroine getting back in touch with, and embracing, the “feminine” aspect of who she is.
Reveal her acceptance of the following:
She is not completely self-sufficient.
She actually needs help.
Show the Heroine reclaiming the best of her initial values, skills, or attributes but seeing these traits differently, not as weaknesses but as positives.
Give the Heroine a moment of reflection, peace, and an opportunity to reset.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 25-50% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 4:

This is a moment of reconciliation after the major crisis and conflict have finally been overcome. This is often a return to reconnection and the Heroine is able to assist others in coming to terms with themselves and the world around them as she has.
Show the Heroine making peace with the “masculine” approach to the world and gaining a better understanding of how it applies to her and what need is filled inside her.
Ensure that your Heroine recognizes that while the masculine was not her true goal, it was an important part of her journey.
Breakdown:
Act 4 makes up 75-100% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
The End of Act 4:
In this beat, the Heroine returns to the original world, but changed.
Show the Heroine returning to the original world, understanding it is not perfect but that she can make it better by sharing her journey with others.
Reveal the Heroine's spiritual and internal reward. Show how the Heroine now sees the world for what it is, and the new strategies for living that have come from that understanding.
Breakdown:
Act 4 makes up 75-100% of the story.

cards.title: Seeing the World Through New Eyes

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 2 Continued:

Your Heroine will begin to form connections throughout her journey. We see a pattern as to when she is most vulnerable and weak (isolation) and when she is most strong and powerful (forming new connections and networking). It doesn't mean she has all the answers, but her journey is about saving others which also saves herself. It stands to reason that as a Heroine, she can't go it alone, and finds herself powerless if she does so. Our Heroine isn't out of the woods yet, though. Her flawed belief system can be a hindrance when attempting to achieve goals.
How do her attempts at solving her problems fail? Showcase that when she is alone she is not nearly so powerful as when she forms connections.
We're still operating under some flawed beliefs. Highlight those and watch all attempts at resolution crumble.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 25-50% of the story.

cards.title: Withdrawal: A Visit to the Underworld

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 2 Continued:

A main theme for the Heroine's journey is that of withdrawal and consequences that follow. Your Heroine's descent into a different world is similar to a metaphorical descent into the underworld. It can be one of the ways our Heroine may withdraw after a particularly nasty fail at achieving her goal. Remember that isolation and separation from familial connections and networks only weaken your Heroine. Her withdrawal and desire to simply have things the way they once were is a painful yet necessary step, as is her desire to continually attempt to rebuild networks and community.
How does your Heroine withdraw after failing to achieve her goal?
How does she attempt to rebuild community and reconnect with loved ones?
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 25-50% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
The Beginning of Act 3:

The Heroine begins her ascent toward reconnection and achieving her goals by pursuing a second family and a constant network of people to assist her. Demonstrate her as a civilizing force throughout this beat and the rest of the beats in your story.
Show your Heroine getting back in touch with, and embracing, connection.
How does your Heroine negotiate for reunification and compromise to achieve the results necessary?
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up 50-75% of the story.

cards.title: Reconnection and Renewal of Community and Family

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 3 Continued:

Your Heroine still has a network to rely on and mentors from the past to assist as well. As we near the end this section, it is time for our Heroine to rally with the support of friends, family, and with those she has been able to build community.
Show the Heroine realizing that her original coping strategies will not work in this new role.
Allow her to realize that what worked before won't work now.  It's time to rely on her network and approach the solution in a different way.
Have the Heroine's family and network begin to function as a team to change the status quo and achieve what everyone needs regardless of what was originally wanted.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up 50-75% of the story.

cards.title: Ascent to Power or Something More?

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 4:

This is a defining moment for the Heroine as to how she will move forward. Does she ascend to her previous position wiser and more prepared? Does she change her own role or seat of power for a different seat of power? Where does this resolution leave our Heroine?
Show the heroine making peace with herself, her circumstances, and the world and gaining a better understanding of how it applies to her and what need is filled inside her.
Where does she go from here?
Breakdown:
Act 4 makes up 75-100% of the story.

cards.title: The Power of Connection in Action

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3:
Show how this network assists the Heroine to achieve the story goal. How do they begin to work together to battle this last and greatest obstacle facing them?
Have the Heroine's family and network begin to function as a team to change the status quo and achieve the true goal.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up 50-75% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 4:

The Heroine and her team are now unified and will thwart their enemy. This is a time of strategy and togetherness as well as eventual resolution and compromise. The Heroine has to give a little to get a little to achieve the main goal. How is the main conflict resolved?
Show how the Heroine and her team stand together in this final battle and eventually achieve their goal.
Show how certain compromises must be made to solve the main conflict and achieve the main goal.
Breakdown:
Act 4 makes up 75-100% of the story.

pl10.name: Hero's Journey
pl10.description: Based on the classic story structure by Joseph Campbell and Christopher Vogler

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:

This section introduces the reader to the Hero and their normal, everyday life – as well as something that will soon come to disrupt it, thrusting them into the Journey. This is the hook that makes the reader care about your character and compels them forward.
Introduce readers to the Hero and their world.
Establish a three-dimensional character with flaws, desires, problems, and a unique personality.
Showcase the Hero's comfort with their everyday life and activities.
Hint at something that displeases them about their life/world (e.g. a problem or a dramatic event/question that bothers the Hero and must be solved).
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Ordinary World should take approximately 12% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1:

In this section, the Hero is driven out of their everyday life and into the adventure. Some Heroes may be hesitant and require more than one Call of Adventure to raise the stakes and convince them to respond, while others are willing to answer the Call and need only an opportunity. The Call introduces a challenge, mission, or quest that must be conquered before the Hero can return to the Ordinary World; these are the inciting incident(s) that hooks the reader and set the scene for the rest of the book.
Introduce a tangible disruption to the Hero's everyday life (e.g. discovery of new knowledge, being sent on a mission, a threat to a family member).
Show how this incident makes the Hero's world uncomfortable.
To consider: is the disruption interesting enough to hook the reader into the story?
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Call of Adventure occurs around the 12% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1:

A willing Hero may skip this step and take up the Call to Action immediately. However, most Heroes need a little convincing; after all, it is dangerous, and the challenge or quest often comes at great personal risk. Some challenges are so threatening the Hero has no choice but to accept quickly, while other challenges may need to gradually build to become dire enough to pressure the Hero into action. Ultimately, the Hero is left with no choice but to agree to the challenge.
Have the Hero hesitate or try to refuse the Call (e.g. they may say it is too dangerous, they feel too old, they don't believe it, etc.)
More than one Call may be necessary to pressure the Hero.
Raise the stakes after each refusal.
Include the Hero's emotional response to the refusal – are they feeling guilty, angry, annoyed? This helps show their motivations and builds their character.
Force the Hero's hand with an inciting incident which can no longer be ignored.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Refusal of the Call occurs around the 15% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1:

This is the introduction to the person or item which gives the Hero the confidence and tools to succeed. The Mentor must work with the Hero to overcome their previous objections, which often takes the form of a (not so) gentle nudge. The Mentor, for example, can be someone with the wisdom and experience to guide the Hero, someone with technical expertise who can provide tools and specialized equipment, or someone who can train the Hero to ready them physically and mentally.
Identify the knowledge, tools, training, or other forms of support provided by the Mentor.
Show the Hero gaining confidence due to the Mentor's help in procuring a magical item, a particular item or equipment, or new knowledge, etc.
Show how the Mentor works with Hero to help change their perspective, carrying the Hero into the story and taking up the Call.
Create an awe-inspiring moment (e.g. showcase an amazing discovery, magic, or superhuman abilities).
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Meeting the Mentor occurs around the 20% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1:

The Hero has gained (or almost gained) all the knowledge, confidence, and tools needed to begin the journey. However, their training and work with the Mentor may be cut short due to the Antagonist's actions or another external force which pressures the Hero out of the Ordinary World and into the Unknown World. This is the first point of no return, which tests the Hero and has them officially commit to the challenge before them. Often this is an abrupt moment with high stakes and tension.
