What external or internal forces push the Hero into the journey? Consider killing the Mentor, having a critical item stolen, or destroy a part of the Hero's world (e.g. a kidnapping or an explosion).
Show the Hero leaving the comfort of their world and setting out to face the task before them.
Re-establish the central issue or Hero's task.

Ensure the Hero's character is well developed and that they respond appropriately to the challenge before them (e.g. a previously timid Hero will not suddenly transform into a brash Hero; the reader must see the growth over the course of the story).
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Crossing the First Threshold occurs around the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

The Hero's first step into the Unknown World produces a series of challenges which quickly tests their new abilities. While the Hero has new tools and confidence, they have not yet learned how to harness them. The dangers and enemies of this new world overwhelm the Hero, leaving them in need of the assistance of Allies. By the end of this section, the reader may doubt if the Hero can succeed.
Introduce enemies and harsh challenges to showcase how dangerous this new world is.
Give the Hero reason(s) to doubt their abilities.
Introduce Allies to support and strengthen the Hero (e.g. a partner, a group, or a newly forged team who face multiple challenges with the Hero).
Test the Hero and their Allies to show how they function together.
Not all Allies may survive past this section.
Not all Allies may remain loyal, and not all Enemies may remain foes.
Note:
This is an opportunity to add more characters to the story.
Plan the character development of the supporting characters to ensure they are strong as well. What are their goals, motivations, and strategies? They may not always align with the Hero.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Test, Allies, Enemies occurs around the 30% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

The Hero and (most) Allies have survived the previous Tests and journey into the Unknown World and can pause for a moment. If they have been hit by setbacks during the Tests, this is an opportunity for them to regroup and create their plan for the final confrontation by gathering tools, preparing plans, or cutting down the enemy's ranks. It may also be a good place for a morale booster or a visit from the Mentor to reconfirm the Hero's faith in their abilities. By the end of this section, the Hero should be entirely separated from the Ordinary World and have survived an event that reconfirms their commitment to the quest.
Allow the Hero to pause after surviving their introduction to the new world.
Demonstrate that the Hero and their band are on the way to their final goal (e.g. have them gather needed supplies and intelligence).
Highlight them creating a plan but encountering hardships along the way.
Show that the Hero is prepared and ready to face the Antagonist.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Approach to the Inmost Cave occurs around the 40% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

Once the Hero has entered the Inmost Cave, they must face their biggest test, which leads them to their darkest moment. The Ordeal is a critical moment and the central conflict in the story. The Hero must draw upon all they have learned and their new skills to be victorious in the face of a dangerous task. Often the Hero faces a large sacrifice, a death, or a significant loss which breaks them down to their lowest. The Hero must transition through a form of death and rebirth, transforming into a stronger, more powerful version of themselves. If the Hero is successful, this rebirth grants them the strength to defeat the Antagonist and new insights which alter their perception for the rest of the story, giving them the strength to fulfill their duties. If the Hero fails, the Journey's success is thrown into question, while the tension and the stakes heighten.
Show the Hero facing their biggest test so far (e.g. a confrontation with the Antagonist or their forces),  leading to their darkest moment.

Dramatize the darkest moment: a painful sacrifice, the death of a Mentor or Ally, the Hero's death, the loss of an important artifact, or knowledge that shakes the Hero's faith in themselves and their world.
Highlight the emotional, mental, and/or physical work the Hero must do to rebuild after being broken down to their lowest so that they can be "reborn" to face the Antagonist.
Show the Hero transformed into a stronger, more powerful version of themselves, with renewed confidence in their abilities.
Hint at how the Hero's perception for the rest of the story is altered by these events (e.g. a death drives them toward the final confrontation, or new knowledge inspires new determination).
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The Ordeal occurs around the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2:

The Hero has been broken down by the Ordeal, but they have survived, meaning the Reward is at hand. The Reward is the item or knowledge the Hero has been fighting for all along the Journey. It is the key to the Hero's ultimate success against the Antagonist, and finally obtaining it is a moment of celebration. Give the Hero (and reader) a moment to stop, celebrate, and catch their breath.
The story has not yet reached its climax, and this moment allows an emotional reset for all involved. However the Hero receives the Reward, it is a victory in the face of sacrifice – and
propels the Hero on to the climax of the story.
Show the Hero acquiring their Reward after facing the Ordeal – this can be an object, knowledge, new abilities, or reconciliation.
The Reward may be rightfully claimed, given, or stolen depending on the circumstances.
Indicate how this Reward will aid the Hero in the rest of their journey and plays a central role in the Hero's defeat of the Antagonist and their forces.
Allow a moment for the Hero to celebrate and perhaps reflect back on all they have been through to get to this point.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Reward (Seizing the Sword) occurs around the 70% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 3:

The Hero aims to return to the Ordinary World, but must face further dangers and the consequences of obtaining the Reward. The Road Back sees an increase in tension and heightened stakes as the Hero is pursued by danger, understands their mission is not yet complete, or uncovers an even more dire circumstance that must be dealt with before returning home. This moment serves as the catalyst for the Hero to complete their mission and transitions them towards the final battle, forcing them across the threshold to ultimately lead them back to the Ordinary World.
Dramatize the consequences the Hero faces for overcoming The Ordeal and acquiring the Reward (e.g. a pursuing army, the need to reclaim an object from the villain, or a sense of time running out).
Use this section to re-confirm the danger and urgency of the mission – it is also a good time to remind the reader of the central dramatic event/question which started the Hero on their Journey.
The danger faced by the Hero may act as a turning point, creating an unexpected turn in the story.
Make clear how these events compel the Hero to finish the adventure before returning home to the Ordinary World, leading them to the Climax and final confrontation.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Road Back occurs around the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 3:

This is the true climax of the story, the final and most dangerous encounter. This is the definitive and greatest test of the Hero's abilities and all they have learned along the journey. With the stakes heightened during the Road Back, the Hero is now fighting for more than themselves; they are fighting to save others or perhaps the world. With time running out and pressure at its highest, the Hero draws upon their new abilities and finally strikes down the Antagonist, sometimes at great sacrifice. After this battle, they are fully transformed into the role of Hero and can return home.
Dramatize the final battle – show how the Hero uses all they have learned to be victorious.

Demonstrate the Hero's resurrection, as they are transformed into a new, stronger version of themselves (e.g. a physical death and rebirth or a figurative death and rebirth of the mind, changing the Hero's perspective).
The Hero may need to sacrifice their life to save the lives of others and the world.
Prepare the newly transformed Hero to return home again.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Resurrection occurs around the 85% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3:

The Hero returns home a changed person with new strength and confidence, and the Elixir. This is an opportunity to reaffirm the Hero's growth, the reasons for the journey, and offers new hope. The Hero is celebrated by those they left behind in the Ordinary World and are accepted back with newfound respect as a reward for facing terrible dangers and risking it all. The Hero can choose to settle into a life of comfort until the next crisis arises, or they may find home too small, leading to a search for further adventures.
Present the Hero's return home: showcase how they are different from when they were first introduced in the Ordinary World.
Reaffirm the Hero's growth, the reasons for the journey, and their new hope.
Highlight the Hero's new strength and the Elixir, which can be a prize, object, knowledge, or abilities.
Show how the Hero can use the Elixir to help those at home, provide more safety, or offer a new perspective, thereby making the journey and their sacrifices worthwhile.
Decide if the Hero chooses to settle in or if their journey has made their home feel too small, leading them to seek other adventures.
If Part of a Series:
Leave some loose threads and room for further character development for the Hero.
Consider leaving tantalizing unfinished story lines or setting the hook for the next book.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Return with the Elixir occurs around the 95% mark.

pl20.name: Horror Beat Sheet
pl20.description: A beat sheet for horror novels and films by T.L. Bodine

cards.title: Evil Cannot Be Conquered, Only Delayed

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3: The Prestige

There is often a final scare or glimpse of the Monster, reminding us that victory in a horror story is only ever temporary. Whether the Hero have won or lost, their ordinary world has changed. Now is the time to showcase the outcome of the story and wrap any final storylines.
If the Hero failed in Beat 13, show the Monster relishing its victory in a changed world. Will the world stay like this, or is there another Hero in the wings?
If the Hero succeeded, show the new world and include a hint that the Monster may yet return.
No matter how good things seem, danger always lurks around the next corner...
Example – Wes Craven's Scream:
This is kept brief in Scream because it’s the first in a franchise – but the final image is a fraction of a second glimpse of our monster Ghostface, giving the monster the final word.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Beat 15 occurs around the 95% mark, concurrent with Beat 14.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Late Act 3: The Prestige

Now that the climax has been reached, the story must show the consequences of the sacrifice or decision the characters made. Did the Hero emerge victoriously, or did they succumb to weakness? Whatever the answer, this is the beat where the consequences are explored.
Show the consequences of whichever choice was made.
If a standalone book/film, wrap the character arcs for the Hero and all remaining characters.
If the Hero is victorious, show how they have transformed.
Example – Wes Craven's Scream:
In Sidney’s case, we keep this brief because it’s the first film in a franchise – we’ll be dealing with these consequences for quite a long time. In a stand-alone movie, this might be longer.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Beat 14 occurs around the 90% - 95% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 3: The Prestige

Faced with the ultimate choice, the Hero either succeeds in defeating their internal conflict and winning against the Monster, or fails and ultimately succumbs to their weakness. Will the Hero make the choice to move forward or slide back to the comfort of their old ways? The higher the stakes, the higher the reward. This is a moment to once more put the reader on the edge of their seat in anticipation of what may happen. The outcome should not be obvious.
This is the climax of the story – make it dramatic and rewarding.
If the Hero succeeds in defeating their internal conflict and overcomes the Monster, show how they use all they have learned along the way to succeed.
If the Hero fails in defeating their internal conflict and succumbs to their weakness, show how/why they chose to slide back and not complete their transformation into a stronger character.
Example – Wes Craven's Scream:
Sidney has to kill her own boyfriend, and come to terms with the realization that she put an innocent man on death row for her mother’s murder.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Beat 13 occurs around the 90% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 3: The Prestige

Victory comes at a cost. Both the internal and external conflict must be confronted together, and their defeat will leave the Hero irrevocably changed. They will need to confront their conflicts and fears to emerge victorious, but the choice may not be as easy as it seems.
While confronting the Monster, the Hero realizes that their internal conflict must be encountered and defeated to overcome it.
This is the hidden cost, which will irrevocably change the Hero.
Example – Wes Craven's Scream:
For Sidney, she now knows now that she was right all along to distrust Billy, and that the internal struggles – her mother’s death, her problems with intimacy – were all his fault, not hers.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Beat 12 occurs around the 85% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Early Act 3: The Prestige
Armed with knowledge, the hero is emboldened to succeed at last. Where previously they had been running for their lives, the Hero now seeks out the Monster.
For the first time, the Hero approaches the Monster, rather than fleeing it.
They intend to enact their new solution to defeat it.
Example – Wes Craven's Scream:
Sidney turns the tables on the killers, using their own methods against them.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Beat 11 occurs around the 80% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 3: The Prestige
Some new piece of information comes to light that makes it clear how to defeat the Monster. This is usually the placement of a big twist.
The Hero gains new information on how to defeat the Monster.
This new information may be delivered by a Mentor or someone they seek out for help, or it may come through soul-searching and observation.
The Hero use their new information and tools to prepare for the next confrontation.
Example – Wes Craven's Scream:

In Sidney’s case, we have the revelation that not only is Billy not dead, but – GASP! – he was the killer all along. Or, well, one of them. The whole scheme comes to light here. And, most shocking of all, we discover that Billy killed Sidney’s mother as well, which ties up all of those internal and external conflicts together into a tidy package with a neat little bow.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Beat 10 occurs around the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2: The Turn

The confrontation has failed, the Monster is on the move, and the Hero is more isolated and in greater danger than ever before. The chase reaches a feverish pitch. The characters (that remain) come to the darkest moment of the story. The reader should feel there is no hope and no way to destroy the Monster.
Hope appears lost – perhaps someone very important has died, or the Hero has tried everything they can think of doing.
The link between the internal conflict and the Monster may become clear to the Hero.
Example – Wes Craven's Scream:

Sidney’s best friend is dead; almost everyone from the party has left; she’s alone with Billy and then – OH NO! – Billy gets stabbed, leaving her to fight off the monster on her own. Every attempt she makes to get help fails as the people she seeks help from are taken out one by one.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Beat 9 occurs around the 65% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2: The Turn

As the second act approaches its close, the Hero attempts to solve their problem, but fails due to not having all of the important information – in other words, the link between the internal and external struggle has not yet become clear to them. This may be a conflict with the Monster itself, or it may be an attempt to reconcile the character’s interior trouble; but either way, this confrontation is doomed because the character isn’t ready yet.
The Main Character attempts to destroy the monster.
They fail at the attempt as they do not yet possess the ability or needed skills/tools to do so.
Example – Wes Craven's Scream:

This is the portion of Scream where Sidney gives in and has sex with Billy in hopes that it might return some sense of “normal” to her life and allow her to move past her mother’s murder. But after they’re finished, Sidney realizes that didn’t fix her problem at all. Things are still weird with Billy, and she doesn’t feel any better.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Beat 8 occurs around the 60% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Early Act 2: The Turn

Beat seven is the longest part – and the heart – of the story, the part where the problems brought up in the first act are teased out and examined. It’s what Blake Snyder would call the “Promise of the Premise,” or what the Hero’s Journey would call “The Road of Trials.” But in a horror movie, it’s the part of the story where the Monster grows increasingly dangerous and comes ever closer to catching hold of the Hero – hence The Chase. It’s also the part of the story where the link between the character’s internal and external struggle begins to become clearer as the character battles against both.
The Monster chases the characters.
The characters lack the skills to fight the Monster.
One or more people may die here.
Example – Wes Craven's Scream:

In Scream, we see Sidney continue to wrestle with the specter of her mother’s murder. Billy has been ruled out as a suspect by the police, but their relationship is still in trouble. And the audience is teased with glimpses of the killer and a few murders to keep things going. Once again, the characters make a decision that puts them on an isolated collision course – in this case, a party invitation that defies the curfew that’s meant to keep everyone safe.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Beat 7 occurs around the 40% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2: The Turn

The moment where the threat becomes evident to the characters involved. This happens about 1/3rd of the way into the story, or at the beginning of the second act. In The Hero’s Journey, this is the “crossing the threshold” moment.
The first death or when the seriously spooky activity begins.
The danger becomes evident and unavoidable.
There's a marked increase in tension.
Example – Wes Craven's Scream:
Sidney gets attacked in her house, an event which also leads her to become suspicions of Billy, putting even more pressure on their strained relationship.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Beat 6 occurs around the 30% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1: The Setup

Whether through a close encounter or just a quick brush, Act 1 ends with the first meeting of the characters and the Monster. The audience of course has seen the Monster in action already – but the fifth beat is about introducing it to the character who, up to this point, has only been struggling with their own inner demons. What’s important about plot point five is that the character doesn’t immediately realize how dangerous the threat really is.
Give the characters their initial contact with the Monster.
Show the characters unaware of the true threat the Monster poses.
Example – Wes Craven's Scream:
Sidney receives a threatening phone call and at first fails to take it seriously, going so far as to attempt to provoke it.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Beat 5 occurs around the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Late Act 1: The Setup

The characters have an opportunity to walk away before crossing the point of no return and fully entering the story. However, they decide to ignore the warning and proceed. This section provides a chance to show the thought process of the characters, build interpersonal tensions, and raise the overall stakes of the story.
Give the characters the opportunity to turn back, but show them choosing not to.
This beat can occur before or after the First Contact with the Monster.
Beats three and four often happen close together or are bundled into a single event.
Example – Wes Craven's Scream:

In this case, after we meet the rest of the important supporting characters – Sidney’s best friend, her insensitive boyfriend, and the weird tag-along friend Randy – we hear a literal warning from the school advising teens not to spend time alone or go out at night until the murderer is found.

But Sidney is on a collision course with the monster anyway. We know that horror relies on isolation, and we’re treated to a long sequence establishing just how alone she is as she returns to an empty house while her father is away on a business trip. She arranges for a friend to come get her, but for a moment, she is totally isolated. We also learn more crucial information about Sidney’s history, namely that her mother was brutally raped and murdered a year ago – an event that starts to make sense of some of her struggles with intimacy in her relationship.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Beat 4 occurs around the 20% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1: The Setup
The characters make a choice that inadvertently isolates them or places them on a collision course with the monster. This is often where they decide to investigate the spooky house or go on a trip.
What choice do the characters make?
How does it lead to their isolation?
How does the decision put them on a collision course with the Monster?
Beats three and four often happen close together or are bundled into a single event.
Example – Wes Craven's Scream:

In this case, after we meet the rest of the important supporting characters – Sidney’s best friend, her insensitive boyfriend, and the weird tag-along friend Randy – we hear a literal warning from the school advising teens not to spend time alone or go out at night until the murderer is found.

But Sidney is on a collision course with the monster anyway. We know that horror relies on isolation, and we’re treated to a long sequence establishing just how alone she is as she returns to an empty house while her father is away on a business trip. She arranges for a friend to come get her, but for a moment, she is totally isolated. We also learn more crucial information about Sidney’s history, namely that her mother was brutally raped and murdered a year ago – an event that starts to make sense of some of her struggles with intimacy in her relationship.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Beat 3 occurs around the 15% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Early Act 1: The Setup

Now that we’ve made our contract with the audience, it’s time to introduce the Main Characters (if we haven’t already met them) and reveal their primary internal conflicts. All monsters are mirror images of the Main Character’s internal conflict.
Introduce the important characters.
Show their primary internal conflict.
Example – Wes Craven's Scream:

We’re introduced to tender young Sidney Prescott, and quickly learn everything we need to know: She lives alone with her father; she has a boyfriend, Billy, who is upset at their lack of sexual intimacy and is bad at respecting boundaries. We don’t know exactly what’s happened yet, but we know from their introduction that something big has happened in Sidney’s recent past and that the baggage is causing trouble in her relationship.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Beat 2 occurs around the 5% mark.

cards.title: The World is Not What it Seems

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1: The Setup

The opening beat is where the audience catches their first glimpse of the monster, or at least an early hint that the monster exists and of where the story will go. This may occur right away – often as a prologue – or after the Main Characters have been introduced. The opening is a promise to the audience, who will now eagerly wait to see that promise fulfilled.
Give the reader an early glimpse of the Monster or a hint that the Monster exists.
Allow the reader to see that the Ordinary World has something sinister just below the surface.
Example – Wes Craven's Scream:
In Scream, we’re introduced to Casey – who, in an iconic 11-minute opening sequence, receives an ominous phone call, discovers the caller is in her house, and is brutally murdered.

This opening sets up everything we need to know about the story’s premise: We know what to expect from the monster, catch a few hints of the darkly comedic tone of the film, and see plenty of blood and guts.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Beat 1 should comprise approximately 5% of the story.

pl23.name: In Media Res
pl23.description: A classic plot structure that begins in the middle of the story

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
End of Act 3:

The story's Central Conflict is resolved, the Antagonist is defeated or driven off, and the Protagonist is newly transformed with a changed perspective. This beat wraps up all the loose ends and character arcs, and returns the Protagonist back to the Ordinary World as a changed person.
Tie up any remaining loose ends from the Climax and Falling Action.
Finish the story arcs of all Main Characters.
Demonstrate the Protagonist's transformation and show how they fit in their new Ordinary World.
Give the reader a dramatic and satisfying resolution.
If part of a series, leave some room for growth for the Protagonist and set the hooks for the next installment.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Resolution occurs around the 90% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Beginning of Act 3:

The Falling Action explores the aftermath of the Climax and its consequences for the Protagonist. If they escaped their dire situation or stole something, they may have enemies chasing after them. If they lost an important item, they might be facing the challenge of recovering it. After the darkest moment, the Protagonist is fully committed to resolving the Central Conflict and defeating the Antagonist. The tension increases as things seem to worsen for the Protagonist, but there is a glimmer of hope.
How has the fallout from the Climax has changed the perspective of the Protagonist?
What drove them to commit fully to the challenge before them?
Continue adding stress and pressure on the Protagonist as they work toward the story's final confrontation.
Offer any final exposition through flashbacks and dialogue.
Demonstrate how the Protagonist is using all they have learned and acquired to resolve the Central Conflict.
Keep the suspense/tension high to ensure the reader stays engaged through the end.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Falling Action occurs around the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
End of Act 2:

In this beat, the story naturally approaches the Climax, brings the reader back to the opening scene, and offers the resolution to the opening scene while leading to the story's Falling Action. The Climax is the turning point of the story and the Protagonist. The fallout from the Climax changes the Protagonist's perspective for the remainder of the story and often leaves them at their darkest moment, where all seems lost.
Bring the reader back to the opening scene and provide an exciting and satisfying solution to the Climax.
Address the story's Central Conflict and demonstrate the fate of the Protagonist.
How does the Climax impact the Protagonist's internal/external goals and overall transformation?
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Climax occurs around the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

The story now enters the Rising Action, where the Protagonist faces challenges and obstacles on their way to the Climax. Each challenge or obstacle leads the Protagonist closer and closer to the dire situation the reader found them in at the beginning of the story. The action, tension, and stakes continue to rise as the Protagonist is put through their paces, and more context is given via Exposition. As with traditional story outlines, the Protagonist will face successes, failures, and setbacks along the way, teaching them and helping them grow.
Create a series of challenges and obstacles for the Protagonist – some will be overcome, while others will make things worse for the Protagonist as they learn and grow from them.
Consider how these steps lead to the Climax.
How do the challenges and obstacles impact the Protagonist's story arc, goals, and motivations?
Tantalize the reader as the tension rises and the story climbs closer to the opening scene.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Rising Action occurs around the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
End of Act 1:

After the attention-grabbing and emotional first scene, the story enters the Exposition. This can be done via flashbacks, dialogue, or time-jumps, but it must be done in a way to keep the tension rising without info dumps. With the reader hooked and curious, the Exposition takes the reader back before the Climax and begins to explain how the Protagonist ended up in such a dire situation. This beat does not have all the Exposition; it is scattered throughout Beats 2, 3, and 4 to maintain interest.
Will you reveal the backstory through flashbacks, dialogue, time-jumps, or a combination?
Give the reader context by showing the Protagonist in their Ordinary World before everything went sideways.
Present the inciting incident and the Protagonist's reaction – did they take up the adventure willingly or not?
Keep raising the tension and the stakes to generate curiosity and a strong emotional connection for the reader.
Don't forget to consider the Protagonist's character arc and how it will transform throughout the story – where did they start, where will they end?
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Exposition occurs around the 5% - 10% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:
In Media Res is Latin for Into the Middle, a story structure that starts in the middle of the action before circling back to the beginning.

Unlike traditional story structures, this one drops the reader into the middle of the story's Climax and offers tantalizing details to hook the reader before returning to the Exposition of the story. As such, it is important to have the beginning, middle, and end of the story planned before attempting this format. The opening scene must be attention-grabbing and provoke curiosity, driving the reader to wonder not only how the story got to this point but how it can be resolved.
Write an amazing first line, something that catches attention and immediatly intrigues.
Do not present the entirety of the Climax, but rather enter a scene in progress and leave before its resolution.
The scene must be pivotal to the story – for example, consider having the Protagonist in a life-or-death situation or doing something unusual like hiding in the wheel hub of an airplane.
Make the reader ask: What's going on here? Who are the characters? Where are we? How did we get here? What will happen next?
Remember, when starting in the middle of the action, the reader has very little context, so it is essential to make the first scene attention-grabbing and full of emotion.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Climax Hook should take approximately 5% - 10% of the story.

pl8.name: Romance Beat Sheet
pl8.description: A beat sheet for romance novels developed by Jami Gold

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1:

An event or a situation brings the Protagonists together and forces them to spend time cooperating to achieve a goal. This event raises the tension and stakes and allows for a clear definition of each of the Protagonist's goals. While still at odds with each other, sparks are starting to fly. In Romance stories, attention must be paid to the External (outside forces that impact the relationship) and Internal Relationship Arcs (beliefs, decisions, and actions of the Protagonists that impact the relationship).
External: What event forces the Protagonists to spend time together? (e.g. snowstorm, disaster cleanup, work project, or competition.)
Internal: What action or choice do the characters make that reflects their desire for each other? (e.g. defending each other, being extra helpful, or thoughtful action.)
Remember, sparks are beginning to fly, but the Protagonists are still in a state of denial.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
End of Beginning should occur at around the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3:

The Protagonists are now together and moving into their happily ever after that readers have been waiting for. They are now fully committed and perfect for each other, with new perspectives in life. (Unless it is a happily ever... for now.)
Show how the Protagonists have changed over the course of the story and how they now interact with each other and their ordinary world. They must be in an opposite state from the beginning.
Allow the Protagonists a moment of enjoyment and celebration – they have earned it.
If part of a series, consider leaving a hook for the next installment.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Resolution should occur at around the 99% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2:

This beat raises the stakes to their highest level yet, bringing a low for the Protagonist(s) and their relationship. An event or betrayal occurs which breaks the bond of trust, and the Protagonist falls back into their fear or false beliefs from before as they see them manifest before them. This often leads to a breakdown of the relationship and gives the reader the impression they will never be together.

External: What event or betrayal triggers the characters' fear about their relationship, forcing them back into their false beliefs? (e.g. one choosing their external goals over their internal, like accepting a job in another city; or one sees the other with an ex-partner; or life interferes in other ways, like a family member planting seeds of doubt.)

Internal: How do the characters realize the relationship is over? This is often a confirmation of doubts or false beliefs. (e.g. they knew the other cannot be trusted, and this event proves it; a Protagonist lets their guard down and the other takes a job in another city; or when faced with a decision, a Protagonist chooses their external goal over their internal goal.)
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Crisis should occur at around the 68% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 3:

Both of the Protagonists are forced to decide if they will succumb to their false beliefs or work through their inner conflicts to save the relationship. They work to fix the internal and external problems and learn the lesson which brings them to their transformation. The central question of will the two Protagonists end up together is finally answered.
External: What inner conflicts continue to threaten the relationship? These are the conflicts that must be addressed and solved.

Internal: How do the Protagonists prove they want to continue in a relationship together? This can be refusing the job, choosing to trust, or having a conversation to clear up misconceptions. Forgiveness is often a theme.
Resolve the conflict of internal and external desires and show how the Protagonists have transformed.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Climax should occur at around the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

Pinch Point 2 introduces another glance at the inner conflict of the Protagonists. The intimacy and relationship are continuing to grow, but inner struggles and doubts begin to resurface. These are the inner conflicts that must be resolved before the Protagonists can receive love.

Introduce the next Pinch Point (e.g. perhaps one Protagonist does not fully trust the other, feels they cannot have both a career and a relationship, or past relationship traumas create doubt and fear).
How does the Pinch Point affect their relationship?
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Pinch Point 2 should occur at around the 62% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

The tension continues to rise as another new development raises the stakes. This section sets the Protagonists on a false victory or false defeat. In a false victory, it appears as though the Protagonists will commit to each other; a false defeat will give the impression they will never find their way together.

External: What visible sign of commitment do the Protagonists offer? (e.g. one or both could profess their love, they could surrender to the idea that it is true love, or they may have their first intimate moment.)

Internal: How are the Protagonists doomed to fail due to internal struggles or dedication to their goals? (e.g. one Protagonist may refuse the profession of love, may recommit to their external goals, or back away due to inner conflict like feeling unworthy/unprepared for love.)
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Midpoint should occur at around the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

The Protagonists are starting to admit to their feelings for each other and may even begin considering a relationship. Enter Pinch Point 1: the reader is granted a first glimpse at the opposition or conflict between the Protagonist's inner and outer conflict. Each Protagonist is still working toward their own goals, but the growing relationship begins to create conflict, raising the tension.

What events occur in Pinch Point 1? The Protagonists may share a kiss, an intimate moment, a fun moment, or have feelings grow due to watching the other be selfless, trustworthy, or capable of achieving a goal.
How does the Pinch Point affect their relationship?
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Pinch Point 1 should occur at around the 37% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1:

Through external forces, chance, or a life event, the Protagonists meet for the first time. Occasionally there will be an instant attraction, in which case there should be an obstacle preventing them from being together; however, typically there is instant dislike, and one or both Protagonists refuse the relationship. Readers should be able to glimpse the Protagonists could be romantically right for each other... in time.
Pick an Inciting Incident that brings the Protagonists together (e.g. a vacation, new job, family introduction, or a stressful moment like severe weather or natural disaster).
Create conflict between the Protagonists (e.g. different life perspectives, different values, personality clashes, or an external obstacle like a disapproving family).
Demonstrate how right the Protagonists could be right for each other and why/how they are not ready.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Inciting Incident should occur at around the 15% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:
The Hook introduces the protagonists, grabs the reader's attention and draws them into the story, while setting up the romance conflict.
Introduce the Protagonist(s) by showing them in their everyday life and offer a glimpse at the internal struggle that is holding them back from love.
Create empathy for the Protagonist(s) – demonstrate their desires, flaws, positive traits, and something they lack.

Foreshadow the coming conflict that will challenge any potential romance with a collision between external goal and internal goal (e.g. the Protagonist is succeeding in their career and is expecting an upcoming promotion that may take up all of their time).
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Hook should occur around the 10% mark.

pl37.name: Larry Brooks Short Story
pl37.description: Based on ideas by Larry Brooks, adapted for short stories

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Setup:
This section sets up the short story by introducing the main character, their world, the situation they are in, and/or the problem they face.
Introduce readers to the main character and an interesting world.
Introduce a problem that disrupts their ordinary world, which the main character must solve.
Give the main character a clear goal that will allow them to solve the problem and a clear motive that drives them toward that solution.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The setup should take approximately 15% of the story, or 750 words, into a 5,000-word story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Shift:
This section reveals how the problem and the goal related to it cause a shift in the main character's world.
Show the character's emotional shift and reaction to the problem.
Reveal how the problem has made them uncomfortable and why they are the ones to solve it.
Show the main character preparing to take action to pursue their goal and solve the problem.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The first shift occurs around the 15-25% mark, from 750-1,250 words in a 5,000-word story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Response:
This beat is where the hero takes action. We've seen their goals and motivation, and now we see the character moving toward the conflict.
Show the character physically taking action and responding directly to the problem they face.
Show the character moving out of their comfort zone and into a new world or situation.
Show the conflict, tension, and stakes increase as a result of the character's response.
Use this section to further develop the character and reveal their strengths and weaknesses.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up the first 50% of the story.
The Response occurs around the 25-35% mark, from 1,250-1,750 words in a 5,000-word story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

The midpoint is the second shift or plot point. If things have been going well for the main character, here they take a turn for the worse. If they have been going poorly, the main character may experience a false victory here.
Show the shift for better or worse for the main character and reveal how it changes their perspective.
Allow your main character to learn a lesson from their response in the previous beat and this shift.
Reveal the character's new approach to their goal and the solution to the problem.
Restate the character's motive and show how it has changed from the initial shift to this one.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story, from 25% - 75%.
Shift (Midpoint) occurs around the 45-55% mark, from 2,250 to 2,750 words in a 5,000-word story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Attack:
The hero now turns to attack the problem with their new knowledge and a fresh approach.
Show the main character renew their attack on the problem and show them facing it in a new way.
Raise the stakes and the danger. This is the most difficult challenge the main character has faced thus far.
Show the main character fail in their attack and reach the darkest moment of the story.
Show the main character in despair, but leave them a glimmer of hope as they move toward the climax of the story.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story, from 25%-75%.
Attack takes up around the 55-75% mark, from 2,750-3,750 words in a 5,000-word story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Third Shift:
After the darkest moment, there is one final shift for the main character, and now they move toward victory, or at least the final resolution.
Show how the main character solves their problem.
Show the final change in the main character's perspective.
Show any sacrifice the main character has to make to achieve their goal and solve the problem.
Show the main character preparing to return to a new normal, whatever that looks like.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Third Shift occurs around the 75-95% mark, from 3,750 to 4,750 words in a 5,000-word story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Resolution:

Show the main character's return to normal, whatever that might look like, depending on the type of story you are trying to tell. The ending can be happy if the main character and their circumstances have changed for the better, or tragic if things have changed for the worse.
Show the changes the character has experienced and show how the outcome of the story has affected them.
Show the resolution of the conflict one way or another.
Wrap up all the elements of the story and resolve any loose ends.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Resolution occurs around the 95% mark, or 4,750 words in a 5,000-word short story.

pl25.name: Lester Dent Master Plot Formula
pl25.description: The classic short story formula for pulp fiction by Lester Dent

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 2: Second 1,500 Words

The tension increases and the stakes continue to rise, as the Hero struggles to deal with the grief piling on them. At this point, minor surprises can keep the reader engaged and add to the mystery. These can take the form of misleading scenes, such as a door across the room suddenly closing. When the Sleuth opens the door, it leads to a closet. But why did the door close? Is there a secret passage in the closet?
Add more grief and stress to the Hero.
Show the Hero struggling to deal with the situation.
Add another physical conflict – try to use a different form of physical conflict than before.
Include a surprise plot twist at the end of this section.
Is there suspense and a growing sense of menace?
Build the plot so there is continuous action that proceeds logically.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up the second 25% of the story.
Second 1,500 Words brings the story to the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 4: Fourth 1,500 Words

The final section of the story, where things reach their lowest point for the Hero before being wrapped up in a neat package. The Hero uses their skills and knowledge to escape a dire situation and defeat the Villain, demonstrating their character transformation. Any remaining mysteries looming over the story are cleared up over the course of the final conflict as the Hero takes hold of the situation – ending with a final twist in the plot, and a snappy punch line.
Create even more difficulties for the Hero.
Have the Hero be practically buried in their troubles (e.g. the Villain has them prisoner, the girl is assumed dead, all seems lost, and the Hero is about to die from a unique murder method).
Add one final surprise twist to the story near the end of this section (e.g. the Villain has a surprise identity or the treasure is worthless).
Wrap up and explain all storylines.
Add a final snappy punchline to conclude the story.
Does the suspense and menace continue to the last line?
Breakdown:
Act 4 makes up the last 25% of the story.
Fourth 1,500 Words brings the story to its conclusion.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 3: Third 1,500 Words

After the situation initially worsens, a glimmer of hope appears – the Hero seems to be getting closer to the solution to the looming menace / mystery. But this turns out to be a false hope, and the tension and stakes rise while the reader is swept along with swift, vivid action.
Add more grief and stress onto the Hero.
Let the Hero make some headway, perhaps cornering the Villain.
Add another physical conflict different from before.
Include a surprise twist which makes things much worse for the Hero, to end this section.
Does this section maintain suspense, deepen the menace, and place the Hero in a tough spot – while happening logically?
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the third 25% of the story.
Third 1,500 Words brings the story to the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 1: First 1,500 Words

The story begins with the Hero in a heap of trouble, and proceeds to get worse from there. Regardless of genre, a pulp story must have physical conflict and plot twists, suspense, and a genuine sense of menace.
Introduce the Hero as early as possible and stick them in a very difficult situation – hint at the mystery, menace, or problem they will have to solve around the first line.
Show the Hero jumping into action to attempt to grasp the mystery, defeat the menace, or solve the problem.
Introduce all of the characters and bring them in on the action.
Have the Hero enter into a physical conflict near the end of this section.
Add a surprise twist in the plot at the end.
Does the story have suspense, create menace to the Hero, and proceed logically?
A genuine pulp story should also contain at least one (or more) of the following elements:
A unique murder method for the Villain to use
A unique thing for the Villain to be seeking
A unique location
A unique menace to hang over the Hero
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
First 1,500 Words brings the story to the 25% mark.

pl33.name: Limerick
pl33.description: A template for writing humorous short form poetry in five lines with a strict rhyme scheme.

children.text: A Limerick is a lighthearted and often silly type of poem, created to make people laugh or smile. Characterized by a five-line structure and an AABBA rhyming scheme. The first, second, and fifth lines typically have 8–9 syllables and rhyme with each other, and the third and fourth lines have 5–6 syllables and also rhyme with each other. Limericks are a fun, playful, and often humorous form of poetry that people of all ages have enjoyed for centuries.
Fill in each part of this template to successfully complete your limerick.
Example:
To write a poem is not a feat,
So said the woman on the street.
I wanted to agree,
But she had a degree,
And was writing for people she'd meet.

Use the first line of a Limerick to set the scene or introduce the main subject of the poem. This line sets the stage for the stage for the rest of the poem, while providing the reader with a sense of the overall tone and atmosphere.

Use the second line of a Limerick to expand upon the main subject of the poem and provide a more detailed description of the scene or moment. This line provides additional details or imagery related to the first line while establishing the rhyme scheme.
Each line should have 8–9 syllables.
Example:
To write a poem is not a feat,
So said the woman on the street.
Write lines 1 and 2 of your limerick below:

The third and fourth lines of a Limerick often introduce a new character or event, and provide a twist or unexpected turn in the story. Usually the humor and wordplay of the Limerick come into play, and these lines are often the most memorable parts of the poem.
Each line should have 5–6 syllables.
Example:
I wanted to agree,
But she had a degree,
Write lines 3 and 4 of your limerick below:

Use the fifth line of the Limerick to conclude the poem. This line often brings the story full circle, resolves any conflicts or surprises introduced in the previous lines, and provides a sense of closure to the poem while completing the rhyme scheme.
This line should have 8–9 syllables.
Example:
And was writing for people she'd meet.
Write line 5 of your limerick below:
Write your final poem below:
What is the message or humor your limerick is trying to convey? Is it successful? Why or why not?
Note your thoughts below:

pl27.name: Propp Folktale Structure
pl27.description: A story structure for folktales  based on the teachings of Vladimir Propp

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Hero's Return
The Hero accomplishes a difficult task.
What makes the task difficult?
How does the Hero accomplish the task?
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Hero's Return
The Hero marries and is rewarded or promoted by the family or community, typically ascending to a throne.
What is the Hero's reward?
How does the reward help to reinforce the Hero's transformation?
What is the Hero's new status?
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Hero's Return
The Villain suffers the consequences of their actions, perhaps at the hands of the Hero, the avenged victims, or as a direct result of their own ploy.
Who punishes the Villain?
What form does the punishment take? (e.g. banishment, death, jail, or other)
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Hero's Return

The Hero gains a new appearance. This may reflect aging and/or the benefits of labour and health, or it may constitute a magical remembering after a limb or digit was lost (as a part of the branding or from failing a trial). Regardless, it serves to improve their looks.
How is the Hero transformed?
Does the Hero regain something lost, or is it a result of their work?
Is it a physical transformation or a transformation of life, like granted nobility and an easier life?
Is the transformation natural or provided via magical means?
Examples:
Cinderella is transformed into a member of the nobility.
In The Frog Prince, the frog is transformed into a handsome prince.
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Hero's Return
The False Hero and/or Villain is exposed to all and sundry.
How is the False Hero exposed? Is it self-revelation, or is it at the hand of the Hero or others?
What is the reaction of the False Hero being exposed?
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Hero's Return
The Hero is given due recognition – usually by means of their prior branding.
How does their branding relate to their being recognized?
What form does the public recognition take?
Who recognizes the Hero?
Examples:
Snow White gets to marry a prince.
In Puss in Boots, the cat is awarded the ogre's castle.
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Hero's Return
A trial is proposed to the Hero – riddles, test of strength or endurance, acrobatics and other ordeals.
What is the proposed task?
Is there more than one task?
How will this task prove the Hero is who they are?
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Hero's Return

A False Hero presents unfounded claims or performs some other form of deceit. This may be the Villain, one of the Villain's underlings or an unrelated party. It may even be some form of future donor for the Hero, once they've faced their actions.
Who is the False Hero?
What claims do they make?
How do they attempt to deceive people into believing they are the Hero?
Examples:
Cinderella's stepsisters pretend to be her when the Prince comes calling.
In The Golden Bird, the older brothers try to kill their younger brother and steal his prizes.
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Hero's Return
The Hero arrives, whether in a location along their journey or in their destination, and is unrecognized or unacknowledged.
Where does the Hero arrive?
Why are they unrecognized?
Are they forced into hiding?
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Hero's Return

The Hero is saved from a chase. Something may act as an obstacle to delay the pursuer, or the Hero may find or be shown a way to hide, up to and including transformation unrecognizably. The Hero's life may be saved by another.
Who or what interferes with the chase?
Is the Hero saved by another?
Is magic used to assist the Hero or something physical, like a well-timed rock slide?
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Hero's Return
The Hero is pursued by some threatening adversary, who perhaps seeks to capture or eat them.
What adversary is chasing the Hero?
What is the threat to the Hero?
How does the Hero attempt to elude the new danger?
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Hero's Return
The Hero travels back to their home.
How does the Hero travel back home?
How long is the journey expected to take?
Examples:
Hansel and Gretel return home to their lamenting father.
Odysseus heads home to Ithaca.
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Donor Sequence
The earlier misfortunes or issues of the story are resolved; the objects of search are distributed, spells broken, captives freed.
How is the earlier misfortune resolved?
What steps are required after the resolution? (e.g. returning stolen items, dispensing food, sharing new abilities)
Examples:
The witch burns in the oven and Gretel frees her brother, and they find a vase of treasures.
Grandmother and Little Red Riding Hood are freed after the woodcutter kills the wolf.
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Donor Sequence
The Villain is defeated by the Hero – killed in combat, outperformed in a contest, struck when vulnerable, banished, and so on.
How does the Hero kill the Villain?
How has the Hero used what they learned, were granted, or found, to succeed?
Is the Villain killed, banished, or simply the clear loser of a contest?
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Donor Sequence
The Hero is marked in some manner, perhaps receiving a distinctive scar or granted a cosmetic item like a ring or scarf.
What brand is bestowed upon the Hero?
Does the brand tie into the story? (e.g. it was foretold the chosen one would have this scar.)
Does the brand grant greater power, or is it symbolic?
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Donor Sequence
The Hero and Villain meet and engage in conflict directly, either in battle or some nature of contest.
In what type of conflict do the Hero and Villain face off?
How close to death does the Hero come?
Is the brush with death physical or literal?
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Donor Sequence

The Hero is transferred, delivered or somehow led to a vital location, perhaps related to one of the above functions such as the home of the donor or the location of the magical agent or its parts, or to the Villain.
Where is the Hero transferred?
How is the Hero transferred?
How does the location relate to the story?
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Donor Sequence

The Hero acquires the use of a magical agent as a consequence of their good actions. This may be a directly acquired item, something located after navigating a tough environment, a good purchased or bartered with a hard-earned resource or fashioned from parts and ingredients prepared by the Hero, spontaneously summoned from another world, a magical food that is consumed, or even the earned loyalty and aid of another.
What is the magical agent acquired by the Hero?
How is the magical agent acquired? (e.g. found, offered, magically brought forth, or stolen.)
How will it aid them in their journey?
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Donor Sequence

The Hero responds to the actions of their future donor, perhaps withstanding the rigours of a test and/or failing in some manner, freeing a captive, reconciles disputing parties or otherwise performing good services. This may also be the first time the Hero comes to understand the Villain's skills and powers, and uses them for good.
How does the Hero react?
How does the Hero come to understand the Villain's true powers?
What tests does the Hero pass / which do they fail?
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Donor Sequence
The Hero encounters a magical agent or helper (donor) on their path, and is tested in some manner through interrogation, combat, puzzles or more.
What form does the magical agent take? (e.g. talking animal, magical item, fairy godmother, or wizard.)
How does the Hero find the magical agent?
How is the Hero tested?
What are the rewards for success and the punishments for failure?
What is being offered to the Hero as the final reward?
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 2: Story Body
The Hero leaves the home environment, this time with a sense of purpose. Here begins their adventure.
How has the Hero prepared themselves for the adventure?
Where are they heading?
How will their plan unfold en route or once they arrive?
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 2: Story Body

The Hero considers ways to resolve the issues by seeking a needed magical item, rescuing those who are captured or otherwise thwarting the Villain. This is a defining moment for the Hero, one that shapes their further actions and marks the point when they begin to fit their noble mantle.
How does the Hero create their plan to counter the Villain?
What do they need to seek or rescue?
How does the plan attempt to thwart the Villain?
Examples:
In Hansel and Gretel, Hansel offers the witch a thin bone in place of his finger.
In The Miraculous Hen, the children offer the cook gold to not kill them and cook them for dinner.
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 2: Story Body
One or more of the negative factors covered previously comes to the attention of the Hero, who uncovers the deceit/perceives the lacking/learns of the villainous acts that have transpired.
What is the request or command given to the Hero?
Do they leave on their own accord, or are they commanded to go?
Is the Hero a Seeker (going to save a damsel) or a Victim-Hero (a victim that becomes Hero)?
Has the Hero been assisted in escape by anyone?
Examples:
The children are sent into the woods in Hansel and Gretel.
Little Red Riding Hood learns the fate of her Grandmother.
The children learn they are to be eaten in The Miraculous Hen.
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 2: Story Body

The Villain harms a family member, including but not limited to abduction, theft, spoiling crops, plundering, banishment or expulsion of one or more Protagonists, murder, threatening a forced marriage, inflicting nightly torments and so on. Simultaneously or alternatively, a Protagonist finds they desire or require something lacking from the home environment (potion, artifact, etc.). The Villain may still be indirectly involved, perhaps fooling the family member into believing they need such an item.
Which family member has been harmed?
How has the family member been harmed?
What does the Protagonist find they require?
Where does the Protagonist need to go to acquire it?
Examples:
The Wolf hides the Grandmother in Little Red Riding Hood and then dresses as her to fool Red when she arrives.
In King Bear, the dragon kidnaps the Tsar's daughter.
In The Miraculous Hen, the gem-laying hen is ordered killed.
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Introduction

The victim is fooled or forced to concede and unwittingly or unwillingly helps the Villain, who is now free to access somewhere previously off-limits, like the privacy of the Hero's home or a treasure vault, acting without restraint in their ploy.
How did the method of deception work?
What did the Villain gain access to?
How has the Protagonist become mechanical at this point? (e.g. sleeping, in a trance, locked away, poisoned, etc.)
Examples:
The witch gives Snow White a poisoned apple.
While Little Red Riding Hood looks for flowers, the Wolf sneaks to her grandmother's house and pretends to be her.
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Introduction

The Villain attempts to deceive the victim to acquire something valuable. They press further, aiming to con the Hero and earn their trust. Sometimes the Villain makes little or no deception and instead ransoms one valuable thing for another.
What form of trickery does the Villain use? (e.g. disguises, transmogrification, charm, or manipulation.)
What is the Villain trying to take from the victim?
If trickery is not used, how does the Villain use coercion or force to get what they want?
Is magic used? If so, in what form?
Examples:
The Wolf encourages Little Red Riding Hood to pick flowers for her grandmother.
In King Bear, a chisel tells the bear to throw it in the ground and dig where it lands to find the Tsar's children.
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Introduction
The Villain succeeds at recon and gains a lead on their intended victim. A map is often involved in some level of the event.
What vital information is leaked?
Who leaks the information and how?
Was the information leaked by carelessness or by interacting with a magical object?
Examples:
The magic mirror in Snow White provides information to the Queen.
In The Miraculous Hen, the merchant's wife tells the young apprentice the precious gems come from the hen.
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Introduction

The Villain makes an effort to attain knowledge needed to fulfill their plot. Disguises are often invoked as the Villain actively probes for information, perhaps for a valuable item or to abduct someone. They may speak with a family member who innocently divulges a crucial insight. The Villain may also seek out the Hero in their reconnaissance, perhaps to gauge their strengths in response to learning of their special nature.
What is the information the Villain seeks?
Who do they approach for the information?
How does the Villain disguise themselves?
Examples:
The wolf in Little Red Riding Hood asks where she is headed.
The apprentice in The Miraculous Hen asks where the precious stones came from.
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Introduction

The prior rule is violated. Therefore, the Hero did not listen to the command or forbidding edict. Whether committed by the Hero by accident or temper, a third party or a foe, this generally leads to negative consequences. The Villain enters the story via this event, although not necessarily confronting the Hero. They may be a lurking and manipulative presence, or might act against the Hero's family in their absence.
How does the Hero break the rule?
What are the consequences of breaking the rule?
How does the Villain make their appearance?
Examples:
Goldilocks breaks into the Three Bear's house, though she knows it is wrong.
Adam and Eve eat an apple from the Tree of Knowledge.
The Grasshopper plays all summer instead of preparing for winter.
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Introduction
A forbidding edict or command is passed upon the Hero ('don't go there,' 'don't do this'). The Hero is warned against some action.
Who warns the Hero?
What is the Hero warned against doing?
Examples:
Little Red Riding Hood is told not to speak with strangers.
In the Bible, Adam and Eve are warned not to eat apples from the Tree of Knowledge.
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Introduction

After the Hero's initial situation is depicted, a member of their community or family leaves the security of the home environment. This may be the Hero themselves, or some other relation that the Hero must later rescue. This division of the cohesive family injects initial tension into the storyline. This may serve as the Hero's introduction, typically portraying them as an ordinary person.
Who is leaving home?
Why are they leaving home?
Where are they going?
Examples:
The Three Little Pigs leave home after coming of age (at their mother's urging).
Little Red Riding Hood leaves home to visit her grandmother.
Note: Your story may not include every beat in this plot structure.

templates.name: Reactive Scene
templates.description: Inspired by Scene & Sequel and the Snowflake Method

children.text: A major plot twist appears. This keeps the story from just being on the same old, same old track.
This twist can put your character back to square one, rethink everything, even question her ability.

This is hard on your character and the reader, after all they're enjoying your book trying to figure who dunnit, and now your sleuth is really struggling. But you as the author must keep the story moving, the character must continue on despite the bad odds of getting whatever their goal is for the story to come to fruition. Justice, Vengeance,  Settling The Score, Acquittal, Trust etc.
This leads us to the Black Moment.
Scene One
Scene Two
Scene Three
Now that the sleuth has rebounded from the Black Moment and creates the climax, hoping it will work...
What kind of reveal do you want?
A room full of suspects that will act as the denouement?
Or a confrontation with the killer.
To know which is best, be sure you know your sleuth well enough to know they work better one way or the other. Or think they can which could then add complications.
Reveal more about your sleuth, history, conflicts, problems. (Make sure your GMC is built).
Remember your sleuth will move forward, then have to retrace their steps as their ideas DON'T pan out.
This long middle will also:
A. Reveal facts about suspects, through interrogations and the discovery of clues.
Bring more of your town in, repeating characters you're building for future books that perhaps been accused mistakenly and trust will need to be built again.  Or the opposite
B. Flight, or disappearance of one or more suspect.
C. Develop a sense of urgency. Raise the stakes or make it evident that if the mystery is not solved soon, there will be terrible consequences.
All of this leads to the midpoint.
