pl15.name: Romancing the Beat
pl15.description: A story structure for romance novels by Gwen Hayes

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Fighting for Love

It’s up to you, a master at your craft, to manage a scene with little conflict that is still intriguing. This is the return to the ordinary world; each Protagonist has changed and fits in their world a little differently and with a new perspective.
Show how each Protagonist fits back in the ordinary world and how they have transformed.
Have a moment of celebration – the Protagonists have been through a lot, so let them unwind a party a bit.
How do their families react to their relationship and transformed selves?
If part of a series, consider planting a hook or foreshadowing a future difficulty.
Breakdown:
Phase 4 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Epilogue occurs around the 98-100% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Fighting for Love

They kissed and made up in the last beat, but show the reader what wholehearted looks like for the Protagonists. You’ve put them through the wringer. This is your chance to make it up to them and your readers.
Close the character arcs of the two Protagonists and show how they have changed (e.g. from selfish to selfless, arrogant to humble, doubting to trusting.)
Resolve the internal and external conflicts.
Show how happy the Protagonists now are and why this was the outcome that was needed all along.
Ensure you are fulfilling reader expectations – the harder the challenges and difficulties before, the sweeter the reward must be.
Breakdown:
Phase 4 makes up the final 25% of the story.
What Wholehearted Looks Like occurs around the 95% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Fighting for Love

It’s life or death now. The Protagonist must be willing to put it all on the line now or risk losing the one thing they need to become wholehearted. The Grand Gesture, the great sacrifice is here, but will it be enough?
Create a Grand Gesture that makes up for the errors of the past.
Don't let them off the hook too easily -t he Grand Gesture may be accepted right away, or there may be a little more work needed. Use this section to increase the tension for an increased pay-off.
Portray the reconciliation.
Breakdown:
Phase 4 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Grand Gesture occurs around the 90% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Fighting for Love
The Protagonist chooses love over fear and doubt. This is the 'I have been an idiot and need to fix this' moment.
What is the triggering event or moment to make the Protagonist choose love over fear?
Decide which challenges or sacrifices must be made to save the relationship (e.g. refusing the job transfer to another city).
Build tension and excitement as the Heroes decides to fight for love.
Breakdown:
Phase 4 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Wake Up occurs around the 85% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 4: Fighting for Love

The Dark Night is the "what have I done" moment for the Protagonist. It's the beat where think they should feel better than they do about the stupid thing they just did and begin to reconsider. Suddenly, they are staring out windows while montages of Phase 2 play across their mind...
Have happy memories begin to challenge the false beliefs and doubts from before.
Hint at a way back for the Protagonists, though it will be challenging.
Breakdown:
Phase 4 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Dark Night occurs around the 80% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Retreating From Love

The darkest moment. The Protagonist has held onto their false beliefs or doubts, and the relationship is over. The reader is left wondering if the Protagonists will ever find their way back to each other. There seems to be no going back after the betrayal in the last beat.
Always tie the black moment to when the Protagonists choose to hold onto their fears, flaws, wounds, or misconceptions.
The opportunity to transform came, and instead of opening their hearts completely, the Protagonist recoiled back to their old self.
The larger the event, the more dramatic the break-up, and further the distance between the two Protagonists, the greater the buy-in for the reader.
Breakdown:
Phase 3 makes up 25% of the story from 50% - 75%.
Break Up occurs around the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Retreating From Love

The worst-case scenario. The fears and false beliefs of Protagonist 1 seem to have come true, and the relationship is breaking down. The reader is left doubting the relationship between the two Protagonists.
Whatever they foretold in their No Way Beats comes true.
No Way Beat says: I don’t believe in love/will never love again/don’t deserve love because_______.
Shields Up Beat says: I knew better than to believe in love/love again/think I deserve love because when I let my guard down______.
Breakdown:
Phase 3 makes up 25% of the story from 50% - 75%.
Shields Up occurs around the 70-75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Retreating From Love
The Retreat Beat is one where subtext is left behind, and the Protagonists actually say, either in an internal or external dialogue, what they fear and how they are going to protect their hearts.
What is the event that causes the trust to be broken and the relationship to falter?
How does this intersect with their internal fears and false beliefs? How will the Protagonist(s) express this?
Breakdown:
Phase 3 makes up 25% of the story from 50% - 75%.
Retreat Beat occurs around the 65-70% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Retreating From Love
The intimacy is continuing or may even appear to be growing, but the seed of doubt planted in the last beat just poked up through the ground.
Portray the growing relationship.
Expand upon the previous event(s) which planted the seed of doubt.
Breakdown:
Phase 3 makes up 25% of the story from 50% - 75%.
Deepening Doubt occurs around the 60% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 3: Retreating From Love
Everything seems to be riding high until past doubts and false beliefs come back. H1 and/or H2 fall back into their old ways, proving they are not quite ready for a transformation.

Go back to the No Way Beats and give them an inkling of doubt custom made for their wholehearted selves (e.g. if H1 believes that the opposite sex cannot be trusted, have H2 be spotted chatting with an ex).
H1 (and/or H2) begins to pull back from the relationship but is still committed.
Breakdown:
Phase 3 makes up 25% of the story from 50% - 75%.
Inkling of Doubt occurs around the 55% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 2: Falling in Love

This is the false high. It appears as thoughts the Protagonists can have both their internal and external goals at the same time. Why choose when you can have it all? Internal and external goals are clearly restated here.
Show the Protagonists everything they want.
Make their goals just within reach.
Give the reader the impression that all will end well with the Protagonists together, goals achieved, and happy.
Breakdown:
Phase 2 makes up 25% of the story from 25% - 50%.
Midpoint of Love occurs around the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 2: Falling in Love

The Protagonists begin to question their first opinions of each other and their previous No Way arguments against being together. They begin admitting to their feelings for each other. What if they gave in to that temptation? Each Protagonist is still working toward their own goals, but the growing idea of relationship begins to create tension and conflict.
What actions or events cause them to begin questioning their opinions of each other and their previous No Way statements?
Grant a glimpse at the opposition between the Protagonist's inner and outer conflict.
Depict the two Protagonists falling in love.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Maybe This Could Work occurs around the 45% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 2: Falling in Love
The desire between the Protagonists continues to deepen as they begin showing each other glimpses of who they actually are.
What external and internal actions begin to show the other their true selves?
Include further examples of how the deepening desire and positive actions continue to erode the false beliefs discussed earlier.
Breakdown:
Phase 2 makes up 25% of the story from 25% - 50%
Deepening Desire occurs around the 40% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 2: Falling in Love
The attraction between the two Protagonists continues to grow, and they begin admitting their feelings for each other. The false beliefs and arguments of H1 begin to be challenged.
Begin attacking your character’s false belief about what he or she stated in either No Way Beat 1 or No Way Beat 2.
Include little moments between the two Protagonists which show the false beliefs being challenged and their growing connection.
Breakdown:
Phase 2 makes up 25% of the story from 25% - 50%.
Inkling of Desire occurs around the 30% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 2: Falling in Love

Attractions are starting to grow, but H1 once more runs from love. They are too dedicated to their external goals or too entrenched in their false beliefs. The argument against falling in love is restated here, showing that H1 is sticking to their old ways.
Restate the argument against love.
Establish how the external goals of H1 conflict with their internal needs.
Breakdown:
Phase 2 makes up 25% of the story from 25% - 50%.
No Way 2 occurs around the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Set Up
This beat is the plot thrust that brings the story into the second act.

An event or situation forces the two Protagonists together to achieve a goal or solve a problem; this event not only raises the stakes, but also clearly defines the goal of each Protagonist. While still at odds with each other, they begin to grow closer, and sparks start to fly.
The two Protagonists cannot walk away from each other now. Not until they see this conundrum through.
Make sure your glue is sticky here – the event that forces them together must be such that it cannot be resolved on its own, nor by only one Protagonist; they must be stuck together to succeed.
Consider what event forces them together and what actions or choices begin reflecting their desire for each other, even though they still deny it.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Adhesion occurs around the 20% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Set Up

This is the argument H1 voices against falling in love. This sets up the romance arc for the reader. The character basically says, either out loud or in internal dialogue, the reason that he or she will not fall in love. Not now, not ever, but especially not with H2 (the character from the Meet Cute).
What is the reason H1 thinks they will not fall in love?
Depict the argument H1 has against falling in love, either vocally or internally, and make it compelling.
Breakdown:
Phase 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
No Way 1 occurs around the 18-20% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Set Up

The two Protagonists meet for the first time on the page, brought together by external forces, chance, or a life event. There may be an instant attraction, but more often, there is an instant dislike with one or both of the Heroes refusing the relationship.
Decide the Inciting Incident that leads to the Meet Cute.
Make it memorable—this is the story they will share with their grandchildren one day.
Hint at how right the Protagonists could be for each other and why now is not the time.
Hint at some conflict between the Protagonists.
Breakdown:
Phase 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Meet Cute occurs around the 10-12% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Set Up

Continue to hook the reader's attention and draw them into the story by introducing the second Hero/Heroine while showing them in their everyday life. Offer a glimpse of their life and the internal struggle that is holding them back from love.
Introduce H2 in a way that makes that character compelling (e.g. desires, flaws, success, a unique personality).
Show your character’s slice of life but throw a hitch in it.
Give or introduce your character’s external goal – for example, a promotion, vacation, or to attain an object.
Introduce or hint at what your character needs – for example, to find love, courage, or develop patience.
Breakdown:
Phase 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Introduce H2 occurs around the 5-8% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Phase 1: Set Up

Hook the reader's attention and draw them into the story by introducing the first Hero/Heroine while showing them in their everyday life. Offer a glimpse of their life and the internal struggle that is holding them back from love.
Introduce H1 in a way that makes that character compelling (e.g. desires, flaws, success, a unique personality).
Show your character’s slice of life but throw a hitch in it.
Give or introduce your character’s external goal – for example, a promotion, vacation, or to attain an object.
Introduce or hint at what your character needs – for example, to find love, courage, or develop patience.
Breakdown:
Phase 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Introduce H1 should be about the first 4-5% of the story.

pl11.name: Six Stage Plot Structure
pl11.description: An outline formula based on ideas popularized by Michael Hague

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3:

The Protagonist returns to the Ordinary World newly transformed, and the reader is shown a glimpse of their new life. If successful, the Protagonist is now able to use their new persona and abilities to face future events and assist those originally left behind in the Ordinary World. This stage sees the outer and inner conflicts resolved and wraps the character arcs of the Protagonist and all major characters.
Demonstrate how the Protagonist is in an opposite state from the beginning of the story.
How has the Protagonist achieved their internal and external goals?
Allow the Protagonist a chance to celebrate, be celebrated, or otherwise reflect on their new life.
Is the Protagonist happy to return to the ordinary world, or does their transformation create new challenges?
If part of a series, leave room for continued personal growth and consider setting the hook for the next installment.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Stage 6 brings the story to its conclusion.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 3:

This is the ultimate obstacle of the story. The Climax is where the Protagonist must face the Central Conflict one final time. It mirrors the story's opening by restating the Protagonist's difficulty or false belief and shows how they have finally overcome it. The Protagonist will either achieve their goal or fail in the final confrontation with the Antagonist.
Demonstrate how the Protagonist uses all they have learned, gained, and experienced to try to successfully obtain their goal / resolve the Central Conflict.
Decide if the Antagonist is defeated, sent on the run, or successful – and how the Protagonist is transformed.
Resolve the Protagonist's external motivation.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Turning Point 5 occurs around the 90% - 99% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 3:

The stakes and tension continue to rise. The challenges are overwhelming, and the pace of the story increases. Everything seems to be going wrong for the Protagonist as they try to recover from the "all is lost" event and achieve their ultimate goal. To succeed, the Protagonist must fully embrace their transformation, finally leaving their old self behind. They must use all they have learned and gained to face the final goal.
The situation gets worse, driving the Protagonist to their lowest (e.g. perhaps they have lost the support of a key Ally, lost faith in themselves, or the Antagonist is at their strongest).

Determine what new piece of information or ability gives the Protagonist the strength to move on – this can be realizing a truth about themselves or the true capability of an object they possess, or it may be a pep talk from an Ally or Mentor.
Demonstrate how the Protagonist has shed their old persona and accepted the new, emboldening them for the final confrontation of the problem.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Stage 5 brings the story to around the 90% - 99% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 3:

A major event occurs, and the Protagonist is brought to their lowest and darkest moment, giving the impression that all is lost. The Protagonist slides back to the comfort of their old ways and tries to hide from the challenge of the Central Conflict, but they are unable. Often an Ally or Mentor is needed to bring the Protagonist back from the brink and give them the confidence they need to continue. Newly emboldened, the Protagonist takes up the mantle for one final grand push. Maximum effort.
What is the Major Setback in your story? For example, it can be the loss of a loved one, the loss of an important object, the villain getting away, or realizing a great betrayal.
The reader and the Protagonist should doubt whether success is still within reach or even possible.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Turning Point 4 occurs around the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2:

The tension and the stakes rise as the Protagonist risks losing it all if they fail; as the importance of reaching the goal grows, so does the difficulty and risk. The Protagonist moves steadily toward their goal and inner transformation, struggling through increasingly difficult challenges. It looks as though hard-fought success is in reach.
Illustrate the increased risk of failure as the tension and stakes rise.
Have the Protagonist face a series of challenges, which they succeed in overcoming, if barely.
The outside world is closing in, and conflict grows.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Stage 4 brings the story to around the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

The midpoint of the story and where the Protagonist crosses the Point of No Return and becomes committed to the final goal. Another Inciting Incident grants clarity and new insight to the Protagonist, driving them to a state of action rather than reaction. They get a glimpse of what is truly at stake and wholeheartedly take on the challenge of the Central Conflict.

As implied by Point of No Return, this incident causes the Protagonist to fully commit to the goal. They no longer have a choice of returning to their ordinary life and are now on a collision course with the ultimate solution.
The Protagonist must take a bigger risk than they have previously, possibly losing friends, Allies, or Mentors along the way.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Turning Point 3 occurs around the 50% mark.

cards.title: Turning Point 3: Point of No Return

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

The Protagonist works to resolve the central problems of the plot and grow as a person. They appear to be having successes as they pursue their new goal and deal with obstacles before them. However, in the face of challenges, they may begin to waver and revert to the comfort of their old self, recoiling from the growth and transformation they have shown to this point.
Have the Protagonist face obstacles and challenges that they can overcome or avoid.
Consider how the Protagonist is growing toward their internal goal as they work towards the external goal.
Remember the Protagonist is not yet fully committed to their transformation or final goal – their strength and courage may wax and wane.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Stage 3 brings the story to around the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

A new Inciting Incident occurs, creating a turn in the story and a new external goal for the Protagonist to pursue. The new goal presents a challenge the Protagonist cannot achieve without growth and transformation and becomes the end goal of the story.

Use this section to clearly define the central story concept and the Protagonist's outer motivation. (Inner motivation represents a change like gaining courage, finding love, or learning patience; outer motivation represents a tangible objective like finding an object, stopping a plot, or saving someone.)

This Turning Point can be the need to foil an evil plot, prevent something terrible, locate an essential item, or deliver someone/something on time – it must be a big enough event to change the course of the story and deepen the hook with the reader.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Turning Point 2 occurs around the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1:

The Protagonist attempts to adjust to their new situation and the new world they've entered upon leaving the comfort of their Ordinary World. Their views in life are challenged, and they get a glimpse of what life could be like. It is exciting but also daunting and frightening. As life changes and obstacles grow, they quickly realize the solution to the problem is not as straightforward as they anticipated.
Consider how the Inciting Incident has challenged the Protagonist's views in life.
Have the Protagonist leave their ordinary world to create the change they need (e.g. change of job, change of location, change of personal relationships).
Build tension and increase the stakes as the story moves toward Turning Point 2.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Stage 2 brings the story to around the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1:

Turning Point 1 introduces an Inciting Incident that creates a goal / opportunity for the Protagonist; it challenges the Protagonist's views and offers an incentive to act and make a change. This event offers a glimpse of their want or need. They may decide to act upon this desire or run from it at first.
Decide upon an Inciting Incident and whether it fits a want (external desire like leaving town or getting an object of power) or a need (internal desire like finding love, courage, or patience).
Will the Protagonist accept it or run from it? (Running from it eventually leads to accepting it.)
This section should hook the reader to continue reading, as it drives the Protagonist into Stage 2.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Turning Point 1 occurs around the 10% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:

The Setup introduces the Protagonist, how they interact with their Ordinary World, and introduces something that displeases them in their everyday life. The Protagonist must be well developed with desires, fears, flaws, and a unique personality. This section is the hook that draws the reader into the story and allows them to connect with the Protagonist. The reader should see the Protagonist facing a difficulty or false belief that has them mired in place.
Create a sympathetic Protagonist – are they a victim, in jeopardy, likable, skilled, funny, depressed?
What about their world displeases them, or is holding them back, but they have not worked to fix? How are they stuck?
What is the wound, false belief, and/or fear that has them entrenched?
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Stage 1 brings the story to around the 10% mark.

pl29.name: Sleuth's Journey
pl29.description: A mystery novel formula by Troy Lambert, based on the classic Hero's Journey

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2:

While the true motive is now clear, there are still issues the Sleuth must face, and the solution seems to be difficult, if not impossible. Attempts to solve the crime have stymied the Sleuth. Misinterpretation of clues or mistaken conclusions have led them in the wrong direction. While some clues are starting to fall into place, others assumed to be valuable thus far are now meaningless, and logic must be applied to force a new way of grasping an understanding of the uncertainties. This beat is a bit of a roller coaster, as the Sleuth reveals the results of the investigation. The reader, as well as the Sleuth and other characters, are given an opportunity to review what is known and assess the possibilities.

Use this section to re-confirm the danger and urgency of solving the case – it is also a good time to remind the reader of the central dramatic event/question which started the Sleuth on their journey.
The danger faced by the Sleuth may act as a turning point, creating an unexpected turn in the story.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Reveal the Wrong Turn occurs around the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 3:

This is a short beat where the Sleuth takes what they have learned in the last two beats, weighs the evidence and information they have been given, and now look to prove the conclusion they've already come to. The reader may not know what is going on exactly, but they will have a hint as to what the Sleuth assumes and why they assume it. However, they don't know the answer for sure and have no idea how the Sleuth will get the proof they need. Based on what only they now know, the Sleuth must seek positive proof to back up the yet undisclosed conclusion.
Have the Sleuth weigh the evidence and information gleaned from the other characters.
Be sure that at this point, the reader generally does not know the answer.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Resurrection occurs around the 80-85% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1:

This is an optional beat, but one in which the Sleuth meets a new partner, their sidekick for this story. This person, although often their polar opposite, gives them the confidence and tools they need to succeed. The partner must get the Sleuth over their previous objections, which often takes the form of a (not so) gentle nudge. The partner, for example, can be someone with youth or experience, someone with technical expertise who can provide tools and specialized equipment, or someone sent to either train the Sleuth or keep an eye on them and keep them in line.
Identify how the partner will interact with the Sleuth.
Show the Sleuth gaining confidence in the partner because of something impressive they do to help them.
Illustrate how the partner changes their perspective, helping propel them toward the new case.
Create an awe-inspiring moment between the two of them.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The New Partner occurs around the 20% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:
This is the world the Sleuth lives in. It can be action-packed. Think of James Bond movies or the intro to John Wick, or the intro to other thrillers.
Create the setting: Where does the story take place? What time period is the story set in? Be sure to give the reader a sense of place.
Show the character and reveal their job (private eye, cop, photographer, novelist, etc.)
Develop a three-dimensional character with flaws, desires, problems, and a unique personality.
Showcase the Sleuth's comfort with their everyday life and activities.
Hint at something that displeases them about their life/world (e.g. a problem or a dramatic event/question that bothers the Sleuth and must be solved).
If this is a series, these elements are reintroduced for readers new to the series.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Sleuth's Ordinary World should take approximately 0-10% of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:
The Sleuth learns of the crime, and their Ordinary World is disrupted, because:
They are hired to solve the crime.
They are assigned the case.
They are somehow drawn into the investigation.
This should include one clue that the Sleuth receives that will play a role later in the mystery.

Remember, in the case of an amateur sleuth, they must have a Motive to get involved in the case, and officials like police and others must also have a Motive for involving them, unless that is part of the conflict, and they are working contrary to officials involved. This may mean a slow burn in the early section of the story.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Sleuth's World Disrupted occurs around the 12% mark.
-- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1:
The amateur Sleuth feels pulled to investigate, but doesn’t feel qualified or want to dive into the investigation. If the Sleuth is a detective, the refusal of the call
occurs when they don’t want the case or fear they won’t be given the case. Often, the refusal of the call is not the decision of the Sleuth, but of their superiors or those around them.

Have the Sleuth hesitate or try to refuse the case (e.g. I'm retiring, I'm too old, I don't need a partner, I have enough work already, I am not qualified to investigate this kind of case) – and realize that more than one type of pressure may be necessary to persuade our Sleuth.
Raise the stakes after each time the Sleuth refuses.
Include the Sleuth's emotional response to the refusal – are they feeling guilty, angry, annoyed? This helps show their motivations and builds their character.
Force the Sleuth to take the case with an inciting incident that can no longer be ignored: command from their captain, events that involve them directly in the case, etc.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Refusal of the Call occurs around the 15% mark.

cards.title: Set the Sleuth on the Path

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1:

Set the Sleuth on the path toward solving the mystery. Offer plausible suspects, all of whom appear to have had motive, means, and opportunity to commit the crime. Select the most likely suspects, and have the Sleuth question them. One of these suspects will turn out to be the actual perpetrator.

At the approximate end of Act 1, something should occur which makes it clear to the reader that the crime is more complicated than originally thought. Hints may be given to allow the reader to actually see possibilities not yet known to the Sleuth.
Answer the question: what causes the Sleuth to become more interested in the case? A bonus for a P.I.? An assignment from their boss? Perhaps something personal that draws the Sleuth in?
Show the Sleuth beginning to embrace the investigation.
Make it clear what the case is about, at least as far as our Sleuth knows so far.

Ensure the Sleuth's character is well developed and that they respond in a way that aligns with their character. Usually, a detective or investigator becomes very determined at this point in the story.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Set the Sleuth on the Path occurs around the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

Direct the investigation toward a conclusion that later proves to be erroneous. Usually, this conclusion and its failure do provide the Sleuth with some new information that sets them on the path to the correct answer, or at least the next try/fail. This is a good place for a clue the Sleuth does not realize is important but pays off later.
Introduce a challenge to showcase how dangerous this case is.
Make the Sleuth doubt their ability to solve the case.
Introduce dependence on the new partner to provide unique skills.
Show how the relationship between the Sleuth and the partner either gets better or worse.
Someone may die here, and that often provides the clue that the Sleuth uses later on. Not all relationships are what they seem, and we can see hints of that happening here.
Note:
This is an opportunity to add more characters to the story, including a rival detective team, old friends, and even potential suspects.
Plan the character development of the supporting characters to ensure they are strong as well. What are their goals, motivations, and strategies? They may not always align with those of the Sleuth.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The First Erroneous Conclusion occurs around the 25-30% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:
After the first erroneous conclusion, our Sleuth will double down on investigations.
Reveal facts about suspects through interrogations and the discovery of clues.
Introduce the flight or disappearance of one or more suspect(s).
Develop a sense of urgency and increase tension here. Raise the stakes or make it evident that if the mystery is not solved soon, there will be terrible consequences.

This is a great place to take those characters just introduced and let the reader learn more about them. Add suspicion to one or more of them, providing the Sleuth with some false leads to follow, mixed with some meaningful clues.
This is also where the first try/fail in the B-Story happens (if you have one).
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Facts about Suspects occurs around the 35% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

The Protagonist and (most) Allies have survived the previous tests and journey into the Unknown World and can pause for a moment. If they have been hit by setbacks during the tests, this is an opportunity for them to regroup and create their plan for the final confrontation by gathering tools, preparing plans, or cutting down the enemy's ranks. It may also be a good place for a morale booster or a visit from the Mentor to reconfirm the Protagonist's faith in their abilities. By the end of this section, the Protagonist should be entirely separated from the Ordinary World and have survived an event that reconfirms their commitment to the quest. Information gathered through interviews or the discovery of physical evidence, should point toward the solution, although the relevance may not yet be apparent.
Broaden the investigation to put suspicion on other characters.
Allow the Sleuth or perhaps the partner to make a plan that could potentially solve the case.
Show that the Sleuth feels confident about coming to a solution, even if they are wrong.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Broaden the Investigation occurs around the 40% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

Through the subplot and other relationships, we start to learn more about the Sleuth and their background. This establishes what drives them, haunts them, or may be missing in their life. This is a breather for the reader from the action, although there can be some personal action in this scene. It happens right before the midpoint of the story.

Make it clear that the Sleuth has a personal stake in the outcome, either because of threat to their life, or the possibility of revelation of matters deeply disturbing to the Sleuth on an emotional level.

Highlight both strengths (e.g. drive and determination) and weaknesses (e.g lack of personal connections, poor relationships, drinking, drugs, or another kind of obsession). This weakness should play into their struggles to solve the case.
Allow the Sleuth to empathize with the victim or their family, this time related to their own deep-seated issues.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The Sleuth's Background occurs around the 45% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

Once the Sleuth has a plan and a personal reason to solve the case, they must face their biggest test, which leads them to their darkest moment. They have been on the wrong track, and tragic events make that obvious. There may be the appearance of a second body, the death of a major suspect, or the discovery of evidence that rules out the most likely suspect. Either way, the mystery takes a completely different turn. Often the Sleuth faces a large sacrifice, a death, or a significant loss which breaks them down to their lowest. The Sleuth must transition through a form of death and rebirth, whether that is a death of their best ideas, or the literal death of someone close to them. The greater the emotional impact the better. If the Sleuth is successful, this grants them new insights which alter their perception for the rest of the story, giving them the determination to solve the crime. If the Sleuth fails, their success is thrown into question, while the tension and the stakes heighten.
Show the Sleuth facing their biggest test so far leading to their darkest moment physically, emotionally, or both.
Dramatize this through a painful sacrifice, the death of a someone close to them, or new evidence or knowledge that shakes the Sleuth's faith in themselves and their solution.
Highlight the emotional, mental, and/or physical work the Sleuth must do to rebound after this defeat so they can ultimately win.
Show the Sleuth transformed into a stronger, more powerful version of themselves, with renewed confidence in their abilities.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The Change of Focus occurs around the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2:

The Sleuth has really been put through it at the midpoint of our story, and now things turn around for them. The motive for the crime they were chasing may have been wrong, but now new, previously hidden motives are revealed. Formerly secret relationships come to light, such as business arrangements, romantic involvements, scores to be settled, or previously veiled kinships. This can come to light in a number of ways, but should be a result of the action the Sleuth has taken.
Show the Sleuth acquiring new clues to the actual motive for the crime. This can be an object, knowledge, new abilities, or reconciliation.
Indicate how this clue is central and a critical part of the solution to the crime. This is where other clues previously meaningless start to make sense.
Develop and expose meanings of matters hinted at in Act 1 to slowly clarify the significance of earlier clues.
Allow a moment for the Sleuth to celebrate their cleverness again. Their confidence starts to return in this beat just before we head into Act 3.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Reward (Seizing the Sword) occurs around the 70% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 3:

The Sleuth made a wrong assumption about motive. This caused them to take a wrong turn, which they now realize and work to correct. The crucial evidence is something overlooked in Act 1, which appeared to have been of little consequence at the time it was first disclosed. That evidence takes on new meaning with information disclosed in Act 3. The Sleuth (and perhaps the reader, if a keen observer) becomes aware of the error which remains undisclosed to the other characters.
Have the Sleuth review the case to determine where they went wrong.
Reveal the chain of events that provoked the crime.
The story is now headed for the climax, so this beat gives the foundation that sets the Sleuth and the reader up to solve the case.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Reveal the Wrong Turn occurs around the 80% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 3:

Once the Sleuth has the answer, this beat shows them finding the final clue they need to solve the crime and revealing it to the reader. This clue should fulfill a promise made in Act 1 and the reader should feel satisfied that the loose ends have been wrapped up. This is another quick beat and could be combined with the previous one. The only thing left is to catch the Villain, and the final confrontation or chase scene often occurs at this point in the story.
Show that the Sleuth and the reader know the answer now.
Make sure that the clues have all led up to this final solution.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Final Reveal occurs around the 85-90% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3:

This is the true climax of the story, the final and most dangerous encounter between the Sleuth and the Villain. This is the definitive and greatest test of the Sleuth's determination to solve the case. With the solution in hand, it is time for the Sleuth to confront the Villain, often alone and without the support they need. With time running out and pressure at its highest, the Sleuth captures the Villain, but there is often a sacrifice involved. A partner is shot, something valuable is lost, etc.
Dramatize the final showdown – show how the Sleuth uses the final clue and what they now know of the Villain to predict what they will do next and capture them.
Show the change in the Sleuth and how that change has helped them solve the case.
Prepare the Sleuth to return to some kind of normal again.
Establish that the case has been solved and justice has been served to the satisfaction of all involved (except the Villain).
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Caught occurs around the 90-95% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3:

The Sleuth is now a changed person with new strength and confidence. This is an opportunity to reaffirm their growth. The Sleuth can choose to settle into a life of comfort until the next crisis arises, or they seek a new mystery and adventure right away.
Present the Sleuth's return to normal and the routine of their lives. Reaffirm the Sleuth's change and new hope.
Decide if the Sleuth chooses to settle in or if they seek more cases and mysteries right away.
If Part of a Series:
Leave some loose threads and room for further character development for the Sleuth.
Consider setting the hook for the next book.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The Denouement occurs around the 99% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:
The Victim is introduced. Their Ordinary World is disrupted when a crime is committed against them. They are killed, robbed, assaulted, etc.
This should include:
At least one unique trait, so the reader cares about them right away.
The crime itself, and the impact on the victim. (How it disrupts their world).
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Victim's World Disrupted occurs around the 12% mark, and is tied to the disruption of the Victim's world
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1:
The Sleuth, and therefore the reader, learns something about the victim that makes them feel empathy. The Sleuth is more motivated to solve the case because of this information.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Empathy Trigger occurs around the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

Information gathered through interviews, or the discovery of physical evidence should reveal new facts about the victim that will help the Sleuth solve the crime. It also fleshes out their character, so the reader is reminded to care that they were victimized.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The Sleuth and the Victim occurs around the 40% mark, and is a result of broadening the investigation.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3:

Victory is snatched away by the Sleuth... and the Villain is left to face the consequences. They may be destroyed, killed, banished, jailed, or convinced to turn back to the path of good. No matter the outcome, the Villain is no longer a threat.
Finish the final confrontation between Villain and Sleuth.
Outline the consequences for the Villain.
If part of a series, set the hook for the next installment and hint at the Villain's next diabolical plan if they are going to return.

While the Villain's Journey closely mirrors the Hero's Journey, the Villain does not have a reward, a homecoming, or an opportunity to relax in a new world they have created. They have been defeated and are sent off to lick their wounds and devise another plan.

Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Ordeal, Death, Rebirth occurs around the 75% mark.
The Villain's final consequences occur around the 90% - 95% mark.

Beginning of Act 3:
The Sleuth now has many of the facts they will need to solve the case. The Villain is getting close to success and getting away with things. But alas, the Sleuth stands in their way.
Show the Villain's frustration, either in their POV or by what the Sleuth observes.
Take away the Villain's hope and make them desperate for success.

On the Run occurs around the 75% mark.

This is a time of victory for the Villain. Even if we do not see this through their POV, we should see that the bad triumphs at this point when the good is at the lowest. The Villain is always on the opposite track as your Protagonist.

The Villain's Midpoint occurs around the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:

The Villain takes action and commits a serious offense or crime. They may steal, kill, rob, or kidnap, but whatever it is, they are now past the point of no return and are beginning on the path to their ultimate goal. They are now unquestionably the story's Villain.

What action does the Villain take to push them beyond the point of return?
How do these actions make the Villain clearly the Villain?

The Sleuth may be seen preparing a partner or a team if you are showing the reader their POV. Otherwise, the Sleuth may be called to another in a series of crimes or something that clues them into someone or a sinister group behind the crimes. This is also related to the new partner, and the Villain may even know them.
Introduce those behind the crime that partner with the Sleuth.
Identify the strengths of the team.
Show how the team will work together.

Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Criminal Preparation occurs around the 20% mark.

As the story begins, the Villain is in their Ordinary World... and something is not quite right. For example, an important project they've been working on has gone wrong; they feel betrayed by their government; they've witnessed a loved one die, or they've given in to their darkest desires. This section either creates sympathy for the Villain or a feeling of revulsion. Either way, the key is to hook the reader with an emotional response to the Villain's behavior.
Introduce the readers to the Villain and their Ordinary World.
Show something in the Villain's world that displeases them.

This can be a family story, a budding romance, or another mystery or case that is happening at the same time as the main storyline,

This Opening Image/Hook happens by the 10% mark of the story

The love interest or the B-Story is disrupted by the same events that disrupt the Sleuth's Ordinary World. The marriage retreat is postponed, or the beach vacation, or the Sleuth is pulled off another case, forced to postpone retirement, etc. This is a conflict that will always be at odds with and making a mess of the main storyline.

The decision to take the case spells the end of the original plan for the B-Story, whatever that might be. In this case of a romance, this jeopardizes the relationship.

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 3:

The Third Disaster comes at the end of Act 2, approximately 75% of the way through the story. The Third Disaster is something bad that forces your Protagonist AND the Antagonist (if there is an Antagonist) to commit to some final showdown that will decide who wins and who loses. That is, they must both commit to end the story.
Example - Star Wars:

In the original Star Wars movie (Episode 4), at the end of Act 2, Luke and his comrades reach the rebel planet, where they learn that the stormtroopers put a tracking device on the Millennium Falcon. The Death Star is now approaching the rebel planet, and Darth Vader means to destroy the planet and end the Rebellion. This is terrible! The rebels can all run and hide, fragmenting the Rebellion, or they can fight to the death. They choose to make a last stand. The rest of the story is the final showdown, in which the rebels attack the Death Star while it moves into position to destroy the rebel planet. One side will win, and one will lose, and the clock is ticking!
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Third Disaster occurs around the 75% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 2:

The Second Disaster comes approximately at the middle of Act 2, roughly 50% of the way into your story. Your lead Character has spent the first half of Act 2 trying to achieve their story goal, but they've been pursuing a path that won't work. The Second Disaster is a bad thing that happens at the midpoint of the story that forces your Protagonist to try a new approach. This new approach will actually work.
Example – Star Wars:

In the original Star Wars movie (Episode 4), Obi-Wan Kenobi is killed by Darth Vader at the midpoint of the story. Up till now, Luke has been following Obi-Wan and just doing what he says. Now he has to step up and start making his own decisions--and he needs to actually start using the Force. He will never win unless he becomes strong in the Force, and he has the second half of Act 2 to get strong.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% to 75%.
Second Disaster occurs around the 50% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 1:
The First Disaster comes at the end of Act 1, roughly 25% of the way into the story. The First Disaster is something bad that forces the Protagonist to commit to the story.
Example – Star Wars:

In the original Stars Wars Movie (Episode 4), Luke's aunt and uncle are murdered by stormtroopers. This drives Luke to agree to leave the planet with Obi-Wan Kenobi. He's now committed to the Rebellion, and he can't turn back.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
First Disaster occurs around the 25% mark of the story.

pl35.name: Sonnet (Shakespearean)
pl35.description: A template for writing poetry featuring four quatrains and a rhyming couplet.

children.text: The Shakespearean sonnet, also known as an English sonnet, was made famous by William Shakespeare. It comprises 14 lines, written in iambic pentameter, divided into three quatrains (four lines) followed by a couplet (two rhyming lines).

The quatrains present a problem, question, or argument, leaving the couplet to provide a conclusion, resolution, or commentary. The typical rhyme scheme found in a Shakespearean sonnet is ABAB CDCD EFEF GG.

Often exploring themes of love, beauty, and mortality, Shakespearean Sonnets are notable for their focus on the speaker’s personal feelings and experiences. They are also known for their use of literary devices, including metaphor and simile.

Some of the most famous examples of this form of sonnets are Shakespeare’s own, having had a lasting impact on poetry and literary culture. The Shakespearean sonnet form remains an important part of the poetry tradition and continues to be used by many poets to this day.
Fill in each part of this template to successfully complete your sonnet.
Example:
Sonnet 18 by William Shakespeare

Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
    Thou art more lovely and more temperate.
    Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
    And summer’s lease hath all too short a date.

Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
    And often is his gold complexion dimmed;
    And every fair from fair sometime declines,
    By chance or nature’s changing course untrimmed.

But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
    Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st,
    Nor shall Death brag thou wand’rest in his shade,
    When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st.

So long as men can breathe or eyes can see,
    So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

An important part of the Shakespearean sonnet, the first quatrain (four lines) provides the reader with a starting point from which to understand the rest of the poem. Each pair of lines rhyme with each other using an ABAB rhyming scheme and establishes the tone and mood, while introducing the speaker’s perspective. It presents the problem, question, or argument to be addressed by the sonnet.
Use this quatrain to set the scene or introduce the main subject, while providing context for the rest of the poem.
Example:
Sonnet 18 by William Shakespeare

Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
    Thou art more lovely and more temperate.
    Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
    And summer’s lease hath all too short a date.
Write the first quatrain of your sonnet below:

Known as the developing quatrains, the second and third quatrains build on the themes and ideas introduced in the first quatrain and continue to develop the tone and mood. Like the first quatrain, they use rhyming couplets, with each pair of lines rhyming with each other (CDCD and EFEF, respectively).

Crucial in shaping the overall meaning of the sonnet and in leading the reader towards the conclusion presented in the final couplet, the second and third quatrains contain the bulk of the poem’s argument or observation. They provide additional details, imagery, or arguments related to the main subject of the sonnet and expand on the speaker’s perspective, offering a deeper understanding.
Use these quatrains to continue to develop the tone and mood of the sonnet, while providing the reader with a deeper understanding of the speaker’s perspective.
Example:
Sonnet 18 by William Shakespeare

Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
    And often is his gold complexion dimmed;
    And every fair from fair sometime declines,
    By chance or nature’s changing course untrimmed.

But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
    Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st,
    Nor shall Death brag thou wand’rest in his shade,
    When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st.
Write the second and third quatrain of your sonnet below:

The final two lines of a Shakespearean sonnet, the couplet provides a conclusion, resolution, or commentary on the situation presented in the first three quatrains. The couplet is written in rhyming pairs, with the two lines rhyming with each other (GG).

Often seen as the most important part of the Shakespearean sonnet, it couplet provides the reader with the final resolution or insight into the main subject of the poem. It may also provide a punchline, a surprising turn of events, or a resolution to the question or argument presented in the quatrains, while leaving the reader with a memorable conclusion that stays with them long after reading the poem.
Use this couplet to provide a resolution and a memorable conclusion to your poem.
Example:
So long as men can breathe or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

End of Act 3:
...now capable of change.
The Protagonist has undergone a transformation and uses their new abilities, knowledge, perspective, or an item they found, to vanquish the Villain / achieve their goal. Their c
hange must be made visual, often with a final showdown. This is t
he resolution of the story
Create a final showdown – demonstrate how the Protagonist and other major characters have transformed from the beginning of the story (e.g. stronger, more courageous, more capable).
Close the circle – show that the Protagonist,
having emerged victorious,

Example: The Protagonist and Allies lead the villagers in an attack, killing some of the loggers. The Allies hold the remaining logging crew at bay while the Protagonist faces off against their leader, causing grievous wounds. The loggers realize the cost of remaining in the village is too steep and agree to vacate the lands. The Protagonist has thus transformed from a passive protector of the lands to one who is willing to use force.

This step occurs around the 85 - 87% mark.

The Protagonist returns to their normal world with whatever they found / took – along with a new perspective leading to new wants and needs. Show the Protagonist preparing for the final confrontation and returning to their normal world..
Indicate how the Protagonist interacts with the normal world has changed throughout the story.

End of Act 2:
...pay its price...

The Protagonist Takes what they wanted but pay a steep price, creating a new need that pushes them to the brink. The Protagonist is at their lowest, and all seems lost, leading to the Climax where the Protagonist faces their toughest conflict. This is often where the Protagonist's wants and needs collide.
Demonstrate how the Protagonist actions have serious consequences (e.g. putting more lives at risk, triggering a chase, or causing the Villain to speed up the timeline of their evil plans).
Show the tension and stakes rising as the Protagonist deals with new challenges in the wake of a seeming victory.

Have the Protagonist suffer a significant loss to continue the descent to their lowest (e.g. perhaps a key Ally is killed, an essential item is lost, or they lose the support of an Ally or love interest).
Example: With their machines destroyed, the loggers turn to violence and attack the village, killing some and holding the rest hostage, intent on ridding themselves of the disruption.

...find what they wanted...

This section creates a turning point. The Protagonist Finds what they've Wanted and achieves a brief moment of victory, but what once appeared as a direct solution soon devolves into something much more daunting and dangerous.
Show the Protagonist appearing to Find a solution to their goal.
Highlight the Protagonist's brief moment of victory – just before the plot turns and tension increases.

...adapt to it...

The result of Go-ing isn't what was expected, and the Protagonist must adapt to the new situation as things become more complicated. The Search for new solutions sets the stage for the turning point / climax of the story.
Add a set of roadblocks between the Protagonist and their need that test them in their new world.
Introduce Allies that assist the Protagonist in going through their trials.
Consider adding to the tension and raising the stakes by not having all Allies survive this section.

...they enter an unfamiliar situation...
The Protagonist enters a new and unfamiliar situation (or world). They must make a change or Go on an adventure and work towards their goal. This introduces the core conflict of the story.

The Protagonist is not quite comfortable in their new role but is willing to take action.

...but they want something...

In this section of the narrative it becomes clear that something is not perfect in the Protagonist's world – they have some Need (internal or external) which introduces the inciting incident that propels the Protagonist into the story. The Need must be vital so that there is no choice but to Go and deal with it.

Introduce the Protagonist's external and/or internal Need(s). The external Need is often a desire to change or achieve something, while the internal Need may be courage, respect, patience, love, or humility.
Present the inciting incident which propels the Protagonist out of their Zone of Comfort.
Example: Loggers arrive and threaten the Protagonist's village and food source. The Protagonist needs to stop the loggers to protect their home.

A character is in a zone of comfort...
Introduce the Protagonist, establish the status quo of their world, and show them in their zone of comfort.
Ensure the Protagonist is sympathetic to the audience to create buy-in – readers must care about the Protagonist to care about the solution to their forthcoming problem.
Allow the audience to see how the Protagonist functions in their normal world, showcasing their personality and comfort through their interactions.

Beginning of Act 4: The Conclusion Phase
The Conclusion Phase is the most straightforward of the four phases of story structure.

In this phase, the final phase of the book, the Protagonist finds the courage and personal growth to force their way forward with a solution to the problem before them and, at long last, finally defeat the Antagonist and achieve their goal.
Or fail trying.
Simply put, the Protagonist does whatever must be done in order to reach the goal, even if it means giving the ultimate sacrifice.

Act 3: The Proactive Phase

Continue putting the Protagonist through try fail cycles as they use what they learned in the second GCM while they attempt to confront the Antagonist. Remember, the Protagonist is growing stronger and learning more as this progresses, leading them to the next and final GCM. The tension and stakes rise at each attempt to confront the Antagonist.

The Proactive Phase makes up approximately 30% of the story, from 50% - 80%.

End of Act 3: Game-Changing Moment #3 (Connects the Proactive Phase to the Conclusion Phase)
Game-Changing Moment #3 is the beginning of the end.  It is the point where the final piece of information the Protagonist needs to combat the Antagonist comes into play.
With this information, the Protagonist can move from the cycle of attempt and failure to one final, no-holds-barred, all-or-nothing attempt to confront the Antagonist and come out successful.

It is this new information that takes the Protagonist from the attacking warrior forced to face off against their own inner demons (and failing as a result) to the selfless martyr that will do or give anything to come out on top in that final confrontation.
Nothing new should enter your story after this point. The Protagonist should have everything they need to either save the day or fail miserably. Either way, the end is nigh.

Beginning of Act 3: The Proactive Phase
The Proactive Phase is that point in the story when the Protagonist begins to confront the Antagonist with direct thought and action.

Up to this point, the Protagonist has been fumbling about, reacting to events and doing what they can to understand the mess they find themselves in.  Then the information the Protagonist gains in the second GCM parts the curtain just enough so he can see what lies ahead.  A new plan of action forms, and the Protagonist charges off to see it through.
No longer content to sit back and wait for the conflict to happen to him, the Protagonist now goes in search of it directly.
The Proactive Phase is all about the Protagonist trying and failing and trying again.  Each time they attempt to defeat the Antagonist, the stakes grow higher, and the tension grows stronger.

It is at this point that the Protagonist learns who or what is standing in their way. They know the identity of the Antagonist and realize that in order to reach their goal, they will have to prevent the Antagonist from reaching their own. The Protagonist’s goal and the Antagonist’s goal are diametrically opposed.

Beginning of Act 2: The Reactive Phase

The Reactive Phase is focused entirely around how the Protagonist responds to the conflict that has just reared its head in GCM#1. It is, in essence, the Protagonist’s blind response to the problem.  They are not yet organized enough or knowledgeable enough to attack the problem head-on (that’s the next phase of the story structure). Right now, they are just reacting – running, hiding, observing, analyzing, avoiding, and the like.

Put yourself in the Protagonist’s shoes.  If your own world suddenly fell apart, you’d probably spend some time simply reacting to the mess as well.  You’d try to figure out what was going on, buy yourself some time to get organized, plan a response, and regroup, and that is exactly what happens to the Protagonist in this section of the book.
The Protagonist knows very little information at this point, and their emotional response to the problem should reflect that.

End of Act 1: Game-Changing Moment #1 (Connects the Preparation Phase to the Reactive Phase)

Game Changing Moment #1 is the first critical moment in the story. It is that point in the story where the Protagonist can no longer continue doing the same old thing they’ve been doing.  Something has happened that drives them forward into the rest of the tale, and nothing will be the same for them ever again.
This is the point where the story really begins because it is at this point that the conflict of the story is introduced.
Remember, without conflict, you don’t have a story at all, so this is one of the most important points  in the entire plot, if not THE most important point.

Game-Changing Moment #1 lets the Protagonist – and thus the reader as well – know that from this point forward, things will be different.  Something new has entered the Protagonist’s life – a sudden need, a mission, a calling – and once it arrives, they can never go back to the ways things were.  Game-Changing Moment #1 demands attention, for it has now become an obstacle to whatever it is the Protagonist needs to accomplish.

Beginning of Act 1: The Preparation Phase
The Preparation Phase gets the story off to a proper start by introducing the characters, the setting, and the stakes.

It introduces the reader to the hero and lets them glimpse what life is like for that individual prior to the events that send things spiraling out of the ordinary. Doing so allows the reader to connect with the Protagonist, to care about them, before the writer throws them both to the wolves.   The more the reader cares about the Protagonist - their wants and goals, dreams and desires, trials and tribulations before the arrival of the central conflict of the story - the more they will care about what happens to them after that conflict appears.
About The Story Engines Framework:

The Story Engines process uses a four-act (four-phase) structure designed to heighten the emotional connection between the reader and the Protagonist of the story. Each act exists for a specific reason and pushes the story forward in different, but equally important, ways.  Their positions in the story are as important as their content; put the wrong act in the wrong place and you’ll destroy that emotional connection you’re working so hard to build.

Each act is tied to the next through a critical transition scene known as a Game-Changing Moment (GCM.) Each GCM moves the Protagonist forward through the revelation of key information which they need to reach their story goal and puts them into a new emotional stance that is represented by the action that follows.
Seven elements – four acts and three game-changing moments – form the base structure of your story.
Breakdown:
The Preparation Phase makes up approximately the first 20% of the story.

Note that this template is set up as a forty-chapter story, based around 80K word manuscripts with forty scenes of 2k words each. Each chapter also happens to be only a single scene in length. This model can be used to shrink or expand the number of chapters or scenes as needed. This works so long as the proper ratios for each phase (20% - 30% - 30% - 20%) are maintained. You can rearrange this template as necessary to fit whatever length novel you need.

pl41.name: Story Genius
pl41.description: Part of the Story Genius method, the Story Genius Timeline includes crucial scenes and plot points designed to help you create a coherent story after you know your characters, and their backstory, and have established their misbeliefs and desires.

children.text: When did this initial story idea and this idea for your character first grab you?
Did the idea or the character come to you first?
What about each of them grabbed your attention?

Now that you’ve answered all of those questions, write the entire scene and capture the moment when your character’s misbelief took root and colored their worldview moving forward. Do this in the Story Genius Plot Guide template.

cards.title: Create 3 Crossroads Scenes that Reinforce the Misbelief

children.text: Throughout your character’s life, they have made several turning-point decisions that have been guided by the misbelief you established in the previous scene. Sketch them out. To nail down three truly crucial moments for your character, consider that these moments need to have the following:
External events that in some fundamental way—due to intense internal conflict—cause the character’s misbelief to deepen.
Had to make a decision that had escalating ongoing ramifications that further confirm the misbelief.
Must yield the most story-specific info
Sketch them in chronological order.

Once you have sketched them out in the scene cards in the Story Genius Plot Guide, write the scenes fully, either here in these scene cards, or in the character template provided. The goal is to have all of this backstory in one platform for you to keep track of. Make sure to write them in chronological order.
What is the Obvious External Plot Problem of the Story?
Go to the Story Genius Plot Guide
Freewrite in scene cards some potential external plot problems of your story
Be sure to tie these plot problems to the internal conflicts and misbeliefs your character has, and their desires (what they want)
Plot Problem Test #1:
See if your obvious plot problem passes this test:
Can your problem sustain the entire novel from the first page to the last?
Is there a real-world specific impending consequence that this escalating problem will give my character no choice but to face?
Is there a clear-cut deadline, a ticking clock counting down to that consequence?

cards.title: What is the Obvious Plot Problem of the Story?

children.text: Write down why you care about this story and the main character in it.
What drives you to write this story?
Why are you the person who needs to write this story?

cards.title: Make a List of Plot Problems

children.text: Head to the Story Genius Plot Guide, and create a list of potential plot problems.
Do some free-writing about your intended plot and extract possible main story problems that you see based on your “what if” story idea and backstory scenes you’ve created for your character.
Make a list of all of the potential plot problems your character will face.

cards.title: What is the Point of Your Story?

children.text: What do you want your readers to go away thinking about? See if you can nail the point of your story down in two to three concise sentences. Relate this back to the character and ideas that first grabbed you.
Potential Plot Points that Challenge Your Protagonist

Go over all of the material you have created so far and tease out potential plot points or obstacles that your protagonist will face when it comes to getting what she wants. Add them to scene cards on your Idea List timeline in the Story Genius Timeline Template. For any scenes you can actually visualize coming to lie, add those to scene cards on the Scene Cards in Development Timeline.
Secrets & Lies
What secrets and lies follow your protagonist into the novel?
External Obstacles

What external obstacles have you already planted in the past that will keep your protagonist from their current goal? Or possibly help your protagonist attain it? Write them here and then add them to your Idea List or to Scene cards depending on how specific they are.
Three “why” tests for plot points from Idea List

Look at all of your plot points from your Idea List and other Scene Cards and run them through these tests to see if they can be used in your story. Explore them in chronological order as best you can. Get rid of anything that has logic fails and doesn’t pass the test. When this process leads you to fresh ideas and info, add these to your Ideas List. If any specific scene solidifies for you then create a Scene card for it.
Does your plot need it to happen?
Logistically, why can it happen? Is it actually possible?
Why would it happen, given your protagonist’s inner struggle?

Look over your Idea List and your scene cards and identify any potential subplots that pop out at you. Make a list of potentials in order of appearance of your novel…or what you guess would be order of appearance. Look at the list and identify any subplots already in play when your novel starts. Ask yourself, how will this subplot matter to my protagonist?
Use the Plot Problem Evaluation list from the scene template menu.
Plot Problem Test:
Look at each potential plot problem on your idea list and ask yourself these questions:
Is the problem capable of forcing my character to make the inner change that my novel is actually about?
Will the problem force my character to struggle with their misbelief?
Will the approaching consequence cost my character something big emotionally speaking even if he/she doesn’t achieve their goal?
Be sure you have completed these steps and fully understand your character and their backstory.

If you are a discovery writer, start to write your story with some of the ideas you have created in mind, and take into account what you know about your character, their misbeliefs, and their desires.
If you are a plotter, finish developing your plot with the ideas you have added to the Story Genius Plot Guide.
Use the Story Genius Scene template to ensure your scenes are necessary and answer all the necessary questions.
As you further develop your characters, fill out the Story Genius Character template so that the details you have created about your character are consistent and clear.
Continue to use the Story Genius tools in the revision of your work.

Write a detailed and specific “what if” for your character and story. Give it context, a surprise, and some conflict that leads to consequences that will hit on the internal struggle your character is experiencing.

Example from Story Genius: “What if a woman who has spent her whole life believing she’s successfully hedged her bets against love is on the verge of losing everything—the one person she’s felt close to, her lifelong career, and her grasp on reality? Mad with grief, she has one chance to set things right, but first, she must convince those around her that she’s not suicidal. So she devises a scheme to steal a dog for an hour or two, believing that getting a dog will reassure the people in her life that she’s back on the path to emotional stability. But when she can’t get rid of the dog, she’s forced to confront the fact that the very thing she spent her life avoiding—connection—is what makes the inevitable grief of loss endurable.”

cards.title: What is Your Character Like Before the Story Starts?

children.text: Write a thumbnail sketch of who your character is before the story starts. Who is this person on the inside? What do they believe? What do they want? What are they in life before the story starts?

cards.title: What Does Your Protagonist Already Want?

children.text: Write a short paragraph about what your character enters the novel wanting. Be as specific as possible even if the character doesn’t think they have a chance of getting it, still list it.
Why does your character want it, and what will it mean for your character to get it? What does she think it will say about her?

cards.title: Why Does Your Character Want It? (Desire)

children.text: What is the misbelief your character has that is preventing them from getting what they want? What’s the fear fueling this misbelief? Given the misbelief, what is the very worst thing that could happen according to your character?
When Did Your Character’s Misbelief Take Root? (Triggering Event)

Write a paragraph or two (a scene) about the moment your character’s misbelief took root. This is a defining moment that will constantly be at war with the character’s desire or what they want in the book.
What Did My Character Originally Go into the Scene Believing?
What existing, healthy belief does the misbelief topple? Ex: Initial belief: Love is safety vs. Misbelief: Love Destroys.
Why Does the Character Have That Initial Belief?
What experience originally taught the character that old belief such as the belief that love equals safety?
What is My Character’s Initial Goal in the Scene?
What does your character initially want to achieve in this scene? Be specific.
What Does My Character Expect Will Happen in the Scene?

This is different from the initial goal. Your character expects a certain outcome based on the goal. What is that exactly? The character must struggle between what they expected to happen and what is actually happening.

pl30.description: A simple but powerful outlining technique that starts with "Once upon a time..."

Act 3:
Protagonist has new routine established.
Having faced off against the Antagonist and won (or lost), the Protagonist can now return back to the Ordinary World with their new set of skills and perspective.
Have the Protagonist return to the Ordinary World with their spoils and completed character arc.
Don't be afraid to create a few more challenges along the road home.
Establish the Protagonist's new routine in the Ordinary World and how it has changed from the beginning.
Example:

And ever since then, the little penguin has been considered a hero for saving the colony from the seals and for forging a relationship with the whales. Now, the whales keep their homes safe so long as the penguins continue to lead aggressive seals their way.

End of Act 2:
Protagonist succeeds or fails.

This section brings the reader to the climax of the story, where they face off against the Antagonist, and either succeeds or fails. (Failure if the story is a drama or tragedy.) This is the payoff the reader has been waiting for. Make it big.
Have the Protagonist use all they have learned to this point to finally confront the Antagonist.
Show how the Protagonist has grown since the beginning of the story.
Create drama and tension – here is where the stakes are highest.
Example:

Until finally the little penguin remembered being told to avoid the deep depths where the whales lived. The little penguin used its newfound speed and swimming abilities to lead the seal into their territory, where the whales immediately begin chasing the seal, allowing the little penguin to escape home...

How will the Protagonist fare?

Challenges continue to pile up, becoming ever more difficult and dangerous. Here is where the Protagonist - and the reader - become unsure of the Protagonist's ability to succeed and whether they will be okay in the end.
Create a final set of consequences and obstacles facing the Protagonist that directly result from the previous section.
Continue to increase stakes, drama, and tension.
Show how the Protagonist is growing and using the tools they have gained to this point, though they may not be effective.
Example:

Because of that the little penguin was found and chased by a seal, and the penguin had to swim faster and faster to escape, realizing it now couldn't return home without risking the seal discovering where the penguins lived...

Middle of Act 2:
More consequences.
The first set of consequences leads to the next set of challenges, which are more dangerous and difficult to overcome.
Continue increasing the tension and raising the stakes for the Protagonist by adding another set of consequences stemming from the previous section.
Plant seeds of doubt that the Protagonist will be able to succeed in their situation.
Continue to consider the Protagonist's character arc and development.
Example:

Because of that, the little penguin's friends redoubled their efforts to make the penguin comfortable in the water, teaching it to swim faster and longer distances, until one day it swam into seal territory...
