Mid Act 2:
Dire consequences.

Breaking the routine causes dire consequences for the Protagonist, forcing them out of their comfort zone and into a New World of danger and challenges. Each challenge allows the Protagonist to grow, and develops their character arc toward becoming the Hero.
Introduce consequences the Protagonist is not fully equipped to deal with.
Consider how this consequence impacts the Protagonist's growth.
Example:
Because of that, the little penguin faced its fears and went into the water, but needed help from friends after having difficulty getting back on the ice...

Because of That occurs around the 35% mark.

Protagonist breaks routine.
The Protagonist either breaks their routine, or something happens to disrupt their routine, setting them on the path into the story and toward the New World.
Create an event that the Protagonist cannot ignore and cannot be solved on its own.
Create a clear goal or objective for the Protagonist, also known as the central question or goal.
Example:
But one day, the penguin leader decided all penguins must swim and catch food due to a shortage of fish in storage...

But, One Day occurs around the 25% mark.

End of Act 1:
Protagonist's routine is established.
This section introduces a typical day in the life of the Protagonist and how they function in their world.
Establish the Protagonist's routine and daily interactions.
Develop the Protagonist's Ordinary World.
Example:
Every day friends and family would bring the little penguin fish to eat...

Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Every Day occurs around the 15% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:
World is introduced.
This section introduces the readers to the Protagonist and their ordinary world.
Introduce the Protagonist, other main characters, and their ordinary world.
Set clear expectations and an understanding of what life is currently like.
Example:
Once upon a time, there was a little penguin who was afraid of water...

Once Upon a Time should take approximately 10% of the story.

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 3:
The Protagonist is victorious and transformed as they return to their Ordinary World with a new perspective. This concludes the story and character arc and confirms the overall theme of the story.
Present the Protagonist's return home with their new perspective.
Reaffirm the Protagonist's growth, the reasons for the journey, and their new hope.
Show how the Protagonist's new strength, perspective, and object/knowledge/abilities impact the Ordinary World.
Close the character arc for the Protagonist and all major characters, as well as the story arc.
Give a moment of celebration/enjoyment for the Protagonist and decide if home is too small or if they want to stay.
If Part of a Series:
Leave some loose threads and room for further character development for the Protagonist.
Consider leaving tantalizing unfinished storylines or setting a hook for the next installment.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up 25% of the story.
Outcome (New World) occurs around the 95-98% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 3:

The Protagonist finally transforms, leaving their old self and character flaw behind, to achieve their goal and emerge victorious over the Antagonist. The Antagonist may be defeated, driven off to fight another day, or captured. The Protagonist may need to sacrifice in some way to win – perhaps even making the ultimate sacrifice.
Demonstrate how the Protagonist is transformed into a new, stronger version of themselves.
Depict how the Protagonist has left behind their flaw and false beliefs (e.g. fears turns to confidence, arrogance becomes humility, or I can't becomes I can and will!)
Have the final battle end in a dramatic fashion.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up 25% of the story.
Death (of Character Flaw) occurs around the 90% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 3:

It's the final showdown and the biggest test of the Protagonist. The Protagonist and Antagonist confront each other in a dramatic face-off, and the Protagonist must use all they have learned along the way to achieve their goal. The stakes are at their highest; in fact, the fate of the entire world may hang in the balance. Make it impactful. This is the moment the reader has been waiting for.
Dramatize the final battle.
Show how the Protagonist is using all they have learned to be successful.
The higher the stakes, the higher the drama, the more satisfying the payoff.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up 25% of the story.
Battle occurs around the 85% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 3:

The Antagonist is at their most powerful, and stakes are at their highest. An event occurs which changes the Protagonist's perspective switching them from reaction to action. This event changes the Protagonist's mental state and makes them realize how to stop the Antagonist. This is a turning point in the story.

Create an urgent triggering event that changes the Protagonist's perspective (e.g. perhaps the Antagonist has attacked with the full force of their armies, there is an immediate threat to someone close, or it has been realized the true Antagonist was hiding behind a puppet Antagonist).
Reconfirm the danger and urgency of the Protagonist's pursuit of their goal and remind the reader of the central dramatic question/event.
Show that the Protagonist is now ready to face the final confrontation.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up 25% of the story.
Girding the Loins occurs around the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:
Suffering a defeat, the Protagonist regresses back into their character flaw. They are not yet aware that the flaw is an issue, but that will become apparent.
Restate the character flaw and show how it is reinforced by the previous defeat (e.g. I can't do this because I am too out of shape; if I was in better shape, I would have succeeded).
Use this scene to show the Protagonist had been moving toward transformation and their disheartening slide back to the comfortable ways of old.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story.
Revisiting the Flaw occurs around the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

The Protagonist is gaining confidence and suffering a few defeats along the way, but they are close to reaching their Goal – close, but not successful. Something happens to thwart their attempt at success. The Protagonist is overwhelmed by this new world and is left doubting their abilities and in a low place.
How has the Protagonist been thwarted, and what was lost? For example, a vital object, an ally, or faith in themselves.
Consider adding a twist by having the Goal Thwarted by the betrayal of a close Ally or Mentor.
The Protagonist comes to doubt their resolve and ability to succeed in their pursuit of their goal.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story.
Goal Thwarted occurs around the 40% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Early in Act 2:

The Protagonist, presented with trials and obstacles in their new world, now meets or becomes aware of the Antagonist for the first time. This raises the stakes and tension in the story while introducing the power and threat of the Antagonist.
What scene will present the most impactful entrance of the Antagonist?
Show the Protagonist not fully comfortable in their new role.
Introduce enemies and harsh new challenges.
Consider adding Allies to assist the Protagonist in their time of struggle.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story.
Antagonist Revealed occurs around the 30% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

The Protagonist takes up the challenge presented by the Inciting Incident and makes their first attempt at reaching their goal. They are still uncomfortable with their new pursuit, leading to missteps and failures. These are learning lessons for the Protagonist and help in their transformation.
What was the external or internal force that pushed the Protagonist to pursue their goal?
Show the Protagonist leaving the comfort of their Ordinary World as they begin to navigate their new world.
Re-establish the central issue or the Protagonist's task.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story.
Drive for Goal occurs around the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1:
If not already introduced, introduce the Protagonist's character flaw here. If already introduced, expand upon it. This flaw is what will be resolved by the end of the story.
Highlight the Protagonist's character flaw – are they arrogant, set in their ways, lacking confidence, fearful?
This character flaw must be partially overcome or assuaged for the Protagonist to begin their journey in pursuit of their goal, often with the assistance of a Mentor or Ally.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up 25% of the story.
Display of Flaw occurs around the 20% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1:

The Protagonist realizes what their external goal is and decides if they will go after it or not. An external goal could be a job promotion, the pursuit of a Love Interest, or the acquisition of a particular item or piece of knowledge. There may be a false belief or a character flaw, however, that prevents them from immediately pursuing their goal.
Determine what the Protagonist's external goal is and show them becoming aware of its importance.
The Protagonist may not be willing to answer the call of the Inciting Incident, requiring raising stakes and tension until they are willing to fully pursue their goal.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up 25% of the story.
Character Realizes Goal occurs around the 15% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1:

The Inciting Incident is the event that ultimately forces the Protagonist out of their Ordinary World and into an adventure or journey of transformation. This section triggers the rest of the story by introducing a goal that must be achieved before the Protagonist can return to the Ordinary World.
Identify a dramatic triggering event that cannot be resolved on its own (e.g. an attack, a death, a job loss, a threat from a Villain, fighting corrupt powers, or an impending disaster).
Show how this event makes the Protagonist uncomfortable in their Ordinary World.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up 25% of the story.
Inciting Incident occurs around the 12-15% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:
The Opening Scene sets the stage for the story. Here the Protagonist is introduced, their ordinary world is depicted, and the Protagonist's flaw or the story's theme is introduced.
Introduce the Protagonist and showcase their comfort in their ordinary world.
Hint at something that displeases the Protagonist about their life/world.
Hint at the Protagonist's character flaw and/or the story's theme.
Create a Protagonist that readers can connect to with flaws, hopes, desires, and a unique personality.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up 25% of the story.
Opening Scene brings the story to around the 10-12% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2:

The Protagonist has gone through trials and losses and has entered a dark place. Generally, by this point, they are at their lowest and need a confidence boost or a reminder of why they are capable and what they are fighting for. A visit with an Ally aids or gives advice that finally changes the Protagonist. This is often the 'you had it in you the whole time' moment, or the moment an existing object is found to have previously unknown power.
What has brought the Protagonist to their lowest? Who is best to pull them out of their dark place?
Break the Protagonist's doubt – the Protagonist has gone through trials and losses, and this scene needs to be inspirational for the Protagonist and the reader.
Decide if Assistance will take the form of a pep talk, the discovery of new knowledge, learning about the true power of an object, or something else.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story.
Ally Assistance occurs around the 70% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Late in Act 2:

The Protagonist develops a new plan to reach their goal. The Antagonist surprises the Protagonist and makes things worse, causing the Protagonist to fail, forcing the Protagonist to develop a new plan. Repeat.
Have the Protagonist develop a new goal and plan of attack (e.g. the Protagonist will attack the Antagonist at their base of operations).
The Antagonist pulls a surprising maneuver (e.g. the base of operations was simply a safe house, and the actual base is still hidden).
Thwarted, the Protagonist must devise a new plan and deal with their losses (the Protagonist must formulate a plan to locate the actual base).
Repeat several times.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story.
Repeat the Cycle occurs around the 55% mark.

Luke turns off his computer-aided navigation system to use the Force to take the shot at the Death Star’s single vulnerability, successfully blowing it up and saving the day. children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:
The opening section shows us what the hero’s world is like, introduces all the main characters and introduces the hero’s flaw or flaws.
Create a robust picture of the Hero's ordinary world and how they interact within it.
Create a sense of comfort for the Hero, but consider including something about the world that displeases the Hero.
Develop a three-dimensional character with flaws, hopes, problems, and a unique personality.
Identify the Hero's wants (external) and needs (internal).
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
A Day in the Life brings the story to the 8% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1:

Something happens and the Hero’s world is flipped on its head. This is where the hook comes in. You can also consider this the call to adventure, where the Hero is presented the opportunity to go on some kind of adventure.
Decide upon a compelling hook / inciting incident – this should be something that cannot be resolved on its own, and must be interesting to the audience.

Consider whether the inciting incident will be a personal loss like a death in the family, an external attack like a kidnapping, a natural force like a tornado, or based upon a larger disruption to the Hero's world like a war?
This is the hook that carries the audience into the story.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Spark occurs around the 8% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1:

The Hero needs to decide whether to embark on this adventure or take this new opportunity. 99% of the time the Hero will refuse initially, but something will drive them to make a decision and go go go… right into Act 2!
If the Hero initially refuses the call to adventure, increase the tension and stakes until refusal is no longer an option.

Consider creating a willing Hero who wants to take up the call but is facing obstacles to do so (e.g. they want to stop the villain, but their specialized weapons have been confiscated by the government).
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Do I Stay or Do I go occurs around the 15% mark.

cards.title: Do I Stay or Do I Go?

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

Act 2 begins with the Hero boldly venturing into their new world, which is the opposite of the world they have lived in up to this point. Remember, it doesn’t literally have to be a New World — just an unfamiliar place or situation.

Bring the audience into the New World by showcasing what is different about this world versus the Hero's ordinary world highlighted at the beginning (e.g. a tropical rain forest, an alien planet, a spaceship, or a far-off land.)
The New World should be exciting but also a bit daunting to the Hero – what about this New World creates a sense of unease for the Hero or hinders them?
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Into the New World occurs around the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Early Act 2:
The new world often comes with a few new characters, including the Love Interest. The Love Interest usually represents what the Hero needs – not what the Hero wants, but what they actually need.
Introduce new characters, including the Love Interest. Pay attention to your character development, as each major character must have an arc.
How does the love interest represent the Hero's needs? Remember needs are internal (e.g. courage, self-confidence, appreciation, or humility).
The introduction of the Love Interest must be enticing to the audience, who must care about the relationship.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
What is Love occurs around the 35% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Mid Act 2:

Remember that awesome hook you thought up? This is where you pay it off. The hero has fun with her new powers or her new situation. The audience should absolutely love this part. A large portion of a movie’s trailer often comes from scenes in this section.
Experiment with the Hero's new power or situation, showcasing what they can do and how they can still grow.
Have fun with this section – the greater the passion involved, the deeper the buy-in for the audience.
This should be a scene that has the audience talking and telling their friends.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Melt Their Faces Off occurs around the 40% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

At the midpoint of the film (and Act Two), the Hero crosses the point of no return. They do something they can’t undo, which will plunge them into the second half of Act 2, which is the nightmare. But not quite yet...

The trigger for the Hero's point of no return must be something significant (e.g. they kill the Villain's henchman, cause an international incident, disobey the government, or lose a vital item or object).
Consider the possible consequences of this action. How does it impact the story? How does it affect the Hero's mindset?
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Crossing the Rubicon occurs around the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Mid Act 2:

The Hero gets a moment of clarity and everything seems like it’s going to be okay — they thinks they're going to prevail. One small note here — in some movies this is the moment of false defeat. But either way the hero is headed into the Long Journey into Night.
Have the Hero celebrate a victory and gain further confidence (e.g. they foil a portion of the Villain's plan, not realizing it is part of a larger scheme).
Give the Hero and the audience a false sense of victory and relief (e.g. they found the source of the Villain's power and believe they know how to stop it).

Alternatively, consider having the Hero suffer a false defeat (e.g. perhaps the Villain has absconded with an essential item or object, or the Hero's efforts to repair a dam cause another section to fail, threatening a town with a deluge of water).
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
False Victory occurs around the 55% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Late Act 2:

Here’s where things go from bad to worse. The Villains come back far more powerful than before. The Hero’s losing their external and internal battle. Often the Love Interest leaves at this point. Things continue to get dire.

Show the Hero in a severe state of struggle (e.g. the Villain that escaped has returned with a greater army, is more powerful due to an object they stole previously, or all the Hero's efforts just seem to fail).
Have the Hero descend into darkness as everything seems to fall apart around them, such that both the Hero - and the audience - begin to doubt if they can be successful.
Demonstrate how the the Hero's inability to face their flaws continues to hinder them.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Long Journey into Night occurs around the 60% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Late Act 2:
Things could not get worse, the Villains seem unstoppable, and all hope is lost. The Love Interest ditched the Hero, usually because of the Hero’s flaw, and things are at their most hopeless.
Show the Villain wracking up victory after victory – they have unleashed the full force of their might, and all hope for the Hero appears to be lost, as they still struggle to face their flaws.
Use this section to ramp up tension and drama as the Villain appears to be heading toward successfully implementing their evil plan.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Rock Bottom occurs around the 65% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2:

The Hero realizes their flaw, learns their lesson, and formulates a plan to defeat the Villain. Here’s where the A story — the main plot, and the B story — often the Love Interest — meet. This is also the moment when the Hero rushes right into Act 3.
Determine what leads the Hero to finally face their flaws and regain the determination to face the Villain (e.g. an epiphany, discovery of new information, or a pep talk with a Mentor or Ally).
Showcase the Hero's new perspective / abilities and identify how it gives them the strength and confidence to face the Villain.
Have the newly inspired Hero make amends with the Love Interest and devise a plan to foil the Villain.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
From the Ashes occurs around the 70% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 3:

The Hero faces the Villain, who is at their strongest, and wins! By winning, they have now changed the world. The Hero is now older and wiser. And every major character has changed —  this can be one of the trickiest parts of writing a screenplay. Every major character has to have an arc and change in some way by the end of the movie.
The final payoff for the audience, this section must be dramatic, exciting, and satisfying.
Vanquish the Villain or stop their vile plan.
Show how the Hero has transformed from the beginning and satisfied their wants and needs.
Wrap up the character arcs for the other major characters and show how they have changed, as well.
Celebrate the Hero as they return to the ordinary world – how has it changed with their victory?
If the film is part of a series, be sure to leave room for further development of the Hero and perhaps set a hook for the next story.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Time to Kick Ass starts around the 75% mark.

pl24.name: Villain's Journey
pl24.description: An outline formula for writing villains based on the classic Hero's Journey

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 3:

Victory is snatched away by the Hero... and the Villain is left to face the consequences. They may be destroyed, killed, banished, jailed, or convinced to turn back to the path of good. No matter the outcome, the Villain is no longer a threat as they were at the beginning of the story.
Finish the final confrontation between Villain and Hero, with the Villain failing and the Hero emerging victorious.
Outline the consequences for the Villain and what they have learned (if they are still alive).
Close the character arc of the Villain and any remaining loose threads from their story.
If part of a series, set the hook for the next installment and hint at the Villain's next diabolical plan.

While the Villain's Journey closely mirrors the Hero's Journey, the Villain does not have a reward, a homecoming, or an opportunity to relax in a new world they have created. They have been defeated and are sent off to lick their wounds and devise another plan.
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Ordeal, Death, Rebirth occurs around the 75% mark.
The Villain's final consequences occur around the 90% - 95% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 2:

After overcoming the trials and challenges of the previous section, the Villain faces their greatest challenge yet. This is the moment they have been waiting for throughout the story, as they prepare to use their devastating weapon, launch their armies, ready their final trap, or otherwise enact their diabolical plan. Only one obstacle remains... the Hero.
Show the Villain's preparations coming close to fruition.
Create a sense of possibility that the Villain will be successful in their plan.
Bring the Villain to the cusp of success before the Hero comes in to ruin their fun.
Create a dramatic and thrilling final showdown – this is the major confrontation of the story.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Approach occurs around the 55% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 2:

The Villain faces a series of tests and challenges, often failing again and again – don't forget, there is a pesky Hero trying to foil their plans! Whether they're seeking a lost item, tracking down the Hero, hunting those that betrayed them, or seeking new information, these challenges block the Villain's path; so, the Villain seeks Allies to assist them in achieving their ultimate goal. At some point, the Villain is offered a chance at salvation, an opportunity to turn back from their chosen path, but they refuse.
Have the Villain face a series of challenges, each offering a lesson and leading directly to the next challenge.
Create empathy for the Villain and show things from their perspective.
Introduce Allies to assist the Villain in facing their obstacles – some of whom may perish, quit the adventure, or be sacrificed by the Villain for the cause.
Create exciting and interesting ways for the Villain to fail.
Offer the Villain some form of victory, which helps lead them to their largest challenge.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Tests, Allies, and Enemies occurs around the 35% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

The Villain officially Crosses the Threshold by taking action and committing a serious offence or crime. They may steal, kill, rob, or kidnap, but whatever it is, they are now past the point of no return and are beginning on the path to their ultimate goal. They are now unquestionably the story's Villain.
Re-establish the Central Issue of the story.
What action does the Villain take to push them beyond the point of return?
How do these actions further the Villain's diabolical schemes?
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
Crossing the Threshold occurs around the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
End of Act 1:

The Villain's Mentor may be a more powerful Villain, a figure of command, or another form of assistance: an object of power; a book; or access to dangerous information. The knowledge, skills, or objects they gain will assist them on their Journey. The Mentor helps the Villain feel prepared enough to begin.
Introduce the Villain's Mentor or guiding force.
Identify the knowledge, tools, or other forms of support provided by the Mentor.
Show how the Mentor works with the Villain to change their perspective.
Demonstrate how the new knowledge or abilities can assist the Villain in their mission.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Meeting the Mentor occurs around the 20% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1:

The Villain may not be willing to jump at the Call to Adventure immediately: they may hesitate or refuse to kill someone, attempt to find another solution to their problem, or rationalize the event which upset their world. By contrast, a willing Villain will be ready to jump into the action but may be prevented by obstacles that first need to be overcome.
Have the Villain hesitate or refuse the call – perhaps include a twinge of conscience (e.g. hesitating to take action against an old friend or ally).
Present the Villain's counterarguments to taking up the challenge.
Raise the stakes so that the Villain ultimately has no choice but to act.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Refusal of the Call occurs around the 15% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Middle of Act 1:

The event which upset the Villain in Beat 1 becomes their Call here. For example: they may need to repair their project at all costs; avenge the death of a loved one; fight the allies that betrayed them; or feel the urge to put an evil plan into play. Villains usually do not see themselves as evil or wrong-doers; they generally see themselves as trying to right a wrong or make the world a better place. But most people do not agree with their methods or sense of reality.
Turn the displeasing event in Beat 1 into a Call to Adventure, a reason for the Villain to be thrust into the story.
Give the Villain a unique perspective that makes it clear they do not see themselves as evil.
Introduce the overall theme of the story and the Central Issue to be resolved.
How will succeeding in this Journey make the Villain's world better?
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Call to Adventure occurs around the 10% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:

As the story begins, the Villain is in their Ordinary World... and something is not quite right. For example: an important project they've been working on has gone wrong; they feel betrayed by their government; they've witnessed a loved one die; or they've given in to their darkest desires. This section either creates sympathy for the Villain or a feeling of revulsion. Either way, the key is to hook the reader with an emotional response to the Villain's behavior.
Introduce the readers to the Villain and their Ordinary World.
Show something in the Villain's world that displeases them.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
Ordinary World brings the story to about the 10% mark.

pl14.name: W Plot
pl14.description: A five point story structure for novelists and screenwriters

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Act 3:

The Protagonist begins to resolve their problem with the assistance of new hope, ideas, new/returning Allies, or a personal change – and the action starts to rise once more to the Resolution. A moment of epiphany may serve as another minor complication but ultimately leads to a resolution. The problem's solution leads to a sense of completion or change for the Protagonist.
Offer new hope which begins to solve the problem (e.g. the Ally who purchased the replacement ticket remains calm in the face of this new dilemma and begins to look for other options).

Include an epiphany moment (e.g. it is not possible for a direct flight, but they find a series of connecting flights from a different airline which will get the Protagonist to the funeral on time, at an added expense).
Show that problem is resolved and the Protagonist attains their goal (e.g. after trials and tribulations, the Protagonist arrives in Europe just in time to attend the funeral).

Demonstrate how the Protagonist has grown (e.g. The Protagonist learns the value of enlisting the support of others and also learns to stay calm in the face of difficulties, making it easier to find solutions).

Spend time with the Protagonist following their newly attained goal (e.g. they attend the funeral, reminisce with family, and perhaps meet a new love interest or discover something that sparks a new adventure).
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
The moment of epiphany occurs around the 85% to 90% mark.
The Resolution brings the story to its conclusion.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
End of Act 2:

The lowest point in the story. The Protagonist has tried and failed to resolve the problem, but it looks as though all hope is lost as they face their worst-case scenario. They cannot solve the problem on their own; they need help in the form of new hope, ideas, new/returning Allies, or a personal change within themselves.

Deepen the problem and raise the stakes to make it appear as though all hope is lost (e.g. the issue with the landing gear is that it is broken, and the plane must be pulled from service, cancelling the flight. The next available flight leaves too late, and the funeral will be missed).
Identify a path forward for the Protagonist to resolve the problem (e.g. the Protagonist turns to the Ally that purchased the new ticket and enlists their assistance once more).
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The 2nd Turning Point occurs around the 75% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Beginning of Act 2:

The 2nd Triggering Event is a reversal of fortune in the story – though a lesser event than the 1st Triggering Event, it deepens the Protagonist's problem. It initiates downward action in the story once more, creating a new conflict or dilemma. The tension and the stakes are rising, leading to the lowest point in the story.
Introduce the 2nd Triggering event that threatens the Protagonist's goal once more (e.g. there is an announcement at the airport that there is an issue with the plane).
Increase drama and tension by raising the stakes and deepening the problem (e.g. the issue with the plane is broken landing gear).
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% - 75%.
The 2nd Triggering Event occurs around the 50% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
End of Act 1:

The 1st Turning Point occurs at the first low point in the story, when it looks like the Protagonist may not attain their goal. This turning point takes the story in a new, positive direction, as a change in the situation appears to increase the likelihood of success. The tension eases as the Protagonist starts recovering from the problem (for example, with the help of Allies or new information), and the story begins to climb again toward the middle of the book.
Introduce a low point for the Protagonist (e.g. they realize they accidentally shredded their ticket with a pile of old documents. They cannot afford a new ticket).
Introduce Allies, a new idea, or other solution to the problem (e.g. a wealthy friend hears about the unfortunate events and offers to buy a new ticket).
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The 1st Turning Point occurs around the 25% mark.
--- Add Your Details Above This Line ---
Beginning of Act 1:

Begin your story with the setup in the Protagonist's ordinary world, leading to the Triggering Event, an external event that sets the story in motion. This could be discovering new knowledge, a job loss, a birth/death, a trip, or an invitation to adventure. It must be a critical event for the story, which introduces a problem that interferes with the character's goal and increases drama, bringing the story to its first low point.
Begin the story in the ordinary world and introduce the Protagonist (e.g. they live in Canada and work a mid-range job).
Choose the most important event from the series of events in the story to launch it (e.g. the Protagonist needs to fly to Europe for the funeral of a close family member).

Set up a problem to begin lowering the action and increasing drama. This will bring the story to the 1st Turning Point (e.g. the Protagonist needs to leave for their flight but cannot find their tickets).
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
The Trigger Event should occur approximately around the 10% mark.
This entire section should bring the story approximately to the 25% mark.

proj2.name: Write Your First Nonfiction Book
proj2.description: Based on the book with step-by-step instructions by Honorée Corder.

children.text: You want your reader to feel like they absolutely can create their desired results. They picked up your book because they want what you have as easily and quickly as possible, without pain and suffering. Chapter One is designed to give them the confidence to keep striving for their goal.

Because we find ourselves in others, sharing the success stories of others is helpful. It’s likely that Chapter One didn’t do the job entirely because you are the expert, so your readers will think you’re a magical unicorn, and they can’t possibly get the same results as mere mortals. This chapter can help them get a better sense that they, too, can be successful.

You’ve figured something out, and this is what you are sharing in your book. This is the instructional part of your book, the meat, and its purpose is to provide what your reader can do, step-by-step, to duplicate your results.
Your readers will get the best results if they have a simple formula they can read, remember, do, and share. Take your process and make it a “no-brainer” for your reader.
How can they put what they’ve learned from you into practice? Give them more information so not only will they achieve success, but they can also avoid failure.
On your journey, you’ve probably also figured out or discovered a few additional pieces of information they will find invaluable. Include these distinctions and goodies in this chapter.
Do you have some additional secret sauce? Pointers for avoiding mistakes or accelerating results? Put them in this chapter, a little of both if you’re feeling generous.

You got ’em fired up in Chapter One, send them off to do great deeds, and, as my friend Jay Papasan says, Eat tacos. Okay, not really about the tacos, but you do want them to feel empowered, inspired, and well equipped to take immediate action. (This can, and may, include eating tacos. Who’s to say?)
What’s your subject matter?
What aspect of your subject matter are you talking about, and what point of view are you taking
What is your reader going to read and learn, and their potential takeaways.
Amp up the excitement! End your Introduction in such a way your reader is excited and ready to turn the page and dive into the book.
Back Matter

A book’s back (or end) matter provides an opportunity for the relationship started in the front matter and the main content of the book to continue outside of the book. I call this maximization or monetization.
The back matter of a book can include any or all of the following (or just simply provide an author’s bio, including their website):
Author Notes
Acknowledgments
Special Invitation
Glossary
Bibliography
Index
Call to Action

notes.title: Back Matter
Bestselling Book Formula

children.text: The Bestselling Book Formula
consists of four elements or keys, and they are read, remember, do, and share. What that means is that the book’s title, premise, and the formula contained within it are easy to

1. Read. Is the book easy to read?
2. Remember. Is the book’s title or formula easy to remember?
3. Do. Is what the book teaches easy to do?
4. Share. Is the book’s title or formula easy to share?

children.text: Let’s get the bones of your Introduction down:
What’s your subject matter?

Amp up the excitement! End your Introduction in such a way your reader is excited and ready to turn the page and dive into the book.

notes.title: Big Idea
8 Chapters

children.text: Chapter One: Encouragement.

You want your reader to feel like they absolutely can create their desired results. They picked up your book because they want what you have as easily and quickly as possible, without pain and suffering. Chapter One is designed to give them the confidence to keep striving for their goal.
Chapter Two: Stories and examples.

Because we find ourselves in others, sharing the success stories of others is helpful. It’s likely that Chapter One didn’t do the job entirely because you are the expert, so your readers will think you’re a magical unicorn, and they can’t possibly get the same results as mere mortals. This chapter can help them get a better sense that they, too, can be successful.
Chapter Three: An overview of the process.

You’ve figured something out, and this is what you are sharing in your book. This is the instructional part of your book, the meat, and its purpose is to provide what your reader can do, step-by-step, to duplicate your results.
Chapter Four: Short formula in the form of an acronym, process, or alliteration.
Your readers will get the best results if they have a simple formula they can read, remember, do, and share. Take your process and make it a “no-brainer” for your reader.
Chapter Five: The Formula in action.
How can they put what they’ve learned from you into practice? Give them more information so not only will they achieve success, but they can also avoid failure.
Chapter Six: Other tips, tools, resources, and ideas.
On your journey, you’ve probably also figured out or discovered a few additional pieces of information they will find invaluable. Include these distinctions and goodies in this chapter.
Chapter Seven: How to get results in the best possible way.
Do you have some additional secret sauce? Pointers for avoiding mistakes or accelerating results? Put them in this chapter, a little of both if you’re feeling generous.
Chapter Eight: Call to action.

You got ’em fired up in Chapter One, send them off to do great deeds, and, as my friend Jay Papasan says, Eat tacos. Okay, not really about the tacos, but you do want them to feel empowered, inspired, and well equipped to take immediate action. (This can, and may, include eating tacos. Who’s to say?)

A black-and-white mirror image of the book’s front cover
A second title page
Copyright page
Dedication
Acknowledgments (These can also go in the back matter.)
Special Invitation (This is where you can invite your readers to get to know you better by offering something of value in exchange for their email.)

proj4.description: This plot guide is a companion piece to the Story Genius method, and provides you with information on each step you'll take through the process, and where each element you'll create belongs in Plottr.

children.text: Throughout your character’s life, they have made several turning-point decisions that have been guided by the misbelief you established in the previous scene. Sketch them out. To nail down three truly crucial moments for your character, consider that these moments need to have the following:
External events that in some fundamental way—due to intense internal conflict—cause the character’s misbelief to deepen.
Had to make a decision that had escalating ongoing ramifications that further confirm the misbelief.
Must yield the most story-specific info
Sketch them in chronological order.

Once you have sketched them out in the scene cards in the Story Genius Plot Guide, write the scenes fully, either here in these scene cards, or in the character template provided. The goal is to have all of this backstory in one platform for you to keep track of. Make sure to write them in chronological order.

cards.title: Create 3 Crossroads Scenes that Reinforce the Misbelief

children.text: Answer the following questions, and write a scene to "show' them to yourself.

NOTE: This scene is part of pre-writing and may or may not appear in your book, or the information found in it can help reveal more about your character's backstory woven through the book. This scene is more for you as the author than for the reader.
Write the scene in first person
Answer each question below, and use your answers to write the scene
When Did Your Character's Misbelief Take Root? (Triggering Event)

Write a paragraph or two (a scene) about the moment your character’s misbelief took root. This is a defining moment that will constantly be at war with the character’s desire or what they want in the book.
What Did My Character Originally Go into the Scene Believing?
What existing, healthy belief does the misbelief topple? Ex: Initial belief: Love is safety vs. Misbelief: Love Destroys.
Why Does the Character Have That Initial Belief?
What experience originally taught the character that old belief such as the belief that love equals safety?
What is My Character’s Initial Goal in the Scene?
What does your character initially want to achieve in this scene? Be specific.
What Does My Character Expect Will Happen in the Scene?

This is different from the initial goal. Your character expects a certain outcome based on the goal. What is that exactly? The character must struggle between what they expected to happen and what is actually happening.
Breakdown: Pre-Writing
This scene happens before your story begins
Writing these and other backstory scenes helps you construct your plot based on your characters and who they are as they enter the story.
Nail down one truly crucial moment for your character, including the following:
An external event that in some fundamental way—due to intense internal conflict—cause the character’s misbelief to deepen.
A time when your character had to make a decision that had escalating ongoing ramifications that further confirm the misbelief.
This scene must yield story-specific information about your character
Write this scene as the first event that impacted your character after the initial misbelief triggering scene

Explore the external plot problem that will encompass your story and cause your main character to face their misbelief in order to get to their core desires. If you have done all the work so far, this external plot problem will likely be obvious.
Make sure this problem is the overall big problem, and one it will take an entire novel to solve.
Make sure this problem solidly hits the "third rail" of your character's misbelief and desires
Make sure this external plot problem will take plenty of work to solve and will cause your character both internal and external conflict

If you have several ideas, freewrite a scene card about each, labeling it OEPP (to set it apart from other plot problems you will add to this idea timeline) and evaluate it based on the above criteria
Trust your instincts and choose the problem that you want to write and that will make your character and therefore your reader consider their misbeliefs and cause them to face them head on

This problem helps define the theme and dirction of your story
Defining this External Plot Problem will guide the rest of your Plotting process.

cards.title: What is the Obvious External Plot Problem?

children.text: Sketch out ideas of possible scenes or story ticks that will build to the opening scene of your book. Opening scene and hook. You need to figure out what event or hook puts your character on a path of no return so to speak. The hook is not to be confused with the inciting incident, although those two moments can happen fairly close together. Consider the hook the invitation to action and the inciting incident is when the character, willingly or unwillingly, finally accepts that call to action.
So what ticks or scenes occur before the book starts that lead to the big tick or hook wherein we invite the character to take action or accept the call?

You can have as many ticks or scenes as you want that lead to the beginning scene of your book. We have a few scene cards (ticks) in the template, but feel free to add more scene cards based on how many ticks you have before your novel begins.

These are ideas that are too fuzzy for you to conceptualize. You have a vague notion of what will happen but no real specifics. Remember, generalizations kill your story and cause writer's block. Be as specific as possible with your ideas, but don't be afraid to add vague ones here and try to flesh them out.
Any scene that you can envision but doesn’t seem to have a connection to your character’s internal struggle. These are romping around ideas.

Cards that you’ve determined are story specific and eligible for a place in your novel’s cause-and-effect trajectory. Give these cards a scene number to help you put your ideas in chronological order.
The first point of conflict and the moment that propels the Protagonist into the story. This event begins the Central Conflict of the story and must be one that cannot be resolved on its own.
Tie the Inciting Incident to the basic conflict within the story, revealed in the Unavoidable Problem.
Create a strong Inciting Incident that ultimately forces the Protagonist's hand to take action.
Ensure the Incident and the Protagonist's reaction impact the third rail and hook the reader deeper into the story.
Breakdown:
The Inciting Incident occurs around the 10-15% mark in the story.

The crux of the story and the height of suspense and tension. This is the turning point for the story and Protagonist. This is where everything starts to fall apart, and the attitude of your protagonist toward their misbeliefs and desires changes. Now they must take action based on this change, and determine how to move forward.
Consider how their actions at this juncture will transform the story and impact their character arc and the third rail.
Restate the Unavoidable Problem, and show you character contemplating the potential solution to it.
Show the reader how your main character could either succeed or fail here, depending on what decisions they make.
Breakdown:
The Midpoint (something changes) occurs around the 50% mark.

Believing their desires are now unattainable, the main character is forced to examiine their misbelief more closely. Was it true in the first place, or is it entirely false? If it is false, what is the truth? For them, this is the Dark Night, the worst it can get. They underestimated the power of the external events or antagonist that has led them to this point, and because of this they may also feel guilt and responsibility for the outcome.
How did they underestimate the Antagonist?
Display the Protagonist's mental state and their relationship with their misbelief and desires– are they angry, depressed, forlorn, or wracked with guilt?
Further increase the stakes and create the impression that victory is impossible.
Breakdown:
The Dark Night generally occurs between the 70-80% mark of your story.

cards.title: The Dark Night (The Worst It Can Get)

children.text: Create the “aha!” moment (usually happens right before, during, or right after the final conflict of your story) when your protagonist realizes what they have been taught. When does your protagonist’s struggle end and the misbelief debunked? What allows the character to resolve the external problem or make peace with it? When you create the “aha!” moment answer the following questions.
Will your character achieve the external goal at the end?
What will change for your character internally?
What will happen externally in the scene that forces your protagonist to confront and hopefully overcome the misbelief?
Breakdown:
The "Aha" moment can occur right before, during, or right after the final conflict of your story.

The story's Unavoidable Problem is resolved, and the Protagonist has either succeeded and transformed or failed and remained stagnant. They challenged their misbelief and changed their thinking, resulting in both an internal and external victory. While they may or may not have attained their initial desires, they have gotten what they needed.
Tie up any remaining loose ends in your story..
Conclude the character arcs for all characters and their relationship with their misbeliefs.
This is the final payoff for the reader – make it dramatic and memorable.
Breakdown:
The Resolution generall occurs around the 80-90% mark of your story.

Lisa Cron, the author of Story Genius, is not big on story structure or story structure books. Not any of them. So we have added here some of the common major plot points and some of the one's Lisa mentions in her book to provide a loose roadmap to help you construct your story.
Most often, the Story Genius Plot Guide will work best combined with another story structure based on your genre, personal preferences, and how "structured" you like your outline to be.

cards.title: NOTE: Story Structure and Lisa Cron
Floating in the Ocean (The Ordinary World)

children.text: This is your character's ordinary world, where they are simply floating in the ocean of life. Things might not be great, but they are okay. Give us a glimpse of who they are and what matters to them.
Create an ordinary world where your character is either content with life or ignorant of oncoming disaster.
Throw a hitch in their ordinary life hinting at the trouble to come
Don't allow your ordinary world to be boring. Show a daily routine that portrays who your character is.
This is the start of your story. Be sure your character is interesting and empathetic right away.
Breakdown:
Floating in the ocean generally makes up the first 5% of your story.

A problem arises that your character must face. It cannot be solved on its own, but it requires your character to intervene in some way. This problem must impact your character's misbelief and threaten their desires.
Introduce the primary problem of the story.
Show that this is the overall problem your character must resolve by the end of the story, even if they don't realize how large of a problem it is at this moment.
State the theme of your story here, either through a character verbalizing it, or showing it clearly to your reader.
Be sure this problem drives your character toward the inciting incident and the start of the story.
Remember to use the Story Genius Scene template to ensure that this scene impacts the third rail (misbelief and desire) and pulls the reader immediately into the story.
Breakdown:
The unavoidable problem usually arrives somewhere between 5-10% of the way into your story.

proj1.name: Snowflake Method
proj1.description: Based on the Snowflake Method by Randy Ingermanson

children.text: --- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 3:

The Third Disaster comes at the end of Act 2, approximately 75% of the way through the story. The Third Disaster is something bad that forces your Protagonist AND the Antagonist (if there is an Antagonist) to commit to some final showdown that will decide who wins and who loses. That is, they must both commit to end the story.
Example - Star Wars:

In the original Star Wars movie (Episode 4), at the end of Act 2, Luke and his comrades reach the rebel planet, where they learn that the stormtroopers put a tracking device on the Millennium Falcon. The Death Star is now approaching the rebel planet, and Darth Vader means to destroy the planet and end the Rebellion. This is terrible! The rebels can all run and hide, fragmenting the Rebellion, or they can fight to the death. They choose to make a last stand. The rest of the story is the final showdown, in which the rebels attack the Death Star while it moves into position to destroy the rebel planet. One side will win, and one will lose, and the clock is ticking!
Breakdown:
Act 3 makes up the final 25% of the story.
Third Disaster occurs around the 75% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 2:

The Second Disaster comes approximately at the middle of Act 2, roughly 50% of the way into your story. Your lead Character has spent the first half of Act 2 trying to achieve their story goal, but they've been pursuing a path that won't work. The Second Disaster is a bad thing that happens at the midpoint of the story that forces your Protagonist to try a new approach. This new approach will actually work.
Example – Star Wars:

In the original Star Wars movie (Episode 4), Obi-Wan Kenobi is killed by Darth Vader at the midpoint of the story. Up till now, Luke has been following Obi-Wan and just doing what he says. Now he has to step up and start making his own decisions--and he needs to actually start using the Force. He will never win unless he becomes strong in the Force, and he has the second half of Act 2 to get strong.
Breakdown:
Act 2 makes up 50% of the story from 25% to 75%.
Second Disaster occurs around the 50% mark of the story.
--- Add Your Details Above this Line ---
Act 1:
The First Disaster comes at the end of Act 1, roughly 25% of the way into the story. The First Disaster is something bad that forces the Protagonist to commit to the story.
Example – Star Wars:

In the original Stars Wars Movie (Episode 4), Luke's aunt and uncle are murdered by stormtroopers. This drives Luke to agree to leave the planet with Obi-Wan Kenobi. He's now committed to the Rebellion, and he can't turn back.
Breakdown:
Act 1 makes up the first 25% of the story.
First Disaster occurs around the 25% mark of the story.

notes.title: Introduction to the Snowflake Method, by Randy Ingermanson

children.text: I invented
the Snowflake Method in the summer of 2002.
The problem
the Snowflake Method solves is "How do you get the first draft of your novel written?"
Note that there are many possible answers
to that problem. The Snowflake Method is my answer, and it's been immensely popular.
My  "Snowflake Method" page
on my website has been viewed more than 6.5 million times over the years, and it's made me famous around the world as a teacher of "how to write fiction."
I've also written
a best-selling book,
How to Write a Novel Using the Snowflake Method,

which you can buy at any of the usual online retailers. The book is written as a story. It's the story of a young woman who always wanted to write a novel, but didn't know how. The story is written in fairy tale format, and it's pretty crazy and very silly. That's for a reason.
The crazy, silly story makes it easy to remember.
Let's remember

that there are other ways to write your first draft. If the Snowflake Method works for you, then that's a win. If some other method works for you, that's also a win. In the end, your reader won't care how you wrote your first draft. Your reader only cares if your novel gives them a powerful emotional experience.
You might be wondering
why it's called the Snowflake Method. I'm glad you asked...
The answer
is in the next note.

notes.title: Why It's Called the "Snowflake Method"

children.text: I have a PhD
in theoretical physics and have worked as a software developer to write many complex scientific software projects over the years.
When faced
with a new challenge, a software developer starts with something small and builds out.
Here's a metaphor
for how to do that.
Imagine you're asked
to draw the following complicated "Snowflake fractal":
How could you
possibly draw that?
You could just put
your pencil down on the paper and start drawing, but ... it's complicated! There must be an easier way.
There is an easier way
. Instead of trying to draw the whole complicated image in one shot, you can start with a simple triangle:
That's not much
, but it's a start. You can build from that. All you have to do is erase the middle part of each side and then add a triangle projecting out. Like this:
That's still not much
, but it's more than what you started with. Now you can again erase the middle of each edge and replace it with a triangle again. Like this:
That's starting to look
like something! Now you just keep repeating the process, erasing the middle of each edge and adding more tiny triangles. Like this:
You can see that

in just a few steps, you've made enormous progress. At each step, all you did was either erase a bit of a line segment or draw a triangle. Each step was easy, but the whole is so much more than the sum of the parts.
You can take as many steps
as you like, but very soon, you'll be adding triangles smaller than the thickness of your pencil. That's when it's time to stop. And you'll have this:
All of this
is a deep metaphor for how you design a novel
before you begin writing it.
You start

with the basic idea of the novel. Then you make it a bit more complex. Then a bit more complex. Then a bit more. After doing that just a few times, you have the skeleton of a beautiful, perfectly-designed novel.
Once you have that
, you can sit down and start writing.
The Snowflake Method
has 10 steps. Step #10 is to write your novel.
Here in this template
, we'll work through the other 9 steps. You can do each of these nine steps right here in Plottr.
Just follow

the guidelines in the notes below. Each step will tell you to do one task, and it will tell you which part of Plottr to use to complete that task. Just follow your nose, and in a few hours of intense, creative work, you'll have a beautiful and elegant design for your novel.

notes.title: Step 1: Explanation of the One-Sentence Summary

children.text: Take an hour
and write a “Storyline” — a one-sentence summary of your novel. Something like this: “A rogue physicist travels back in time to kill the apostle Paul.” (This is the summary for my first novel,
Transgression
.) Your Storyline will serve you forever as a ten-second selling tool. This is the big picture, the analog of that big starting triangle in the snowflake picture.
When you write your book proposal

, this Storyline should appear very early in the proposal. It’s the hook that will sell your book to your editor, to your publishing committee, to the sales force, to bookstore owners, and ultimately to readers. So make it the best one you can!
Some hints
on what makes a good Storyline:
Shorter is better. Try for fewer than 15 words.
No character names, please! Better to say “a handicapped trapeze artist” than “Jane Doe”.
Tie together the big picture and the personal picture. Which character has the most to lose in this story? Now tell me what he or she wants to win.
Read the one-line blurbs on the New York Times Bestseller list to learn how to do this. Writing a one-sentence description is an art form.
If you want more details
on the one-sentence summary, see Chapter 3, "Your Story in One Sentence," in my book
How to Write a Novel Using the Snowflake Method

notes.title: Step 2: Explanation of the One-Paragraph Summary

children.text: Take another hour

and expand your one-sentence summary to a full paragraph describing the story setup, major disasters, and ending of the novel. This is the analog of the second stage of the snowflake. I like to structure a story as “three disasters plus an ending.” Each of the disasters takes a quarter of the book to develop, and the ending takes the final quarter. I don’t know if this is the ideal structure, it’s just my personal taste.
If you believe in the Three-Act Structure,

then the first disaster corresponds to the end of Act 1. The second disaster is the mid-point of Act 2. The third disaster is the end of Act 2 and forces Act 3, which wraps things up. It is OK to have the first disaster be caused by external circumstances, but I think that the second and third disasters should be caused by the protagonist’s attempts to “fix things”. Things just get worse and worse.
You can ultimately use this paragraph
in your proposal. I recommend that you write a paragraph with five sentences:
The first sentence tells the backdrop and story setup.
The second sentence explains the beginning up to the first disaster.
The third sentence describes the first half of the middle, up to the second disaster.
The fourth sentence describes the second half of the middle, up to the third disaster.
The fifth sentence explains the ending.
If you want more details
on the one-paragraph summary, see Chapter 5, "The Importance of Being Disastrous," in my book
How to Write a Novel Using the Snowflake Method

notes.title: Step 3: Explanation of Your Character Definitions

children.text: In the first two steps

of the Snowflake Method, you’ve worked out a high-level view of your novel. Now you need something similar for the storylines of each of your characters. Characters are the most important part of any novel, and the time you invest in designing them up front will pay off ten-fold when you start writing. For each of your major characters, take an hour and fill out the beginnings of a character sheet. You don't need to define everything about these characters. Just the really important stuff, such as:
The character’s Name
The character's Role in the story (Hero, Villain, Love Interest, Sidekick, or whatever role you want to assign. Or none at all.)
The character’s Storygoal (what does the character want concretely?)
The character’s Ambition (what does the character want abstractly?)
The character's Values (each Value can be summarized in a single sentence of this form: "Nothing is more important than _________.")

A one-sentence summary of the character’s Storyline (write this as if this character is the Hero of the story. Remember that every character thinks they are the Hero of their own story. Even the Villain thinks so.)
A one-paragraph summary of the character’s storyline (again, write this as if this character is the Hero of the story.)
An important point:

You may find that you need to go back and revise your one-sentence summary and/or your one-paragraph summary that you did in Steps 1 and 2. Go ahead! This is good — it means your characters are teaching you things about your story. It’s always okay at any stage of the design process to go back and revise earlier stages. In fact, it’s not just okay — it’s inevitable. And it’s good. Any revisions you make now are revisions you won’t need to make later on a clunky 400-page manuscript.
Another important point:

It doesn’t have to be perfect. The purpose of each step in the design process is to advance you to the next step. Keep your forward momentum! You can always come back later and fix it when you understand the story better. You will do this too, unless you’re a lot smarter than I am.
If you want more details
on the character definitions, see Chapter 6, "Nothing is More Important Than Characters" in my book
How to Write a Novel Using the Snowflake Method

notes.title: Step 4: Explanation of your One-Page Synopsis

children.text: If you’ve done
the first three steps of the Snowflake Method, you should have a good idea of the large-scale structure of your novel. So now just keep growing the story.
Take several hours
and expand each sentence of your one-paragraph summary (from Step 2) into a full paragraph. All but the last paragraph should end in a disaster. The final paragraph should tell how the book ends.
Write your one-page synopsis
in the present tense, like this: “Jack sells his cow in town for some magic beans. When he comes home, his mother throws the beans out the window . . .”
This is a lot of fun,

and at the end of the exercise, you have a pretty decent one-page skeleton of your novel, which we’ll call a short synopsis or a one-page synopsis. notes.title: Step 5: Explanation of Your Character Synopses

children.text: Take a day or two

and write up a one-page description of each major character and a half-page description of the other important characters. These “character synopses” should tell the story from the point of view of each character.
As always

, feel free to cycle back to the earlier steps and make revisions as you learn cool stuff about your characters. I usually enjoy this step the most. I find it effective to put the resulting “character synopses” into my proposals in addition to a plot-based synopsis.
Editors love
character synopses, because editors love character-based fiction.
If you want more details
on the character synopses, see Chapter 8, "Your People's Secret Stories," in my book

notes.title: Step 7: Explanation of Your Character Charts

children.text: Take another week

and expand your Character definitions into full-fledged Character charts detailing everything there is to know about each character. Some writers call this the Character “bible.” You’ll want to include the standard stuff such as birthdate, description, history, motivation, goal, etc. Most importantly, how will this character change by the end of the novel?
This step

is an expansion of your work in Steps 3 and 5, and it will teach you a lot about your Characters. You will probably go back and revise Steps 1 through 6 as your Characters become “real” to you and begin making petulant demands on the story. This is good — great fiction is Character-driven.
Take as much time

as you need to do this because you’re just saving time downstream. When you have finished this process, (and it may take a full month of solid effort to get here), you should know your characters inside out.
If you want more details
on Character charts, see Chapter 12, "Your Character Bible," in my book
How to Write a Novel Using the Snowflake Method

notes.title: Step 7: Where to Write Your Character Charts

children.text: In Steps 3 and 5

Snowflake Method Character Template
for each of your Main Characters.
However
, you didn't fill in everything yet. You only filled in the Character's Name, Role, Storygoal, Ambition, Values, One-Sentence Summary, One-Paragraph Summary, and the Character Synopsis.
There's much more
to your Characters than that!
The Snowflake Method Character Template

has some basic attributes defined for things like Date of Birth, Age, Height, Weight, and a number of other obvious ones. If you don't care about these, you can actually delete them from the template.
More importantly
, you can add custom attributes. You can make your own Character template that has exactly the things you care about. Go ahead and do that first, and then fill in the charts for each Character.
Always remember

that these charts are for your benefit, to help you think deeply about your Characters. Don't fill them in just because they're there. Fill them in only if they help you get a clear understanding of your Characters.
And have fun
, always!

notes.title: Step 8: Explanation of Your Scene List

children.text: Your next step

is to take either your long synopsis or your short synopsis (or any other synopsis you may have made) and make a list of all the scenes that you’ll need to turn the story into a novel. All you need is one sentence that tells what happens in each scene.
Every scene
should have a "Point of View" Character. You can set up a Timeline for each of your POV Characters.
For our purposes,

every Chapter in the Timeline should be a single scene in your story. (Ultimately, when you write your novel, you'll cluster your scenes into chapters, but you can make that decision very late in your story development. For right now, just consider each Chapter as a single scene.)
It can take a week
to make a good scene list. In Step 8, you only need to write up a single sentence for each scene, telling what happens. (Later in Step 9, you can flesh this out with more details.)
If you want more details
on scene lists, see Chapter 14, "Your List of Scenes," in my book
How to Write a Novel Using the Snowflake Method

notes.title: Step 8: Where to Create Your Scene List

children.text: Click on the Timeline menu entry
in the menubar at the top of this window.
That will show
you your Timeline, where you can fill in scenes and move them around.
This template
contains one pre-made Timeline named "Three Disaster Structure."
That just provides
you with the boundary points that mark off the three main disasters in the story. These happen approximately at the 25%, 50%, and 75% marks in your story.
If you know
the Three-Act Structure, then the first Disaster comes at the end of Act 1. The second Disaster comes in the middle of Act 2. The third Disaster comes at the end of Act 2.
These three Disasters

mark major turning points in your story. The first Disaster commits your lead Character irrevocably to the story. The second Disaster causes your lead Character to rethink what isn't working and to choose a new approach that will actually work. The third Disaster causes your lead Character (and the villain, if you have one) to BOTH commit to end the story in some sort of final showdown.
If you want to know more
about the Three-Disaster Structure, see chapters 5, 9, and 13 in my book
How to Write a Novel Using the Snowflake Method

notes.title: Step 9: Explanation of Your Scene Details

children.text: You may want to make

some extra notes about each of the scenes in the scene list that you created in Step 8. You can select any scene from the list here. If necessary, you can change the Point-of-View character and edit the summary of the scene. Then you can add any extra notes that you want to remember for the scene. You might want to write notes on the setting, characters, cool dialogue, or anything else related to your scene. Write as many notes as you need to.
Scenes generally
fall into two types, and you may want to classify each scene as one of these types and make notes on the various parts:
A Proactive Scene
has the following pattern:
Goal
Conflict
Setback
A Reactive Scene
has the following pattern:
Reaction
Dilemma
Decision
The structure of scenes
is very important, because the scene is the fundamental unit of fiction. If you’d like a quick survey on scene structure, see chapter 17 of my book in my book
How to Write a Novel Using the Snowflake Method
If you want to become an expert
in scene structure, I've written a whole book that goes into great detail on exactly how scenes work, with lots of examples. So check out my best-selling book
How to Write a Dynamite Scene Using the Snowflake Method

notes.title: Step 9: Where to Write Your Scene Details

children.text: In step 8,
you already made your scene list using the Timeline tool.
Now you can return

to your Timeline and edit each scene card with all the details you need. I personally like to put in info on whether the scene is Proactive or Reactive, and then write a short sentence describing the Goal, the Conflict, and the Setback (if it's a Proactive Scene) or the Reaction, the Dilemma, and the Decision (if it's a Reactive Scene).
If the scene

is neither a Proactive Scene nor a Reactive Scene, then you should think very hard about whether this scene is pulling its own weight. Why is this scene in your story? What does it do for your story? Is it advancing the conflict? If not, maybe you don't need the scene, or you can revise it to be either Proactive or Reactive, or you can combine it with some other scene that contributes to the conflict.
Of course
, you can do whatever you want, but when a scene is neither Proactive nor Reactive, that's a big red flag. Proceed with caution.
Have fun!
Always have fun. Writing should be fun.

notes.title: Step 10: Write Your Novel

children.text: If you've completed
all the first 9 steps of the Snowflake Method, you now have a well-balanced strategic plan to write your novel.
You can now export
this Plottr project to a Microsoft Word document or a Scrivener document, and that'll give you a place to start writing.
Now that
you have a plan for your novel, you can write each scene with confidence. You know it's in the right place. You know it serves the story.
Write fast
and write well.
And
have fun!
